7.s: The Early Vedic family is best described as:
7.x: The family was patriarchal, patrilineal and joint; sons were preferred.

7.s: The transition from a cattle-based tribal economy to a settled agrarian economy is significant because it helps explain the later rise of:
7.x: The shift from a cattle-based tribal economy to an agrarian territorial society contributed to the emergence of territorial kingship and a more established varna hierarchy.
7.tq: Apply the cause-and-effect relationship between economic change and political-social formation.
xs: The shift to a settled agrarian economy explains the later rise of **territorial kingship and varna hierarchy** — option **(2)**.
It was a move from a **cattle-based tribal economy** to a **settled agrarian territorial** society.
xa: Later Vedic = **birth-based varna**, **iron**, rice/wheat.
Early Vedic: the cow was the **standard unit of value**.

7.s: The Vaishya group is described as having developed from which group?
7.x: Vaishyas were described as emerging from vis, meaning the mass of the people or tribespeople.
7.tq: Match the social category with its stated origin term.
xs: The **Vaishya** grew out of the **Vis** — option **(3)**.
**Vis** = the mass of the people / tribespeople.
xa: Purusha Sukta: Vaishya came from the **thighs**.
**Rajanya** = Kshatriya, from the **arms**.
**Dasa/Dasyu** captives were slaves.

7.s: The Purusha Sukta occurs in which Mandala of the Rigveda?
7.x: The Purusha Sukta (Rigveda 10.90), a late addition, is in Mandala X and is the first statement of the four-fold varna.
xa: Gotra in the lineage sense first appears in the **Atharvaveda**.
Body parts: Brahmana = **mouth**, Kshatriya = **arms**, Vaishya = **thighs**, Shudra = **feet**.

7.s: The distinction between Arya varna and Dasa varna in the early Vedic period primarily reflected a:
o: Cultural and linguistic distinction between groups
Religious division between two priestly orders
7.x: Arya and Dasa varna reflected a cultural, linguistic and partly colour-based distinction between Vedic groups and conquered local groups; it was not yet a rigid caste system.
7.tq: Distinguish an early cultural distinction from the later birth-based caste structure.
xs: **Arya varna vs Dasa varna** was a **cultural and linguistic** (and colour-based) distinction — option **(1)**.
It separated Vedic groups (conquerors) from conquered local groups — **not rigid caste**.
xa: Early society was tribal and largely **egalitarian**.
Broad groups: **priests, warriors, common people**.
Occupations were **not birth-based**.

7.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched with the body part mentioned in the Purusha Sukta?
7.x: The Purusha Sukta describes Brahmana as originating from the mouth, Kshatriya from the arms, Vaishya from the thighs and Shudra from the feet.
7.tq: Start with the sure body-part association and eliminate the reversed pairs.
xs: **Brahmana — mouth** is correctly matched — option **(1)**.
Kshatriya/Rajanya = **arms**; Vaishya = **thighs**; Shudra = **feet** — so options 2, 3 and 4 are wrong.
xa: The **Purusha Sukta** is in **Mandala X** (hymn **10.90**), a late addition.
The **Vaishya** grew out of the **vis** (the mass of the people).
The word **Shudra** first appears in the **10th Mandala**.

7.s:
Consider the following statements about gotra:
1. Gotra exogamy was fully established in the Rigvedic period.
2. In the Rigveda, the word gotra means cow-pen.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
7.x: In the Rigveda gotra means cow-pen; it appears in the lineage sense in the Atharvaveda, and gotra exogamy is a Later Vedic development.
xa: The word **varna** first appears in the **Rigveda**.
**Shudra** first appears in the **10th Mandala**.
**Untouchability** was also absent.

7.s: The word 'Shudra' first appears in which Mandala of the Rigveda?
7.x: The word Shudra first occurs in the 10th Mandala, which also has the Purusha Sukta.

7.s: The term 'gotra' in the sense of lineage first appears in the:
7.x: Gotra as lineage first appears in the Atharvaveda; in the Rigveda the word means cow-pen.

7.s: In the Purusha Sukta, the Kshatriya is said to have emerged from the Purusha's:
7.x: Brahmana from the mouth, Kshatriya from the arms, Vaishya from the thighs and Shudra from the feet.

7.s: Who among the following was a Brahmavadini who composed some hymns of the Vedas?
7.x: The term Brahmavadini referred to women scholars in the Vedic period who possessed and expounded Vedic knowledge. Such women, also known as rishikas, composed hymns addressed to deities. Among the notable Brahmavadinis was Lopamudra, the wife of sage Agastya, to whom several hymns of the Rigveda are attributed, indicating her role as a composer of Vedic hymns.

7.s: Which one of the following is not related to the Rigvedic period?
7.x: Ghosha, Apala, and Vishvavara are female seers credited with hymns in the Rigveda; therefore, they are considered related to the Rigvedic age. In contrast, Gargi is a philosopher of the Later Vedic/Upanishadic period, not the Rigvedic period.

7.s: Compared with the Early Vedic period, the position of women in the Later Vedic period:
o: Improved in assemblies but declined in rituals
7.x: Women's position declined in the Later Vedic period: they were excluded from Upanayana, rituals and assemblies.
xa: The **Aitareya Brahmana** calls daughters a source of **misery**.
Early Vedic women attended the **Sabha** and **Vidatha**.

7.s: Which one of the following does NOT belong to the group of Rigvedic women seers?
7.x: Gargi was a later Vedic scholar associated with Upanishadic dialogue, whereas Apala, Ghosha and Vishvavara were Rigvedic women seers.
7.tq: Use period discrimination to separate a later scholar from Rigvedic seers.
xs: **Gargi** is **not** a Rigvedic woman seer — option **(3)** (**BPSC 2025** odd-one-out).
**Apala, Ghosha, Lopamudra, Vishvavara** composed Rig Vedic hymns.
xa: Gargi held a **dialogue with Yajnavalkya** in the **Brihadaranyaka Upanishad**.
**Maitreyi** was also a later (not Rigvedic) scholar.
Women attended the **Sabha** and **Vidatha**.

7.s: Marriage in Early Vedic society was largely:
7.x: Early Vedic marriage was largely monogamous; adult marriage and choice in marriage were recognised and child marriage was absent.
xa: **Swayamvara** was practised.
**Niyoga** = union of a childless widow with her husband's brother.
Later, the **Aitareya Brahmana** called daughters a source of misery.

7.s: The practice of niyoga in the Vedic context referred to:
o: The selection of a king by the Sabha
The exchange of cattle during marriage
The union of a childless widow with her husband’s brother
The marriage of a girl before puberty
7.x: Niyoga was a levirate practice in which a childless widow could unite with her deceased husband’s brother.
7.tq: Test the exact meaning of a specialised marriage custom against nearby social practices.
xs: **Niyoga** = **union of a childless widow with her husband's brother** (levirate) — option **(3)**.
Child marriage was **absent**; the king's selection involved the **Samiti**, not niyoga.
xa: **Widow remarriage** was allowed.
**Swayamvara** was practised.
Marriage was largely **monogamous**.

7.s: Early Vedic society preferred sons, yet women could:
o: Take no part in household religious rites
Receive education and take part in sacrifices and assemblies
7.x: Early Vedic women received education, took part in sacrifices and assemblies and could own cattle; there is no evidence of land ownership.
xa: Women seers: **Apala, Ghosha, Lopamudra, Vishvavara**.
Women attended the **Sabha** and **Vidatha**.
Debate: texts praise women seers, but society stayed **patriarchal** with son-preference.

7.s: Which Rigvedic woman seer was the wife of sage Agastya?
7.x: Lopamudra, a Brahmavadini, was the wife of sage Agastya.

7.s: Gargi's famous dialogue with Yajnavalkya occurs in the:
7.x: Gargi was a Later Vedic / Upanishadic scholar; her dialogue with Yajnavalkya is in the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad.

7.s:
Consider the following statements about women in the Rig Vedic period:
1. Women could own cattle.
2. Child marriage was common.
3. Widow remarriage was possible.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
7.x: Women could own cattle and widow remarriage was possible; there was no child marriage, as adult marriage was the norm.

7.s: Which Mandala of the Rigveda is wholly devoted to Soma?
7.x: The whole of Mandala IX is devoted to Soma, the sacred drink.

7.s: The gambler's hymn of the Rigveda is:
7.x: The gambler's hymn on dicing is Rigveda X.34; X.90 is the Purusha Sukta.

7.s: In the Rig Vedic age, 'sura' was a:
7.x: Sura was a fermented drink with few Rigvedic references; soma was the sacred drink.

7.s: Who among the following was the most popular God of the early Vedic Aryans ?
The religion of early Vedic Aryans was primarily of
7.x: The religion of early Vedic Aryans was mainly related to worship of the nature and performing of Yajnas. The Aryans in the early Vedic period described life as a manifestation of nature. Worship of different forces of nature formed a part of their religious belief. They believed that some divine power works behind the objects of nature such as fire, water, wind etc.

7.s: In context on Indian culture 'Rita' means
7.x: The concept of 'Rita' i.e., the universal principle of natural order, is of Vedic origin. The 'Rita' has been the basis of Indian culture, legal theory, politics and philosophy. God Varuna was supposed to uphold 'Rita' or the natural order which is why he was also called as 'Ritasyagopa'.

7.s: Rig-vedic religion was–
7.x: The most interesting aspect of Rig Vedic religion was its polytheistic character in which a number of Gods were worshipped. The Rigvedic Aryans worshipped nature with intense feelings and endowed it with an animated soul. Vedic Gods were mainly classified into three groups- (1) God of sky-Varuna, Mitra, Surya, Vishnu, etc. (2) God of space- Indra, Rudra, etc. (3) God of the earth- Agni, Brihaspati, Soma, etc. Whenever these Vedic saints worship any God, they consider him to be the Supreme God, this is known as Ekeshwarvaad. Other than this in Rigveda Ekeshwarvaad is supported by saying Ekam Satt Vipra bahudha badanti". Ekeshwarvaad of Rigveda included vision of Advaityavaad, Sarvadevtavaad and Bahudevatavaad. But the concept of one supreme God of Vedas is different from the modern Ishwarvaad.

7.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Agni – Ninth Mandala of the Rigveda
Boghaz-Koi inscription – Indra, Varuna, Mitra and Nasatya
7.x: The Boghaz-Koi inscription names Indra, Varuna, Mitra and Nasatya. Agni has about 200 hymns, Soma has the ninth Mandala, and Aghanya means a cow not to be killed.
n: Agni was a Rigvedic deity. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 121-126]
Around 200 hymns were dedicated to Agni. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 121-126]
Soma was a Rigvedic deity. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 121-126]
Soma is associated with the ninth Mandala of the Rigveda. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 121-126]
Aghanya refers to a cow. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 121-126]
An Aghanya cow was not worthy of being killed. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 121-126]
The Boghaz-Koi inscription mentioned Indra. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 121-126]
The Boghaz-Koi inscription mentioned Varuna. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 121-126]
The Boghaz-Koi inscription mentioned Mitra. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 121-126]
The Boghaz-Koi inscription mentioned Nasatya. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 121-126]
xa: ⚠ **250 – 200 – 3** hymns = **Indra – Agni – Vishnu**.
**Agni** was the **intermediary between gods and men**.
**Aditi** was the **mother of the gods**; **Dyaus** = Greek **Zeus**.

7.s: The religious outlook of the Rig Vedic people is best described as:
o: Monotheism with exclusive worship of one god
Ancestor worship centred on royal tombs
Naturalistic polytheism with each god praised as supreme in turn
7.x: Rig Vedic religion was naturalistic polytheism. Its tendency to regard each god as supreme in turn is called Henotheism or Kathenotheism.
7.tq: Use the exact conceptual distinction between polytheism and Henotheism.
xs: Rig Vedic religion was **naturalistic polytheism**, with **each god praised as supreme in turn** — option **(4)**.
Gods personified **forces of nature**; praising each as supreme is **Henotheism / Kathenotheism**.
Many gods were worshipped, so it was not monotheism, and there were **no temples, no idols**.
xa: Worship: hymns and **yajnas in the open air**.
**Male gods dominate**; cult of the **domestic hearth**.
**Rita** = cosmic and moral order upheld by **Varuna**.

7.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Rig Vedic worship?
o: Temples and idols formed the normal basis of worship
Worship was conducted through hymns and yajnas in the open air
Its principal aims included cattle, sons and victory
The cult of the domestic hearth was significant
7.x: Temples and idols were absent in Rig Vedic worship, which used hymns and open-air yajnas for material ends such as cattle, sons and victory.
xa: Each god praised as supreme in turn = **Henotheism / Kathenotheism**.
**Male gods** dominate.

7.s: Which Rig Vedic god was called Purandara, 'destroyer of forts'?
7.x: Indra, called Purandara, is the most mentioned Rig Vedic god with about 250 hymns.
xa: Varuna is the **ethically highest** god.
**Vishnu** was minor — only **3 hymns**.

7.s: Which Vedic god was called Ritasyagopa, the guardian of Rita (cosmic order)?
7.x: Varuna guards Rita, the cosmic and natural order, and is therefore called Ritasyagopa.
n: Varuna was a Rigvedic deity. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 121-126]
Varuna upheld Rita. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 121-126]
Rita was a Vedic concept. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 121-126]
Rita means cosmic order. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 121-126]
Rita means natural order. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 121-126]
Varuna was called Ritasyagopa. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 121-126]
xa: Varuna held **third place** and was the **ethically highest** god.
**Indra** (**250 hymns**) was the most important god; **Agni** (around **200 hymns**) second.
**Mitra**, a solar god, was Varuna's ally.

7.s: Which one of the following pairs is incorrectly matched?
7.x: Vishnu was a minor deity in the Rig Vedic period and is associated with three hymns, not about 250. About 250 hymns are associated with Indra.
7.tq: Use the numerical contrast between a major god and a minor deity.
xs: **Vishnu — about 250 hymns** is wrongly matched — option **(4)**.
**Vishnu** was minor with only **3 hymns**; **250 hymns** belong to **Indra**.
The others are right: **Maruts** = storms, **Rudra** = destruction and healing, **Parjanya** = rain.
xa: ⚠ **250 – 200 – 3** = **Indra – Agni – Vishnu**.
**Aranyani** = forest; **Pushan** = cattle, roads.

7.s: Dyaus, the celestial father, was regarded as the counterpart of:
7.x: Dyaus was the sky or celestial father and corresponded to Greek Zeus and Roman Jupiter.
7.tq: Test the cross-cultural equivalence rather than the deity’s Vedic function alone.
xs: **Dyaus**, the sky/celestial father, is the counterpart of **Greek Zeus and Roman Jupiter** — option **(4)**.
Exam angle: "**Dyaus = Zeus/Jupiter**" is a correct statement.
xa: ⚠ "**Prithvi** was mother of all gods" is wrong — that is **Aditi**.
**Prithvi** = earth, fertility.
Gods personified **forces of nature**.

7.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Rig Vedic gods?
o: Agni ranked second among the Rig Vedic gods
Agni acted as intermediary between humans and gods
Agni was the deity who upheld Rita
7.x: Agni was second in rank and the intermediary between humans and gods; it was Varuna, not Agni, who upheld Rita.

7.s: In the Rigveda, which deity was regarded as the mother of the gods?
7.x: Aditi was the mother of the gods; calling Prithvi the mother of all gods is a common error.

7.s: How many hymns of the Rigveda are addressed to Vishnu?
7.x: Vishnu was a minor god with 3 hymns, against about 250 for Indra and 200 for Agni.

7.s: Which Rig Vedic deity is associated with forests?
7.x: Aranyani was the forest deity; Pushan was of cattle and roads, Prithvi the earth and Parjanya rain.

7.s: The largest number of Rigvedic hymns are devoted to:
7.x: ‘Indra’ has been described as the most powerful deity in the Rigveda. ‘Indra’ is the most important divinity in the Rig- Veda. A very large number of Rigveda hymns (as many as 250 hymns) are devoted to him followed by ‘Agni’ (200 hymns).

7.s: The largest hymn of Rigveda is dedicated to which Vedic god?

8.s: The name of scripture in which ‘’Purusha Medha’ was mentioned is:
8.x: It is believed that Saraswati was the scene of the activities of the famous Vedic tribes - the Bharatas, the Purus, and the Kurus. The Shatpatha Brahmana narrates the story of King Videgha Madhava (a king of Videha) accompanied by his priest Rishi Gautama Rahugana, carrying the sacred fire to the east preserving thereby the tradition that the Kosalas and the Videhas received from their culture.

8.s: In the post-Vedic period which was considered as the axis of Aryan Culture
8.x: In the post-Vedic period, this region of Kuru, Panchala was considered as the axis of Aryan culture because here great achievements happened in science, mathematics, astronomy, religion and philosophy.

8.s: King Asvapati of the Upanishadic period was the ruler of:
8.x: The Upanishads state that some Kshatriya kings who were great scholars and philosophers also imparted knowledge to Brahmins. Some of them were- King Janak of Videha, King Pravahanjabali of Panchal, King Asvapati of Kekaya and King Ajatshatru of Kashi. Asvapati was a Kshatriya king. He was well known as a learned teacher of the age. The Kekaya kingdom was situated on the bank of river Beas, east of Gandhara kingdom. King Asvapati ruled Kekaya when Janak was the king of Videha.

8.s: Which one of the following represents the broad sequence of the Later Vedic eastward expansion?
o: Punjab → Ganga-Yamuna Doab → Kosala, Kashi and Videha
8.x: The movement proceeded from Punjab into the Ganga-Yamuna Doab, including Kurukshetra and the Delhi-upper Doab, and then towards Kosala, Kashi and Videha by about 600 BCE.
8.tq: Solve the sequence by identifying the western starting point and the eastern endpoint.
xs: The expansion ran **Punjab → Ganga-Yamuna Doab → Kosala, Kashi and Videha** — option **(1)**.
In the Doab: **Kurukshetra**, then the **Delhi-upper Doab**; the east was reached by **c. 600 BCE**.
xa: **Kosala** = eastern UP; **Videha** = north Bihar.
**Kosala, Kashi, Videha** were the **new kingdoms** of the east.
**Iron weapons and horse-drawn chariots** helped the eastward push.

8.s: The legend of Videgha Madhava is narrated in the:
8.x: The Shatapatha Brahmana narrates how Videgha Madhava and Gautama Rahugana followed Agni Vaishvanara eastward from the Sarasvati.
xa: The land beyond the Sadanira was settled as **Videha**.
The legend reflects **iron axes and fire** clearing the Ganga forests.

8.s: The Kurus were formed by the union of which two groups?
8.x: The Kurus resulted from the union of the Bharatas and Purus; Kuru-Panchala, with its capital at Hastinapur, became the centre of Aryan culture.
xa: **Hastinapur** is also a PGW and iron site.
Upanishadic king **Pravahana Jaivali** ruled **Panchala**.

8.s: Which of the following pairs of Upanishadic king and kingdom is correctly matched?
8.x: Ashvapati ruled Kekaya. Janaka ruled Videha, Ajatashatru was associated with Kashi and Pravahana Jaivali with Panchala.
xa: **Videha** was settled beyond the **Sadanira** in the Videgha Madhava legend.
**Kuru-Panchala** (capital **Hastinapur**) was the centre of Aryan culture.
Upanishads date to **c. 800-600 BCE**.

8.s: The legend of Videgha Madhava is associated with which use of iron technology?
o: Clearing the forests of the Ganga region with iron axes and fire
Introducing bronze metallurgy into the Indus cities
Constructing stone megaliths in the far south
8.x: The Videgha Madhava legend is connected with the clearing of Ganga-region forests through the use of iron axes and fire. It illustrates the role of iron in eastward expansion.
8.tq: Link the named legend with the specific technological process it illustrates.
xs: The legend reflects **clearing the forests of the Ganga region with iron axes and fire** — option **(2)**.
**Agni Vaishvanara** "burnt the forests" eastward from the **Sarasvati** to the **Sadanira (Gandak)**.
**NBPW** is post-Vedic (from **c. 600 BCE**), so option 1 is wrong.
xa: Source: **Shatapatha Brahmana**; priest **Gautama Rahugana**.
Land beyond the Sadanira = **Videha**.
8.fixed: stem carried a duplicated A-D list in a different order from the options

8.s: Who was the priest of Videgha Madhava in the Shatapatha Brahmana legend?
8.x: Videgha Madhava and his priest Gautama Rahugana followed Agni Vaishvanara eastward from the Sarasvati.

8.s: In the Videgha Madhava legend, which river was crossed before Videha was settled?
8.x: They crossed the Sadanira, identified with the Gandak; the land beyond it was settled as Videha.

8.s: Ajatashatru, the Upanishadic scholar-king, ruled which kingdom?
8.x: The Upanishadic Ajatashatru was king of Kashi, not the Magadha king of the same name.

8.s: Which Upanishadic king is correctly matched with his kingdom?
8.x: Pravahana Jaivali ruled Panchala; Ashvapati ruled Kekaya, Janaka Videha and Ajatashatru Kashi.

8.s: The Kuru-Panchala region of the Later Vedic period had its capital at:
8.x: Kuru-Panchala, the centre of Aryan culture, had its capital at Hastinapur in Meerut district.

8.s: The earliest evidence of the use of iron in India has been discovered from :
8.x: Atranjikhera is a prehistoric and historic excavated archaeological site on the bank of Kali river, a tributary of Ganga. This site was first identified by Sir Alexander Cunningham in his survey report in 1861-62 but excavated by R.C. Gaur. A Trial trench put in 1962, was followed in the next year by digging on a small scale. Regular excavation was started in 1964. The earliest evidence of iron used in the region dates back to around 1000 B.C.

8.s: In Later Vedic texts, iron is referred to as:
8.x: Iron is called krishna ayas or shyama ayas ('black metal') in Later Vedic texts. Lohita ayas denotes copper, plain ayas in the Rigveda meant copper or bronze, hiranya is gold and nishka was a gold ornament later used as a unit of value.
8.tq: Krishna/shyama ayas = black metal = iron; lohita ayas = copper.
xs: Iron is **krishna ayas** (also **shyama ayas**), "black metal" — option **(2)**.
**Lohita ayas** = copper; Rigvedic **ayas** = copper/bronze.
**Nishka** was a unit of value, not a metal term.
xa: Iron was introduced in the north **c. 1000-800 BCE**.
Iron was **common at most PGW sites**.

8.s: Iron technology in North India emerged approximately between:
8.x: Iron technology in North India is dated to about 1000-800 BCE and was common at most Painted Grey Ware sites.
xa: Other sites: **Atranjikhera, Hastinapur, Kaushambi**.
Iron = **krishna ayas / shyama ayas** ("black metal").
New TN dates push Indian iron far before the Gangetic **c. 1000 BCE** date.

8.s: Which archaeological site in Krishnagiri district, Tamil Nadu, has yielded iron AMS-dated to about 2172 BCE?
8.x: Mayiladumparai (Krishnagiri district, Tamil Nadu) is AMS-dated to 2172 BCE and is described as the earliest iron-use evidence in India. Sivagalai (Thoothukudi) is the site with iron dated to about 2953 BCE, Thirumalapuram (Tenkasi) has an Iron Age urn chamber, and Adichanallur is the type-site for urn burials.
8.tq: Link the exact date to the correct site before comparing the nearby South Indian sites.
xs: **Mayiladumparai** (Krishnagiri, TN) is AMS-dated to **2172 BCE** — option **(1)**.
It is noted as the **earliest iron-use evidence in India**.
**Sivagalai** (Thoothukudi) = iron about **2953 BCE**; **Thirumalapuram** (Tenkasi) = urn chamber; **Adichanallur** = urn-burial type-site.
xa: South Indian Iron Age now placed around **2100 BCE**, earlier than the Gangetic Iron Age.
BPSC **2022** asked when iron use began; the key was "**none of the above**".
8.fixed: Mayiladumparai no longer the earliest: Sivagalai iron dated c. 2953-3345 BCE (2025); also removed duplicated A-D list

8.s:
Consider the following statements about the iron dates from Tamil Nadu:
1. They establish that Painted Grey Ware originated in Tamil Nadu.
2. They suggest iron use in India began much earlier than the Gangetic date of about 1000 BCE.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
8.x: The Mayiladumparai (2172 BCE) and Sivagalai (about 2953 BCE) dates push Indian iron use far earlier than about 1000 BCE; they say nothing about the origin of Painted Grey Ware.
xa: South Indian Iron Age now placed around **2100 BCE** (reported Jun **2026**).
**Adichanallur** (Thoothukudi) = type-site for urn burials.

8.s: In Vedic texts, 'lohita ayas' refers to:
8.x: Lohita ayas was copper; krishna or shyama ayas was iron and hiranya was gold.

8.s: In the Rigveda, the term 'ayas' denoted:
8.x: Rigvedic ayas meant copper or bronze; iron was called krishna ayas in Later Vedic texts.

8.s: Which Tamil Nadu site has yielded iron dated to about 2953 BCE, now the oldest?
8.x: Sivagalai in Thoothukudi district yielded iron dated to about 2953 BCE, older than Mayiladumparai's 2172 BCE.

8.s: Which of the following is NOT an early iron site of North India?
8.x: Adichanallur is an urn-burial site in Thoothukudi, Tamil Nadu; the others are North Indian iron sites.

8.s: Besides krishna ayas, iron in Later Vedic texts was also called:
8.x: Iron was krishna or shyama ayas, the 'black metal'; lohita ayas was copper.

8.s:
Consider the following statements about iron in the Later Vedic period:
1. Iron axes and fire helped clear the Gangetic forests.
2. Taxila in Gandhara has yielded iron of about 1000 BC.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
8.x: Iron axes with fire cleared the Gangetic forests, and Taxila is listed among the early iron sites (c. 1000 BC).

8.s: The pottery from 1000 B.C. to 600 B.C. found in the Gangetic plain is called the ________pottery.
8.src: APPSC 2023 Screening test (Online Mode) to the post of Deput

8.s: The Ochre-coloured Pottery (O.C.P.) was christened at:
8.x: Discovery and Naming (Christen) of OCP was done by B.B. Lal in 1950-52 at Hastinapur. Ochre-Coloured Pottery (known to archaeologists as OCP) as the name implies, its main distinguishing feature was when rubbed it left on ochrecolour on fingers which gives it a first appearance of being badly fired. Other characteristics are its porous character and the fact that it is invariably worn out at the edges.

8.s: Ochre Coloured Pottery is generally placed in which period?
8.x: Ochre Coloured Pottery is post-Harappan and belongs to the second millennium BCE; the hallmark Later Vedic pottery is Painted Grey Ware.
xa: PGW = **c. 1000-600 BCE**, Gangetic plain.
OCP comes **first** in the protohistoric pottery sequence.

8.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the pottery sequence of Indian protohistory?
o: Ochre Coloured Pottery comes before Black and Red Ware
Black and Red Ware comes before Painted Grey Ware
Painted Grey Ware comes after Northern Black Polished Ware
Northern Black Polished Ware begins around 600 BCE
8.x: The sequence runs OCP, Black and Red Ware, Black Slipped Ware, Painted Grey Ware, Red Ware and then NBPW, so PGW comes before NBPW, not after it.
8.fixed: stem carried a duplicated A-D list in a different order from the options

8.s:
Consider the following statements about the Iron Age in Andhra Pradesh:
1. It is associated with the Megalithic culture and Black and Red Ware pottery.
2. It is unrelated to megalithic burial traditions.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
8.x: The Iron Age in Andhra Pradesh is associated with the Megalithic culture and Black and Red Ware, with sites such as Nagarjunakonda cited in this context.
xa: **Sankalia**: rice was first harvested in AP in this era.
BRW also marks the Megalithic/Iron Age south generally.
TN iron dates: **Mayiladumparai** **2172 BCE**; **Sivagalai** about **2953 BCE**.
8.fixed: stem carried a duplicated A-D list in a different order from the options

8.s: Which of the following groups contains the four wares known in the Later Vedic phase?
o: Ochre Coloured Pottery, Black and Red Ware, Northern Black Polished Ware and Red Ware
Black Slipped Ware, Painted Grey Ware, Northern Black Polished Ware and Ochre Coloured Pottery
Black and Red Ware, Black Slipped Ware, Painted Grey Ware and Red Ware
Painted Grey Ware, Northern Black Polished Ware, Red Ware and Amphora Ware
8.x: The four Later Vedic wares are Black and Red Ware, Black Slipped Ware, Painted Grey Ware and Red Ware. Northern Black Polished Ware is associated with the later Mahajanapada and second-urbanisation phase, not the Later Vedic group.
8.tq: Use the exclusion clue: identify the ware that belongs to the later urbanisation phase.
xs: The four wares are **Black and Red Ware, Black Slipped Ware, Painted Grey Ware and Red Ware** — option **(3)**.
Options with **NBPW** or **OCP** are wrong: OCP is post-Harappan, NBPW post-Vedic.
xa: Later Vedic phase: **1000-600 BC**.
⚠ Trap: **not NBPW** (APPSC **2024**).
Sequence: **OCP → BRW → BSW → PGW → Red Ware → NBPW**.
8.fixed: stem's A-D list mislabelled vs options (A in stem = option 3)

8.s: Which pottery leaves an ochre colour on the fingers when rubbed?
8.x: Ochre Coloured Pottery, named at Hastinapur by B.B. Lal, leaves an ochre colour on the fingers.

8.s: Shiny black pottery associated with the Mahajanapadas and second urbanisation is:
8.x: NBPW, from about 600 BCE, is the shiny black ware of the Mahajanapada phase; PGW is grey.

8.s: Adichanallur is associated with:
8.x: Adichanallur is associated with urn burials and is not a Painted Grey Ware site, unlike Atranjikhera, Hastinapur and Bhagwanpura.
xa: Other PGW sites: **Ahichchhatra** (Bareilly), **Noh** (Bharatpur), Kurukshetra.
About **700** PGW sites, mostly in the **upper Ganga basin**.
8.fixed: stem's A-D list mislabelled vs options

8.s:
Consider the following statements about Painted Grey Ware:
1. It is grey pottery bearing linear painted designs.
2. It consists mainly of bowls and dishes.
3. It is a highly polished black pottery.
Which of the above statements are correct?
8.x: PGW is grey pottery with linear painted designs, mostly bowls and dishes (c. 1000-600 BCE). Highly polished black pottery describes NBPW.
xa: PGW = Later Vedic, **c. 1000-600 BCE**, Gangetic plain.
⚠ Some notes wrongly place PGW in the **Early Vedic** period.
Finds: **iron weapons**, earthen bowls and dishes, **copper objects**.
8.fixed: stem carried a duplicated A-D list in a different order from the options

8.s: With reference to the Painted Grey Ware culture, which one of the following statements is NOT correct?
o: The sites are concentrated mostly in the upper Ganga basin.
The culture was confined exclusively to the lower Indus basin.
The sites yielded iron weapons and copper objects.
8.x: Painted Grey Ware sites were found mainly in the upper Ganga basin, not exclusively in the lower Indus basin. They yielded iron weapons, earthen bowls and dishes, and copper objects.
8.tq: Find the geographical extreme that contradicts the known concentration of the sites.
xs: The wrong statement is that PGW was **confined exclusively to the lower Indus basin** — option **(2)**.
PGW sites lie mostly in the **upper Ganga basin**; about **700** are known.
They yielded **iron weapons**, earthen bowls and dishes, and **copper objects**.
xa: Copper possibly came from **Khetri**, Rajasthan.
PGW = **c. 1000-600 BCE**, Gangetic plain.

8.s: Painted Grey Ware was first found at which site in 1944?
8.x: PGW was first found at Ahichchhatra (1944); the Hastinapur excavation (1950-52) established it as a culture.

8.s: The PGW site Bhagwanpura, where a house plan was found, is in:
8.x: Bhagwanpura is in Haryana; Noh is in Rajasthan and Atranjikhera in western UP.

8.s: Which of the following PGW sites is correctly matched with its region?
8.x: Noh is in Rajasthan; Bhagwanpura is in Haryana, Ahichchhatra in Bareilly and Atranjikhera in western UP.

8.s: About how many Painted Grey Ware sites are known?
8.x: About 700 PGW sites are known, mainly in the upper Ganga basin.

8.s: Painted Grey Ware sites are found mainly in the:
8.x: PGW sites lie mainly in the upper Ganga basin, not the lower Indus basin.

8.s: The emergence of the ‘second urbanisation’ is associated with which pottery phase and which group of settlements?
o: Black and Red Ware; Videha and Kekaya
Northern Black Polished Ware; Shravasti, Kausambi and Hastinapur
Painted Grey Ware; Kurukshetra and Bhagwanpura
8.x: True towns emerged after the Vedic period during the Northern Black Polished Ware phase, including Shravasti, Kausambi and Hastinapur.
8.tq: Match the urbanisation phase with its characteristic pottery and town examples.
xs: Second urbanisation = **Northern Black Polished Ware**; **Shravasti, Kausambi and Hastinapur** — option **(2)**.
True towns came only **after the Vedic period**.
**PGW**, **BRW** and **Red Ware** are Later Vedic village-phase wares.
xa: NBPW runs from **c. 600 BCE** with the **Mahajanapadas**.
**Rajghat** (Varanasi) yielded **pre-NBPW** pottery about **3,000** years old.

8.s: In the Later Vedic period, rice was known as:
8.x: Rice (vrihi) became a chief crop with ritual importance, while barley continued to be grown.
xa: Chief crops: **rice (vrihi)** and **wheat**.
Other crops: pulses/lentils, millets, **sugarcane, sesame**.
AP angle: **Sankalia** says rice was first harvested in AP in this era.

8.s: The largest number of oxen mentioned for yoking a plough in the Later Vedic evidence is:
8.x: Ploughs were described as yoked with 6, 8, 12 and even 24 oxen, showing the growing scale of plough agriculture.
xa: **Buffalo** was also used for ploughing.
Iron **ploughshares** came into use.
Agriculture became the **primary** livelihood.

8.s: Which one of the following best characterises settlements during the Later Vedic period?
o: Large cities with extensive burnt-brick architecture were common.
Villages with mud and wattle houses predominated, while true towns emerged later.
All settlements were fortified imperial capitals.
Nomadic camps were the only form of settlement.
8.x: Settlements were mainly villages with mud and wattle houses. Burnt bricks were not prevalent, and true towns emerged after the Vedic period during the NBPW phase.
8.tq: Distinguish the dominant settlement pattern from the later urban phase.
xs: **Villages of mud and wattle houses** predominated; **true towns emerged later** — option **(2)**.
**Burnt bricks were not prevalent**; Hastinapur's mud structures were modest.
xa: True towns came in the **NBPW** phase — "**second urbanisation**": Shravasti, Kausambi, Hastinapur.
BHU's **Rajghat** finds date **Varanasi's urban origins to about 800 BCE**.

8.s: In the Later Vedic context, the term ‘Shresthins’ refers to:
8.x: Shresthins point to merchant groups. Nishka functioned as a unit of value, while barter continued as the main form of exchange.
8.tq: Use the occupational context to distinguish merchant groups from administrative and religious groups.
xs: **Shresthins** = **groups of merchants** — option **(1)**.
They point to growing trade, though **barter** was still the main mode.
xa: **Nishka** = unit of value.
**Ox-drawn wagons** carried goods.
True towns came only in the **NBPW** phase.

8.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Later Vedic agriculture?
8.x: Rice (vrihi) was the main crop and had ritual importance; wheat was grown and barley continued.

8.s:
Consider the following statements about Later Vedic settlements:
1. They were mainly villages of mud and wattle houses.
2. Burnt bricks were commonly used.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
8.x: Settlements were mainly villages of mud and wattle houses; burnt bricks were not common.

8.s: Which Vedic text contains spells and charms against disease?
8.x: The Atharvaveda contains spells and charms; the Samaveda sets Rigvedic hymns to music and the Yajurveda gives ritual procedures.
xa: ⚠ **Udgatri** = Samaveda priest; **Adhvaryu** = Yajurveda priest.
The **Atharvaveda** is the **latest Veda** and records folk practice.
**Brahmanas** = ritual commentaries (**Shatapatha, Aitareya**); **Aranyakas** = "forest texts".

8.s: Which Veda is associated with the Adhvaryu priest?
8.x: The Yajurveda gives ritual procedures in prose, is linked with the Adhvaryu and has Krishna and Shukla branches.
xa: **Samaveda** = hymns set to music, sung by the **Udgatri**.
**Atharvaveda** = spells and charms; the **latest Veda**.
**Upanishads**: **108** in all, **13** principal.

8.s: In Vedic sacrifice, the Adhvaryu was the priest who:
o: Handled the practical, manual work of the sacrifice
Taught the Veda and Vedangas for a living
8.x: The Adhvaryu handled the manual work of the sacrifice; the Hotri recited hymns, the Upadhyaya taught and the Suta was the charioteer.
n: Suta was the charioteer. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #56 · pp 130-131]
Suta was associated with the royal court. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #56 · pp 130-131]
Hotri was a Rigvedic priest who recited hymns. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #56 · pp 130-131]
Hota was a Rigvedic priest who recited hymns. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #56 · pp 130-131]
Adhvaryu was the priest responsible for the practical aspects of sacrifice. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #56 · pp 130-131]
Adhvaryu was the priest responsible for the manual aspects of sacrifice. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #56 · pp 130-131]
Upadhyaya was a teacher who taught the Veda as a profession. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #56 · pp 130-131]
Upadhyaya was a teacher who taught the Vedanga as a profession. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #56 · pp 130-131]
xa: ⚠ **Udgatri** = **Samaveda**; **Adhvaryu** = **Yajurveda**.
**Ratnins**: the king's council of **12 functionaries**, honoured in the **Ratnahavimshi** rite of the **Rajasuya**.
**Bhagadugha** = revenue collector; **Sangrahitri** = treasurer; **Palagala** = messenger.

8.s: Which Vedic texts are called 'forest texts' and give symbolic readings of ritual?
8.x: The Aranyakas are forest texts giving symbolic readings of ritual; the Upanishads deal with Atman, Brahman, Karma and Moksha.
xa: **Brahmanas** = ritual commentaries; **Samaveda** = hymns set to music.
Upanishads date to **c. 800-600 BCE**; **108** in number, **13** principal.

8.s: Which Vedic priest chanted the Samaveda hymns set to music?
8.x: The Samaveda sets Rigvedic hymns to music, chanted by the Udgatri; the Adhvaryu belongs to the Yajurveda.

8.s: Which is regarded as the latest Veda?
8.x: The Atharvaveda, with spells and charms against disease, is the latest Veda.

8.s: The king’s share of agricultural produce, known as Bhaga, was generally:
8.x: Bhaga represented the king’s share and was fixed at one-sixth of the produce. Vaishyas were the tribute-payers.
8.tq: Remember the fraction attached specifically to the king’s share, not to the other taxes.
xs: **Bhaga** was **one-sixth** (**1/6**) of produce — option **(2)**.
It was the **king's share**, collected by the **Bhagadugha**.
xa: Other compulsory taxes: **Bali** (tribute) and **Shulka** (customs/tolls).
**Vaishyas** paid tribute.
Early Vedic bali was **voluntary**; Later Vedic taxes were **compulsory**.

8.s: Which one of the following officials was responsible for collecting the king’s share of revenue?
8.x: Bhagadugha was the revenue or tax collector who collected the king’s share. Sangrahitri was the treasurer, Akshavapa the accountant and superintendent of dice, and Palagala the messenger.
8.tq: Apply the ‘who would do this job?’ method to distinguish related officials.
xs: The **Bhagadugha** collected the **king's share** of revenue — option **(3)**.
**Sangrahitri** = treasurer; **Akshavapa** = accountant / superintendent of dice; **Palagala** = messenger.
xa: Exam angle: Bhagadugha = **revenue collector** (**UPPSC 2023**).
⚠ Older notes say the **Sangrahitri** collected taxes.
**Bhaga** = king's share, **1/6** of produce.

8.s: In the Later Vedic polity, the Sangrahitri was the:
8.x: The Sangrahitri was the treasurer; the Senani was army chief, the Purohita chief priest and the Suta charioteer and herald.
xa: The **12 ratnins** were honoured in the **Ratnahavimshi** rite of the **Rajasuya**.
**Kshata / Kshatri** = chamberlain; **Govikartana** = keeper of game.

8.s: Which of the following correctly lists the taxes that became compulsory in the Later Vedic period?
8.x: The compulsory taxes were Bali, a tribute; Bhaga, the king’s share; and Shulka, customs or tolls.
8.tq: Match the tax names with the Later Vedic revenue context rather than later fiscal terminology.
xs: The compulsory taxes were **Bali, Bhaga and Shulka** — option **(4)**.
**Bali** = tribute; **Bhaga** = king's share (**1/6**); **Shulka** = customs/tolls.
**Rajasuya** is a sacrifice and **Samiti, Vidatha** are assemblies — not taxes.
xa: **Vaishyas** were the tribute-payers.
Collector = **Bhagadugha**.

8.s: The term ‘Ratnins’ in the Later Vedic polity referred to:
o: A body of twelve military commanders
A council of twelve royal functionaries
A group of twelve provincial governors
A group of twelve village assemblies
8.x: The Ratnins, or ‘jewels’, were the king’s council of twelve functionaries. They were honoured during the Ratnahavimshi rite of the Rajasuya.
8.tq: Directly identify the institutional meaning of an important technical term.
xs: **Ratnins** ("jewels") were the king's **council of twelve functionaries** — option **(2)**.
They were honoured in the **Ratnahavimshi** rite of the **Rajasuya**.
xa: List: purohita, rajan, mahisi, senani, **bhagadugha**, **sangrahitri**, suta, kshata, govikartana, gramani, **parivakti**, akshavapa.
Some lists add **palagala** (messenger).

8.s: The Ratnins were honoured in which rite associated with the Rajasuya sacrifice?
8.x: The Ratnahavimshi rite involved offerings at the houses of the Ratnins and honoured the king’s twelve functionaries.
8.tq: Use the sacrifice–rite association to distinguish closely related Vedic rituals.
xs: The Ratnins were honoured in the **Ratnahavimshi** rite — option **(1)**.
It is part of the **Rajasuya** sacrifice.
xa: The ratnins were **12** royal functionaries.
**Bhagadugha** = revenue collector; **Sangrahitri** = treasurer.

8.s: How many Ratnins made up the king's council in the Later Vedic period?
8.x: The Ratnins ('jewels') were a council of 12 officials honoured in the Ratnahavimshi rite.

8.s: In the Later Vedic period, 'Shulka' meant:
8.x: Shulka was customs or tolls; bali was tribute and bhaga the king's one-sixth share.

8.s: Which Ratnin was the charioteer and herald?
8.x: The Suta was charioteer and herald; Senani was army chief, Palagala messenger and Akshavapa accountant.

8.s: Which term for territory or state marks the shift from tribe to territory in the Later Vedic period?
8.x: Tribe gave way to territory, expressed by rashtra and janapadas.

8.s:
Consider the following statements about the Later Vedic Sabha and Samiti:
1. They declined in importance.
2. They came to be dominated by chiefs, nobles and Brahmanas.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
8.x: The Sabha and Samiti declined, dominated by chiefs, nobles and Brahmanas; the Sabha became a royal court.

8.s: Which Later Vedic ritual was a horse sacrifice expressing control over territory?
8.x: The Ashvamedha was the horse sacrifice for control over territory; Vajapeya was a chariot race and Rajasuya royal consecration.

8.s: The Rajasuya sacrifice was performed for:
8.x: The Rajasuya was the royal consecration conferring supreme power.

8.s: Which god became supreme in the Later Vedic period?
8.x: In the Later Vedic period Indra and Agni lost prominence and Prajapati became supreme.
xa: **Pushan** became the god of the **Shudras**.
**Vishnu** was a **minor god** in the Rigveda before his rise.

8.s: The Upanishadic thinkers criticised which tendency of Later Vedic religion?
8.x: Later Vedic worship became centred on elaborate rituals, which prompted the Upanishadic critique.
xa: The Upanishads (**c. 800-600 BCE**) dealt with **Atman, Brahman, Karma, Moksha**.
**Prajapati** became the supreme god.

8.s: In contrast to tribe-based Early Vedic society, Later Vedic society became:
o: Urban and based on coined money
Territory-based with agriculture and compulsory taxes
8.x: The Early Vedic phase meant tribe, cattle and voluntary bali; the Later Vedic phase meant territory, agriculture and compulsory taxes.
xa: Later Vedic crops: rice (**vrihi**) and **wheat**.
Compulsory taxes: **Bali, Bhaga** (**1/6**), **Shulka**.
Collector = **Bhagadugha**.

8.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Rudra — God of animals who later merged with Shiva
Pushan — God of warriors and destroyer of cattle
8.x: Pushan became associated with cattle and was regarded as the god of the Shudras. The other three pairs are correctly matched.
8.tq: Find the pair containing a swapped function rather than a swapped name.
xs: **Pushan — god of warriors and destroyer of cattle** is wrongly matched — option **(4)**.
**Pushan** was a **cattle god** who became the **god of the Shudras**.
The rest are right: **Rudra** (animals, merged with Shiva), **Prajapati** (creator, supreme), **Vishnu** (preserver).
xa: **Indra and Agni** lost their earlier importance.
Ritual-heavy worship **prompted the Upanishadic critique**.

8.s: In the Later Vedic period, Pushan was regarded as the god of the:
8.x: Pushan, a cattle god, came to be regarded as the god of the Shudras.

8.s: Which god, minor in the Rigveda, rose as preserver in the Later Vedic period?
8.x: Vishnu rose as preserver; Indra and Agni lost importance and Rudra was the god of animals.

8.s: Which Later Vedic god of animals later merged with Shiva?
8.x: Rudra, god of animals, later merged with Shiva.

9.s: In ancient period, which Varna was also called as ‘Sarthavaha’?
9.x: Proper rules of conduct for trade were prescribed by the head of trade guilds, known as Sarthavaha or Srenipramukh. The rules were called Samay and Srenidharma. Hence, the term Sarthavaha is associated with the Vaishya.

9.s: Which of the followings customs emerged during the post-Vedic period :
9.x: While living in the Grihastha Ashram (householder stage), a person was required to perform the Pancha Mahayajnas (Five Great Sacrifices). These five sacrifices were: Brahma Yajna ,Deva Yajna ,Pitra Yajna, Bhuta Yajna ,Atithi Yajna. The Grihastha Ashram was considered the foundation of society, as it was during this stage that a person earned wealth and also supported the other three ashramas—Brahmacharya ,Vanaprastha and Sanyasa.

9.s: In which phase, the concept of untouchability was put clearly?
9.x: The concept of untouchability assumed definite shape in the early Christian era which was the period known as the era of Dharmashastra in ancient Indian history. During this period, the Brahmanical religion was in ascendance. Various scriptures were being written and the social customs of different types were practised strictly and untouchability was one of them.

9.s: The literal meaning of which Upanishad is white horse?
9.x: Satyakama Jabala as a boy, and later a Vedic sage, who first appears in chapter IV of ancient Hindu text, the Chhandogya Upanishad challenged the stigma of an unmarried mother.

9.s: According to the Aitareya Brahmana, the Shudra was described as
9.x: The Aitareya Brahmana described the Shudra as ‘a servant of another’ and stated that he could be expelled or struck at will.
9.tq: Link the source text with its distinctive description of social status.
xs: The **Aitareya Brahmana** calls the Shudra "**a servant of another**" — option **(3)**.
He could be **expelled** and beaten/slain at will.
The **tribute payer** in the same text is the **Vaishya**.
xa: Shudras had **no Upanayana**, no right to study the Vedas.
Discrimination existed against **Shudras and Chandalas**.
The Aitareya also calls the daughter a **source of misery**.

9.s: Which of the following occupations were associated with the Vaishyas in Later Vedic society?
9.x: Vaishyas engaged in farming, trade and craft production and paid tribute.
9.tq: Use the occupational cluster rather than selecting a single profession.
xs: **Vaishyas** were **farmers, traders and artisans** — option **(1)**.
They were also **cattle-rearers** and the **tribute payers**.
Warriors/kings = **Kshatriyas**; priests/teachers = **Brahmanas**.
xa: Vaishyas formed **guild-like bodies (gana)** headed by a **shreshthin**.
Vaishyas were **dvija** — entitled to upanayana (metre **Jagati**).

9.s: The first statement of the fourfold varna order is associated with the Purusha Sukta of the
9.x: The Purusha Sukta in the Tenth Mandala of the Rigveda contains the first statement of the fourfold varna order.
9.tq: Test the precise textual location rather than merely the name of the text.
xs: The **Purusha Sukta** is in the **Rigveda, Tenth Mandala** — option **(4)**.
It is the **first statement of the four-fold varna order**.
xa: The words **varna** and **shudra** also occur in the Rigveda.
Upper three varnas = **dvija** (twice-born, via upanayana).
Birth-based occupation and **rigid hierarchy** set in during the **later Vedic period**.

9.s: The term ‘Dvija’ in the context of later Vedic society referred to
o: the three upper varnas entitled to the Upanayana rite
9.x: Brahmanas, Kshatriyas and Vaishyas were collectively called Dvija, or twice-born, because of their entitlement to Upanayana.
9.tq: Distinguish the collective ritual category from the individual varnas.
xs: **Dvija** = **the three upper varnas entitled to the Upanayana** — option **(1)**.
Dvija means **twice-born**; second birth comes through **upanayana**.
**Shudras** and **women** were excluded from upanayana.
xa: Upanayana metres: **Gayatri** (Brahmana), **Trishtubh** (Kshatriya), **Jagati** (Vaishya).
Education (gurukula) was confined largely to the **Dvija**.
**Vratyas and Nishadas** stood outside the varna order.

9.s: The proliferation of jatis is a feature of which period?
9.x: The proliferation of jatis was post-Vedic, including Gupta-era diversification; the later Vedic period saw birth-based occupation and rigid hierarchy.
xa: Jati growth: **Gupta-era** diversification; **post-Satavahana** mixed castes in Andhra.
Exam angle: varna **rigidified after the Rig Vedic phase**.
Rig Vedic society was relatively **fluid and egalitarian**.

9.s: The first reference to money-lending in the Vedic literature is found in the
9.x: The Shatapatha Brahmana contains the first reference to money-lending.
9.tq: Match the economic practice with the specific textual source.
xs: The **Shatapatha Brahmana** has the **first reference to money-lending** — option **(4)**.
It also gives the **elaborate description of Upanayana**.
**Chhandogya** = earliest reference to the first three ashramas; **Aitareya** = Shudra as servant of another.
xa: The Shatapatha says the "**wife is half her husband** and completes him".
Guild-like Vaishya bodies (**gana**) appear in later Vedic texts.

9.s: Which of the following groups stood outside the formal four-varna order?
9.x: Vratyas and Nishadas were groups placed outside the formal four-varna order.
9.tq: Separate excluded groups from the four recognised varnas.
xs: **Vratyas and Nishadas** stood **outside the varna order** — option **(2)**.
**Brahmanas, Kshatriyas (Rajanyas), Vaishyas, Shudras** are the four varnas themselves.
xa: **Rathakaras** kept the **sacred-thread** privilege.
Discrimination targeted **Shudras and Chandalas**.
The **Chhandogya Upanishad** names the Chandala a despised birth.

9.s: Untouchability as a formal rule is associated with the:
9.x: Later Vedic society discriminated against Shudras and Chandalas, but formal untouchability belongs to the post-Vedic Dharmasutras.
xa: The **Chhandogya Upanishad** calls the Chandala a despised birth.
The Aitareya: Shudra could be **expelled** and **struck at will**.
Satavahana Andhra: **anuloma** offspring = **Ugra**; **pratiloma** = **Chandala**.

9.s: The earliest reference to the first three ashramas is found in the:
9.x: The Chhandogya Upanishad first refers to the first three ashramas; all four are first listed in the Jabala Upanishad.
xa: ⚠ **3 – 4** ashramas = **Chhandogya – Jabala**.
**Sannyasa** was **added later**; only the **first three** were prevalent in Later Vedic times.
The **Grihastha** performs the **Pancha Mahayajnas** (MPPSC **2025**).

9.s: In the Later Vedic period, varna increasingly came to be based on:
9.x: Varna became increasingly birth-based in the Later Vedic period, and gotra exogamy became important.
xa: Rig Vedic society was **relatively fluid and egalitarian**.
**Harappan** society had differentiation but **no textual caste**.
In Rig Vedic times women attended the **Sabha**.

9.s: In Satavahana Andhra, the offspring of an anuloma union and a pratiloma union were respectively known as:
9.x: Anuloma offspring were called Ugra, whereas pratiloma offspring were called Chandala. The other pairs refer either to teachers and priests or reverse these two designations.
9.tq: Discriminate between two easily reversed social classifications by fixing their exact order.
xs: In Satavahana Andhra, **anuloma** offspring = **Ugra** and **pratiloma** offspring = **Chandala** — option **(3)**.
Option 2 reverses them; **Acharya/Upadhyaya** are teachers and **Purohita/Adhvaryu** priests.
xa: **Anuloma** = higher-varna man with lower-varna woman (tolerated).
The **Chhandogya Upanishad** names the Chandala a **despised birth**.
Post-Satavahana (**Ikshvaku**) society saw **mixed castes and sub-castes**.

9.s: Which Satavahana ruler claimed to have protected varnashrama dharma?
9.x: Gautamiputra Satakarni claimed to have protected varnashrama dharma.
xa: Jati proliferation is **post-Vedic** (Gupta-era diversification).
**Anuloma** offspring = **Ugra**; **pratiloma** = **Chandala**.

9.s: Varnashrama Dharma combines the varna system with the:
9.x: Varnashrama Dharma denotes the combined framework of varna and Ashrama.
xa: It became the **normative frame** of later Hindu society.
AP angle: **Gautamiputra Satakarni** protected varnashrama dharma and opposed **varna-sankara**.

9.s: The elaborate description of the Upanayana ceremony is found in the
9.x: The Shatapatha Brahmana gives an elaborate description of the Upanayana ceremony.
9.tq: Use the text–ritual association and avoid swapping closely related Vedic works.
xs: The elaborate Upanayana description is in the **Shatapatha Brahmana** — option **(4)**.
**Chhandogya** = three ashramas; **Brihadaranyaka** = Gargi's debate; **Aitareya** = Shudra as servant.
xa: Metres: **Gayatri – Trishtubh – Jagati** = **Brahmana – Kshatriya – Vaishya**.
The Shatapatha also has the **first reference to money-lending**.

9.s: In the varna order, priestly functions belonged to the:
9.x: Priestly duties belonged to the Brahmanas; Kshatriyas were warriors and rulers, Vaishyas farmed and traded, and Shudras did manual work.
n: Brahmana is associated with priestly and religious functions. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #22 · pp 80-82]
Kshatriya is associated with warrior and ruling functions. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #22 · pp 80-82]
Vaishya is associated with agriculture, cattle-rearing, and trade. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #22 · pp 80-82]
Shudra is associated with servile and manual occupations. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #22 · pp 80-82]
xa: Vaishyas were the **tribute payers**.
The upper three varnas were **dvija** (twice-born, via upanayana).
⚠ **Jati** (birth-based groups) is **distinct** from **Varna**.

9.s: Vaishya guilds (gana) were headed by a:
9.x: Vaishya guilds were headed by a shreshthin; the Sarthavaha headed trade guilds.

9.s: The rules of the guilds were known as:
9.x: Guild rules were called Samay and Srenidharma.

9.s: In Satavahana Andhra, the offspring of a pratiloma union was called:
9.x: Pratiloma offspring were called Chandala and anuloma offspring Ugra.

9.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the Shudra in Later Vedic society?
o: Was called 'servant of another' in the Aitareya Brahmana
9.x: The dvija were the upper three varnas; Shudras had no upanayana and no Vedas.

9.s:
Consider the following statements about the ashramas in the Later Vedic period:

2. Sannyasa was added later and was not well established.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
9.x: Only Brahmacharya, Grihastha and Vanaprastha were prevalent in Later Vedic times; Sannyasa was added later.

9.x: Vanaprastha was gradual withdrawal; Brahmacharya was Vedic study, Grihastha household life and Sannyasa complete detachment.
xa: The **Grihastha** performs the **Pancha Mahayajnas**.
Sannyasa was **added later**.
Women followed the ashrama chosen by their **husbands**.

9.s: The Pancha Mahayajnas were regarded as daily duties primarily of the
9.x: The Pancha Mahayajnas were daily duties of the Grihastha, or householder, Ashrama.
9.tq: Apply the social-role clue: regular family and ritual obligations belong to the householder.
xs: The **Pancha Mahayajnas** were daily duties of the **Grihastha** (householder) — option **(3)**.
Exam: **MPPSC 2025**.
xa: The five: **Brahma** (Vedic study), **Deva** (gods), **Pitri** (ancestors), **Bhuta** (living beings), **Nri/Manushya** (guests).
Grihastha duties: **marriage, family, economic** duties.

9.s:
Consider the following statements about the Purusharthas:
1. Dharma, Artha and Kama formed the earlier trivarga.
2. Moksha was added later under Upanishadic ideas of karma, samsara and liberation.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
9.x: Dharma, Artha and Kama formed the trivarga in the Later Vedic-Sutra phase; Moksha was added later under Upanishadic influence.
xa: Dharma = duty; Artha = wealth; Kama = desire; Moksha = liberation.
Core Vedic-Upanishadic legacy concepts: **dharma, karma, moksha**.

9.s: Which of the following Purushartha – meaning pairs is correctly matched?
9.x: Artha means wealth. Dharma means duty, Kama desire and Moksha liberation.
xa: The first three = **trivarga**.
Moksha was the **fourth**, added with Upanishadic thought.

9.s: Which of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched with a Pancha Mahayajna?
9.x: Bhuta-yajna was directed towards living beings. Hospitality to guests was the duty of Nri-yajna or Manushya-yajna.
9.tq: Find the exchanged duties among the five closely related Yajnas.
xs: **Bhuta-yajna — hospitality to guests** is wrongly matched — option **(3)**.
**Bhuta yajna** = for **all living beings**; hospitality to guests = **Nri/Manushya yajna**.
The rest are right: **Pitri** = ancestors; **Brahma** = Vedic study; **Deva** = offerings to gods.
xa: The Pancha Mahayajnas are daily duties of the **Grihastha**.
Exam angle: **MPPSC 2025** asked in which ashrama they are performed.

9.s: All four ashramas are first mentioned in the:
9.x: The first three ashramas appear in the Chhandogya Upanishad; all four first appear in the Jabala Upanishad.

9.s: Among the Pancha Mahayajnas, the Nri (Atithi) yajna refers to:
9.x: Nri or Atithi yajna is hospitality; Bhuta yajna is for living beings.

9.s: Under which phase was Moksha added to the Purusharthas?
9.x: Dharma, Artha and Kama formed the trivarga; Moksha was added later in the Upanishadic phase.

9.s: In the context of ancient Indian society, which one of the following terms does not belong to the category of the other three?
9.x: Kosa is the odd one out because it is not related to kinship or lineage. In Sanskrit usage, kula denotes a family, vamsha (vamsa) signifies lineage or descent, and gotra refers to a clan traced to a common ancestor, often linked with rules of exogamy. All three are kinship-based concepts. By contrast, kosa means a treasury (and in some contexts, a lexicon), making it an economic or literary term rather than a social or lineage category.

9.s: In the context of ancient Indian society which one of the following terms does not belong to the category of the other three?
9.x: In the context of ancient Indian society, Vansha, Gotra and Kula are the words associated with the family system, but the word Kosa is related to the treasury.

9.s: The word 'gotra' literally means:
9.x: Gotra literally means cow-pen; as an institution of descent from a common male ancestor it was established in Later Vedic times.
xa: Rule: **gotra exogamy** — no marriage within the same gotra.
Plus caste endogamy and **sapinda** prohibition ("sasan" rule).

9.s: Who analysed sapinda and gotra rules and divided India into four kinship zones in the work titled Kinship Organization in India?
9.x: Irawati Karve analysed sapinda and gotra rules and divided India into four kinship zones in Kinship Organization in India, published in 1953.
9.tq: Use the author–work association as the deciding clue.
xs: **Irawati Karve** wrote **Kinship Organization in India** (**1953**) — option **(3)**.
She analysed **sapinda and gotra** rules and divided India into **four kinship zones**.
**Gargi** and **Maitreyi** were Upanishadic women philosophers.
xa: **Gotra exogamy** + caste endogamy + **sapinda** prohibition = North Indian pattern.
⚠ **Kosa** (treasury) is not a kinship term.

9.s: Which one of the following is the odd one out in relation to ancient Indian kinship terminology?
9.x: Kula, Vamsha and Gotra are kinship terms, whereas Kosa means treasury.
9.tq: Identify the term that belongs to a different conceptual group.
xs: **Kosa** is the odd one out — it means **treasury** — option **(1)** (**UPSC 1996**).
**Kula** = family; **Vamsha** = lineage/dynasty; **Gotra** = exogamous clan.
xa: Gotra literally means **cow-pen**.
**Irawati Karve** analysed kinship in *Kinship Organization in India* (**1953**).
**Gotra exogamy** = no marriage within the same gotra.

9.s: Gotra exogamy prohibited:
9.x: Gotra exogamy prohibited marriage within the same gotra, operating alongside caste endogamy and sapinda restrictions.
xa: **Irawati Karve** analysed **sapinda + gotra** rules.
Gotra as an institution was established in **Later Vedic** times.

9.s: The lineage sense of the word 'gotra' first appears in the:
9.x: Gotra means cow-pen in the Rigveda; the lineage sense first appears in the Atharvaveda.

9.s: In Later Vedic kinship terminology, 'Vamsha' means:
9.x: Vamsha = lineage, Kula = family and Kosa = treasury (not a kinship term).

9.s: Who is the world's oldest school pupil in Kenya?
There was a provision for reciting which mantra in the Upanayana ritual of the Kshatriya castes?
9.x: During the Upanayana ceremony of the Kshatriya caste, the Trishtubh Mantra was prescribed. It symbolized the martial and heroic qualities associated with Kshatriyas, aligning with their warrior duties and societal responsibilities in Vedic tradition.

9.s: In Later Vedic sacrifice, which priest chanted the Samaveda?
9.x: The Udgatri chanted the Samaveda; the Hotri recited the Rigveda and the Adhvaryu performed sacrificial acts.
xa: **Acharya** taught the whole Veda **not for a fee**.
**Purohita** = family/royal priest and a **ratnin**.

9.s:
Consider the following statements about Upanayana:
1. It was open to Shudras and women.
2. It was the sacred-thread initiation into Vedic study for the upper three varnas.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
9.x: Upanayana was the sacred-thread initiation into Vedic study for Brahmanas, Kshatriyas and Vaishyas; Shudras and women were excluded.
xa: Performed in the boy's **8th year**.
Elaborate description in the **Shatapatha Brahmana**.
It is one of the **16** samskaras.

9.x: The traditional total number of samskaras is sixteen.
9.tq: Recall the exact numerical value from the ritual classification.
xs: There are **16** samskaras (**shodasha samskaras**) — option **(3)** (**MPPSC 2015**).
They run from **Garbhadhana** (conception) to **Antyeshti** (funeral).
xa: Key ones: **Upanayana** and **Vivaha**.
**Pumsavana** = to procure a male child.

9.s: Which of the following pairs of varna and Upanayana metre is correctly matched?
9.x: The Kshatriya Upanayana was associated with Trishtubh. The Brahmana's metre was Gayatri and the Vaishya's Jagati.
xa: Exam angle: "mantra in the Kshatriya upanayana" = **Trishtubh** (**MPPSC 2024**).
Upanayana made one **dvija**; Shudras and women excluded.

9.s: In the gurukula system of education, the pupil generally
o: lived separately from the teacher and studied independently
received instruction only from guild heads
9.x: In the gurukula system, pupils lived with the guru. Education was confined largely to the Dvija communities.

xs: In the **gurukula** the pupil **lived with the guru** — option **(1)**.
Education was confined largely to the **Dvija**.
xa: **Brahmacharya** = student stage — Vedic study under a guru.

**Hotri** = Rigveda reciter; **Udgatri** = Samaveda chanter.

9.s: Which teacher taught the Veda and Vedangas for a livelihood?
9.x: The Upadhyaya taught for a livelihood, while the Acharya taught the whole Veda free.

9.x: Upanayana, the sacred-thread ceremony, was performed in the boy's 8th year.

9.x: Vaishya = Jagati; Brahmana = Gayatri; Kshatriya = Trishtubh.

9.x: The Hotri recited the Rigveda; the Udgatri chanted the Samaveda and the Adhvaryu performed the acts.

9.s: Which was the most popular form of marriage in the Vijayanagara Empire?
Who among the following is considered to be the first law-giver of India ?
In the Arsha form of marriage, the groom gave the bride's father:
9.x: In the Arsha form, the groom gave a token cow and bull to the bride's father.
xa: Arsha is an **approved** form.
⚠ **Asura** = purchase; **Rakshasa** = capture; **Paishacha** = lowest.

9.x: Paishacha, involving the seduction of a sleeping or intoxicated girl, was regarded as the lowest form of marriage.

**Daiva, Prajapatya, Arsha** are **approved** forms.

**Brahma** form: father gives daughter with gifts to a learned man.

**8 forms** in both **Manu** and **Kautilya**.

o: Paishacha — seduction of a sleeping or intoxicated girl
9.x: Rakshasa marriage involved capture or abduction. Marriage by purchase was known as Asura marriage.

xs: **Rakshasa — marriage by purchase** is wrongly matched — option **(1)**.
**Rakshasa** = marriage by **capture/abduction**; purchase = **Asura**.
The rest are right: **Gandharva** = mutual consent; **Paishacha** = seduction; **Asura** = bride price.
xa: Exam angle: "marriage by purchase of bride" = **Asura** (**APPSC 2012**).
There are **8** forms in Manu and Kautilya.

9.x: Manu and Kautilya list eight forms of marriage, of which the first four were approved.

9.x: Rakshasa marriage was by capture; Asura was by purchase.

9.x: Gandharva marriage was based on mutual consent.

Members of the same varna only
A higher-varna man and a lower-varna woman
9.x: Anuloma was a higher-varna man with a lower-varna woman; pratiloma, the reverse, was disapproved.

9.x: In Daiva marriage the daughter was given to the officiating priest.

9.s: In which Upanishad is the famous dialogue of Yagnavalkya and Gargi mentioned?
9.x: The dialogue between Yagnavalkya and Gargi is mentioned in the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad.

9.s: In the Later Vedic period, women lost the right of ____, the initiation ceremony.
9.x: The status of women declined through loss of Upanayana, restricted education and exclusion from religious and public activities.
xa: References to **sati** and **child marriage** appear.
Exceptions: **Gargi** and **Maitreyi**.
In Rig Vedic times women attended the **Sabha**; the **Atharva Veda** mentions women in the **Samiti**.

9.s: References to which of the following practices appear in accounts of the declining status of women in Later Vedic society?
o: Compulsory female military service and polyandry
Abolition of marriage and communal ownership
Female kingship and universal widow remarriage

9.x: The Brihadaranyaka Upanishad records Gargi's debate with Yajnavalkya.

9.x: The Aitareya Brahmana says a daughter is a source of misery; the Shatapatha calls the wife half her husband.

9.x: The Shatapatha Brahmana describes the wife as half her husband.

Consider the following statements about women in the Later Vedic period:

10.s: Which literature refers to Andhras as ‘Andhakaratta '
Which of the following is the correct order of the Vedic literature?
10.x: Each of the Vedas is divided into four parts (or sections). The correct order of them is Samhitas, Brahmanas, Aranyakas and Upanishads. Samhitas and Brahmanas form the Karma- Kanda segment of the Vedas. Aranyakas and Upanishads form the Gyan-Kanda segment of the Vedas. They explicitly focus on philosophy and spirituality.

10.s: Veda Vyasa, also known as Krishna Dvaipayana, is traditionally associated with which of the following?
o: Compilation and classification of the Vedas
10.x: Veda Vyasa, or Krishna Dvaipayana, is traditionally remembered as the person who classified the Vedas.
10.tq: Use the person–work association and eliminate authors of other grammatical and Buddhist texts.
xs: **Veda Vyasa (Krishna Dvaipayana)** is recalled as the **classifier of the Vedas** — so option **(1)** is correct.
The **Ashtadhyayi** is by **Panini**; the **Mahabhashya** is by **Patanjali**.
Vyasa is also the traditional author of the **Mahabharata**.
xa: A **Vijayawada** discourse in **Mar 2026** recalled Vyasa as classifier of the Vedas.
The four Vedas: **Rig** (hymns), **Sama** (melody), **Yajur** (ritual formulas), **Atharva** (spells, charms).
⚠ Priests: **Hotri – Udgatri – Adhvaryu – Brahman** = **Rig – Sama – Yajur – Atharva**.

10.s: What is the literal meaning of Vedanta?
10.x: Vedanta literally means the end of the Vedas, Veda plus anta, since the Upanishads come at the close of Vedic literature and mark its climax.
10.tq: Split the word into its parts.
n: Vedanta means the end of the Vedas or the climax of Vedic ideology. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #53 · pp 127-128]
xs: **Vedanta** literally means the **End of the Vedas** — option **(4)** is correct.
It is the **climax** of **Vedic ideology**; the **Upanishads** are also called **Vedanta**.
xa: Foundations of Vedanta: **Prasthanatrayi** — **Upanishads**, **Brahma Sutra**, **Bhagavad Gita**.
Upanishads were composed c. **800-600 BCE**; teaching: **Atman = Brahman**, **Karma**, **Moksha**.
Upanishads = **Shruti**; Puranas = **Smriti**.

10.s: Vedic texts, regarded as 'heard', are classed as:
10.x: All Vedic texts - Samhitas, Brahmanas, Aranyakas and Upanishads - are Shruti ('heard') and called apaurusheya.
xa: **Puranas** = **Smriti** (later, legend-based).
**Manusmriti** = the earliest Smriti.

10.s: Brahmanas are best described as:
o: Philosophical dialogues concerned exclusively with the jnana-marga
Prose ritual commentaries concerned with the karma-marga
10.x: Brahmanas are prose ritual commentaries or liturgies and are associated with the karma-marga.
10.tq: Distinguish the ritual function of Brahmanas from the philosophical role of Upanishads.
xs: **Brahmanas** are **prose ritual commentaries** concerned with the **karma-marga** — option **(3)**.
They are called "**liturgies**".
Philosophy (**jnana-marga**) belongs to the **Upanishads**; grammar and phonetics to the **Vedangas**.
xa: **Aranyakas** bridge **Karmamarga** to **Jnanamarga**.
Largest Brahmana = **Shatapatha**.

10.s: The 'forest texts' that form the concluding parts of the Brahmanas and bridge karmamarga and jnanamarga are the:
10.x: The Aranyakas are forest texts concluding the Brahmanas and form a bridge from ritualism (karmamarga) to philosophical speculation (jnanamarga).

10.s: The Aranyakas and Upanishads together form the:
10.x: Samhitas and Brahmanas form the Karma-kanda; Aranyakas and Upanishads form the Jnana-kanda.

10.s: Where does the term "Gothra" occur for the first time?
Which one of the following four Vedas contains an account of magical charms and spells?
10.x: The Atharva Veda is distinct for its charms, spells, and healing hymns, unlike the Sama Veda (musical chants) and Yajur Veda (ritual formulas). It is most associated with popular, protective, and therapeutic practices.

10.s: In which one among the following texts does the term kshetra-patni ('mistress of the field') originate?
10.x: The term kshetra-patni, meaning 'mistress of the field', originates in the Atharvaveda (specifically in hymns related to agriculture). • Note: We recommend aspirants avoid unnecessary guesswork in such highly unconventional and obscure questions.

10.s: The compilation of which among the following is based upon the Rig Veda?
10.x: The Samaveda is the shortest among all the four Vedas. It is closely connected with the Rigveda. It has taken many verses from the Rigveda. The Samaveda is compiled inclusively for ritual application and all of its verses are meant to be chanted in ceremonies. Samaveda Samhita consists a total of 1875 verses. Among these except 75 or 99 verses, all of them are compiled in Rigveda.

10.s: Which one of the following four Vedas contains an account of magical charms and spells?
10.x: The earliest description of charms and spells can be found in Atharvaveda.

10.s: Which among the following Vedas was the earliest composition?
Separate Brahmin texts were written for each Veda. The Brahmin texts related to Yajurveda is:
Which of the following is a Samhita of Shukla Yajurveda?
10.x: There are two branches of Yajurveda-Shukla Yajurveda and Krishna Yajurveda. Vajasneyi is the Samhita of Shukla Yajurveda. Shukla Yajurveda is available only in the poetic form whereas Krishna Yajurveda contains both poetic as well as prose form.

10.s: Gayatri Mantra is found in which book?
10.x: The Gayatri Mantra was first written in Sanskrit in the Rig Veda by the Brahmarshi Vishwamitra. Its meaning is “May the Almighty God illuminate our intellect to lead us along the righteous path.”

10.s: In which Veda are Sabha and Samiti declared as separate institutions?
10.x: Among the Vedic texts, Sabha and Samiti are clearly mentioned as separate institutions in the Atharvaveda, although both these institutions (Sabha and Samiti) are also mentioned in the Rigveda. In the tenth Mandal of the Rigveda too, Sabha and Samiti are mentioned and an appeal is made to create unity and consensus between the two. In the Rigveda, the roles of Sabha and Samiti are not clearly separated nor are they established in an institutional form, as we find in the Atharvaveda. In a verse of the Atharvaveda, Sabha and Samiti are shown as two separate institutions and they are called 'two daughters of Prajapati'. Therefore, by mentioning them as two separate institutions in the Atharvaveda, their social and political importance is underlined.

10.s: Rights and Rituals related to Yajnas are mentioned in–
10.x: Yajurveda in Sanskrit means ‘wisdom of sacrificial formulas.’ This Veda, compiled a century or two after the Rig-veda, contains prose and verse formulae that were to be pronounced by the priests performing the manual part of the sacrifice. Pasenadi (also known as Prasenajit) was an immensely popular ruler of Kosala, and a contemporary of the Buddha. 13.s: Who was the first founder of Shwetambar creed during the first partition of Jain creed?
13.x: About 150 years after Lord Mahavira’s departure, when Bhadrabahuswami was the head of the religious order and Maurya was ruling over Magadha. Pataliputra the capital city became the centre of learning and knowledge. At that time there occurred a severe famine that seems to have raged for 12 long years. During that period of shortage and scarcity, it was hard for Jain monks to observe the code of conduct laid down by the Lord. Bhadrabahuswami, therefore, decided to migrate to the South along with many followers. For those who stayed behind, it was hard to remember accurately whatever they learnt. Venerable Sthulabhadra and most of those who stayed in the north used to cover their bodies with a plain, white cloth; while those who had migrated with Bhadrabahuswami were mostly unclad. The latter took pride in their being true unclad followers of the Lord and in due course came to be known as Digamabars which means skyclad. Those on the other side came to be known as Shwetamabars on account of white cloth that they wore.

Which of the above are Jaina texts?
13.x: Parishishtaparvan and Trishashtilakshana Mahapurana are Jaina texts: Parishishtaparvan (12 th century), authored by Hemachandra, provides a historical account of early Jaina teachers along with references to political developments. Nettipakarana and Avadanashataka are Buddhist texts: Nettipakarana belongs to the Tipitaka tradition and explains the teachings of the Buddha, while Avadanashataka is part of Buddhist Avadana literature, which presents moral stories about the Buddha and other figures.

14.x: In Buddhism, Nirvana refers to the ultimate goal of spiritual practice, which is the cessation of suffering (dukkha) and liberation from the cycle of birth, death, and rebirth (samsara). This state is achieved by extinguishing desires, attachments, and ignorance, which are the root causes of suffering. Nirvana is the Summum Bonum of Buddhism, and the person who has attained the ultimate goal is called an Arhat. What is Mokşa to the Hindu, the Tao is to the Chinese mystic, Fana to the Sufi, Eternal Life to the followers of Jesus, that is Nirvāna to the Buddhist. The word Nirvāna literally means, 'blowing out' or 'becoming cool'. It is the blowing out of the fire of lust (rāga), of resentment (dosa), of glamour (moha). It is thus becoming cool, reaching perfect calm, to be reached within the four corners of the present life. An Arhat, after the dissolution of his body and mind, reaches the state of Pari- Nirvāna. Thus, "blowing out" and "cooling" are not complete annihilation but the extinction or dying out of hot passion.

Jainism is founded on the principle of the Triratna (Three Jewels), namely Right Faith (Samyak Darshana), Right Knowledge (Samyak Jnana) and Right Conduct (Samyak Charitra). These constitute the path to liberation (Moksha). Buddhism teaches the Noble Eightfold Path (Ashtanga Marga) as the means to end suffering. It consists of Right View, Right Resolve, Right Speech, Right Action, Right Livelihood, Right Effort, Right Mindfulness and Right Concentration. Shaivism is centred on the worship of Lord Shiva, whose most important symbol is the Shiva Linga, representing both creation and cosmic energy. Animism refers to the belief that natural objects such as mountains, rivers, trees and animals possess spiritual power. Hence, Nature Worship is its defining characteristic. Thus, the correct matching is a–iii, b–ii, c–iv, d–i, corresponding to Option (3).
Exam Note:
• Jainism – Triratna
• Buddhism – Ashtanga Marga
• Shaivism – Linga Worship
• Animism – Nature Worship

17.s: In Kautilya's Saptanga theory, which element comes first in the standard order?
17.x: The standard order is Swami, Amatya, Janapada, Durga, Kosha, Danda/Bala and Mitra, so Swami comes first.
xa: Meanings: **Swami** = king, **Amatya** = ministers, **Janapada** = territory and people, **Durga** = fort.
**Kosha** = treasury, **Danda/Bala** = army, force, justice, **Mitra** = ally.
⚠ Some notes list Durga 6th, Land 7th and add an 8th, **Shatru** (enemy) — learn the standard seven.
Later dynasties (**Eastern Chalukyas**, **Kakatiyas**) used the Saptanga and **18 Tirthas** model.

17.s: Which of the following is NOT one of the seven standard elements in Kautilya's Saptanga theory?

xa: Standard order: **Swami, Amatya, Janapada, Durga, Kosha, Danda/Bala, Mitra**.
