17.s: In Kautilya's Saptanga theory, which element is called 'the ear of the state'?
17.x: Mitra (ally), the seventh limb, is called the ear of the state.

17.s: Which element comes third in Kautilya's Saptanga order?
17.x: The order is Swami, Amatya, Janapada, Durga, Kosha, Danda and Mitra.

17.s: Which Mauryan official was the Collector-General of Revenue and collected revenue in cash and kind with the assistance of the Bhagadhuk?

**Sannidhata** was the **treasurer** and keeper of state stores, not the collector.
**Pautavadhyaksha** handled **weights and measures**; **Sulkadhyaksha** handled **tolls and customs**.

Land revenue was the main income; the king's share (**Bhaga**) was normally **1/6**.

17.s: The Sannidhata in the Mauryan administration was primarily responsible for which of the following?
17.x: Sannidhata was the treasurer and keeper of state stores. The Samaharta, in contrast, was the Collector-General of Revenue.

xs: The **Sannidhata** was the **treasurer and keeper of state stores** — option **(1)**.
**Crown lands and state agriculture** belonged to the **Sitadhyaksha**; **tolls and customs** to the **Sulkadhyaksha**.
**Markets** were under the **Samsthadhyaksha**.

17.s: In the Mauryan administrative system, Dandapala was the head of which department?
17.x: Dandapala was the head of the army department in Kautilya’s Mauryan list of tirthas.

xs: In Kautilya's list, the **Dandapala** headed the **army department** — option **(3)** (APPSC-G1 **2022** key).
**Criminal justice** was the **Pradeshtri**'s charge; the **treasury** was the **Sannidhata**'s.
The **palace household** was under the **Antarvamshika**.
xa: ⚠ Some notes call Dandapala **head of police** — from the Eastern Chalukya **Ashtadasha Tirthas** (Magallu inscription); for the Kautilya question the key is **army**.
The **Senapati** was the commander-in-chief.
Chandragupta's army: **6,00,000 foot** and **30,000 cavalry**, run by **six boards of five**.

17.x: The Eastern Chalukyas (Ashtadasha Tirthas) and the Kakatiyas used the Saptanga and 18 Tirthas model. The Sungas, Kanvas, Indo-Greeks, Sakas, Kushanas and Western Kshatrapas are not linked with it.

xs: The **Eastern Chalukyas** (Ashtadasha Tirthas) and the **Kakatiyas** used the Saptanga and **18 Tirthas** model — option **(1)**.
The notes do not link the Sungas, Kanvas, Indo-Greeks, Sakas, Kushanas or Kshatrapas with it.
xa: ⚠ The Eastern Chalukya list (**Magallu** inscription) makes **Dandapala** a police chief; Kautilya's Dandapala heads the **army**.

Each Mauryan tirtha drew **12,000 panas** a year.

17.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched?

17.s: Among Kautilya's tirthas, the Antapala was in charge of:
17.x: The Antapala was the frontier officer in charge of border forts.

17.x: The Prashasta handled prisons; Dauvarika the palace gate, Nayaka the city guard and Paura the capital.

17.s: Land revenue, which was the chief source of income during the Mauryan period, was collected by which officer?

17.s: In the Mauryan administration, the Akaradhyaksha was in charge of:

17.s: The Mauryan Lakshanadhyaksha was associated with:

17.s: Which one of the following administrative structures in ascending order is correct?

17.x: A study of Ashoka’s inscriptions shows that Pradeshika, Rajuka, and Yukta–all three–were mainly “district-level officers” in the Mauryan administration. 20.s: Who came to power in Magadha after the Mauryas?
20.x:

84.s: The practice of Satavahana kings prefixing their names with their mother's name began during whose reign?
84.x:
The practice of using matronymics (mother's name) became prominent from the reign of Gautamiputra Satakarni, who styled himself after his mother Gautami Balashri. 84.s: According to the Macedonian inscription, who among the following said that the Satavahanas belonged to Bellary?
84.x:
The eminent historian R. G. Bhandarkar proposed the Bellary Theory regarding the origin of the Satavahanas. Based on inscriptional evidence and historical interpretation, he suggested that the early Satavahanas originated from the Bellary region. Although later historians proposed alternative theories placing their origin in the Godavari valley or western Deccan, Bhandarkar's view remains an important historiographical interpretation frequently discussed in ancient Indian history. Hence, the correct answer is Option (2).

• Bellary Theory – R. G. Bhandarkar
• Dynasty – Satavahanas

84.s: The Nasik Prasasti was issued in which regnal year of Vasishthiputra Pulumavi?

Stopper of the mixing of varnas

Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

84.s: Gautamiputra Satakarni's title 'Trisamudra-toya-pita-vahana' refers to:
o: Horses that drank the waters of three seas
Stopper of the mixing of varnas

Trisamudra-toya-pita-vahana – Lord of the southern sea

84.s: The titles 'Dakshinapathapati' and 'Apratihatachakra' in the Naneghat inscription belong to:
84.x: Naneghat gives Satakarni I these titles; Dakshinapatheshwara was Vasishthiputra Pulumavi's.

84.s: Which Satavahana queen ruled as guardian of the kingdom because her son was young?
84.x: After Satakarni I died young, his queen Naganika ruled as regent for her minor sons (Nanaghat inscription).

o: Foundation of the dynasty by a queen
Election of kings by the queen mothers
The high status of royal women, with succession remaining patriarchal

84.s: Gautami Balasri is best described as:
o: The regent of Yajna Sri Satakarni during his minority
The queen of Hala who composed Gathasaptasati
The queen mother of Gautamiputra Satakarni who built a Nasik cave for Bhadrayaniya monks
The wife of Satakarni I who issued the Naneghat inscription

xs: **Gautami Balasri** was the **queen mother** of Gautamiputra, who built a **Nasik cave for the Bhadrayaniya monks** — option **(3)** is correct.

84.x: Naganika, wife of Satakarni I, acted as regent during her son's minority; Lilavati was Hala's queen.

84.x: She built a Nasik cave for the Bhadrayaniya monks; the Karle village went to the Mahasanghikas.

84.x: Gautami Balasri's Nasik prasasti, describing Gautamiputra Satakarni's victories, was engraved in the 19th regnal year of her grandson Vasishthiputra Pulumavi.

84.s: During whose reign did Gautami Balashri issue the Nasik Inscription?

The famous Nasik Prasasti was issued by Gautami Balashri, the mother of Gautamiputra Satakarni, during the reign of her grandson Vasishtiputra Pulumavi. The inscription glorifies Gautamiputra Satakarni as the destroyer of the Sakas, Yavanas and Pahlavas, and is the most important inscription for reconstructing the political history of the Satavahanas. • Nasik Inscription – Gautami Balashri
• Issued during – Vasishtiputra Pulumavi

85.s: During the rule of the Satavahanas, which administration was carried out by the Nigama Sabhas?

85.s: What was the rate of interest during the Satavahana period on the money deposited in a bank run by Shrenis?
85.x:
During the Satavahana period, merchant and artisan guilds known as Shrenis functioned not only as professional organizations but also as banking institutions. Individuals deposited money with these guilds, and the deposited amount was utilized for trade and commercial activities. Historical records indicate that the usual rate of interest on such deposits was 12% per annum. Several inscriptions from the Satavahana and post-Satavahana periods mention permanent endowments deposited with guilds, the interest from which was used for maintaining Buddhist monasteries, feeding monks and supporting charitable activities. Hence, the correct answer is Option (1).
Exam Note:
• Banking Institutions – Shrenis (Guilds)
• Rate of Interest – 12% per annum
• Period – Satavahana

85.s: During the Satavahana period "Kolica Shreni" belongs to whom?
85.x:
During the Satavahana period, occupational guilds known as Shrenis played an important role in economic life. The Kolika (Kolica) Shreni was the guild of weavers. These guilds regulated production, maintained quality standards, organized trade and even functioned as banking institutions by accepting deposits and lending money. The textile industry flourished under the Satavahanas, and weaving guilds contributed significantly to both domestic trade and overseas commerce with the Roman Empire. Hence, the correct answer is Option (3).
Exam Note:
• Kolika Shreni – Weavers' Guild
• Period – Satavahana
• Importance – Textile production and trade

85.s: Which inscription mentions that Rishabhadatta deposited 2,000 Karshapanas in a guild of weavers belonging to Govardhana?

The famous Nasik Inscription of Rishabhadatta (Ushavadatta) records that he deposited 2,000 Karshapanas with the guild (Shreni) of weavers at Govardhana. The interest earned from this permanent deposit was utilized for charitable and religious purposes, especially for the maintenance of Buddhist monks. This inscription is one of the strongest pieces of evidence showing that guilds functioned as banking institutions in ancient India. It also demonstrates the advanced commercial organization that existed during the Satavahana period. Hence, the correct answer is Option (2).
Exam Note:
• Inscription – Nasik
• Deposit – 2,000 Karshapanas
• Guild – Weavers of Govardhana

83.x: 'Vihara' is a Sanskrit and Pali term referring to a Buddhist monastery. Literally meaning "a place for walking or wandering," it originally denoted temporary shelters used by itinerant monks, especially during the rainy season. 83.s:
With reference to ancient India, consider the following statements:
1. The concept of Stupa is Buddhist in origin.
2. Stupa was generally a repository of relics.
3. Stupa was a votive and commemorative structure in Buddhist tradition.
How many of the statements given above are correct?
83.x: Statement 1 is incorrect: A stupa is a mound-like structure that enshrines relics of the Buddha or Buddhist monks and is venerated in Buddhism, though the tradition itself predates Buddhism. In Vedic society, funerary practices such as pitramedha involved collecting ashes or bodily remains in an urn and constructing a memorial mound over it. References to such mound-like structures appear in the Vedic Samhitas, and the term 'estuka' in the Rigveda likely denoted any raised heap or pile on the ground. Over time, especially after the Buddha's passing, stupas became closely associated with Buddhism. Statement 2 is correct: Stupa contained relics regarded as sacred; the entire stupa came to be venerated as an emblem of both the Buddha and Buddhism. 83.s: Which of the following Stupas is the biggest in Andhra Pradesh?
83.x:
The Amaravati Stupa, also known as the Mahachaitya, is the largest Buddhist Stupa in Andhra Pradesh and one of the most magnificent Buddhist monuments in India. Originally constructed during the Satavahana period and enlarged under the Ikshvakus, the stupa became an important centre of Mahayana Buddhism. It was renowned for its exquisitely carved limestone railings, sculptured panels and narrative reliefs depicting scenes from the life of the Buddha and Jataka stories. The Amaravati School of Art, which developed around this monument, is internationally recognized for its artistic excellence and had a profound influence on Buddhist art in Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia. Although important stupas also exist at Bhattiprolu, Jaggayyapeta and Nagarjunakonda, the Amaravati Stupa is the largest among them. Hence, the correct answer is Option (2).
Exam Note:

• Period – Satavahana and Ikshvaku
• Famous For – Amaravati School of Art

They ruled parts of the Northern India including Magadha (current day Bihar). Hence statement 1 is correct. The Paramara dynasty ruled the western and central parts of India including Malwa, between the 9th and 14th century AD, before being captured by Delhi Sultanate rulers. Hence statement 2 is not correct. The Pushyabhutis of Thanesar (current day Haryana) ruled various parts of Northern India during the 6th and 7th century AD. Hence statement 3 is correct. The Maukharis dynasty ruled over parts of Uttar Pradesh and Magadha including Kannauj. The dynasty ruled till around 606 AD when it was reconquered by the Later Guptas. Hence statement 4 is correct. The Yadavas of Devagiri ruled from around 1187 to 1317 AD in western parts of India. Hence statement 5 is not correct. The Maitrakas of Valabhi ruled western and northern parts of current-day Gujarat during the late 5th century to late 8th century AD. Hence statement 6 is correct. Therefore option (b) is correct option.

26.s: Fa-hien (Faxian), the Chinese pilgrim, travelled to India during the reign of
26.x: Fa Xian (Fa Hien) was the first of the three renowned Chinese pilgrim travellers to visit India between the fifth and seventh centuries. The other two are Xuan Zang, or Hsuan Tsang (seventh century), and I-Qing, or I-tsing (seventh century). Fa Xian visited India during the Chandragupta II's reign for around nine years, probably 400-410 CE. The main purpose of his visit was to see the Buddha's land and collect Buddhist manuscripts from India. During his nine-year stay in India, he spent six years in the Gupta Empire. He stayed in Pataliputra for three years studying Sanskrit and copying Buddhist texts.

26.s: Fa-hien (Faxian), the Chinese pilgrim, travelled to India during the reign of
26.x: Fa-hien was a Chinese Buddhist monk and traveller who, travelled via the Silk Route through Central Asia to India and Sri Lanka. between about 399 and 412 CE, During this period, he stayed in India for about ten years, in the early part of the fifth century CE. On the other hand, the reign of the Gupta emperor Chandragupta II (Vikramaditya) is generally considered to be about 375–415 CE, and modern studies of Gupta history clearly mention that the Chinese traveller Fa-hien came to India during the reign of Chandragupta II, but he did not meet the emperor or the court; the main focus of his account is on Buddhistlife and monasteries.

26.s: The Hunas who entered India in the mid-fifth century were also known as:

xs: The Hunas were the **Hephthalites / White Huns** — option **(4)**.

xa: First attack: late **Kumaragupta I**, repulsed by prince **Skandagupta**.

26.s: Yashodharman's victory pillars at Sondani near Mandasor are generally dated to approximately:
26.x: Yashodharman's victory pillars at Sondani are dated to approximately 532 CE. They commemorate his victory over Mihirakula.

xa: He was defeated by **Yashodharman of Malwa**, **Narasimhagupta Baladitya** and the **Maukharis**.

26.s: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
o: The first Huna invasion occurred during Skandagupta's reign.

Skandagupta defeated the Hunas associated with the first Huna invasion.

26.tq: Recall which ruler defeated each Huna leader.
n: The first Huna invasion occurred during Skandagupta's reign. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #67 · pp 143-144]
Skandagupta defeated the Hunas. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #67 · pp 143-144]
Toramana led the second Huna invasion. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #67 · pp 143-144]
Mihirakula was defeated by Yashodharman. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #67 · pp 143-144]
xs: The incorrect statement is **Mihirakula was defeated by Skandagupta** — option **(3)**.
**Mihirakula** was defeated by **Yashodharman** of Malwa (with **Narasimhagupta Baladitya** and the Maukharis).
The others are correct: **Skandagupta** defeated the **first Huna invasion** (Bhitari Pillar); **Toramana** led the **second**.
xa: Mihirakula, son of Toramana, **persecuted Buddhists**.

26.s: Which inference most accurately follows from Yashodharman's victory over Mihirakula?
o: It brought Malwa permanently under direct Gupta administration.
It demonstrated the rise of a regional power and further weakened Gupta authority.

26.x: Yashodharman's victory did not revive the Gupta Empire; his own rise as a regional power undermined Gupta authority and reflected the wider process of political fragmentation.
26.tq: Distinguish the immediate military success from its broader political consequence.
xs: Yashodharman's victory showed the **rise of a regional power** and **further weakened Gupta authority** — option **(2)**.
The notes say his victory over the Hunas **did not revive the empire**.
xa: **Feudatories broke away**: Yashodharman; Bihar, Bengal, MP, Valabhi, Gujarat, western Malwa.
Rise of **Maukharis, Maitrakas, Later Guptas, Pushyabhutis** followed.
The break-up marks the move from a **single empire → regional kingdoms** + feudal order.

26.s: Which of the following inscription–ruler pairs is correctly matched?
26.x: The Gwalior inscription belongs to Mihirakula's rule. Sondani belongs to Yashodharman, the Maukhari seal to Sarvavarman and the Chausath Yogini inscription to Devapala.

Devapala was the ruler associated with the Chausath Yogini Temple Inscription. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-17]

xa: Toramana conquered western India up to **Eran** (near Bhopal).

26.s: Which ruling dynasty donated maximum villages to temples and Brahmins?

26.s: The absence of Gupta coins and inscriptions in western Malwa and Saurashtra after the reign of Skandagupta indicates:
o: The complete end of trade in eastern India
Expansion of Gupta control into western India
Loss of Gupta control over those territories
26.x: The absence of Gupta coins and inscriptions after Skandagupta in western Malwa and Saurashtra is evidence that these areas were no longer under effective Gupta control.
26.tq: Infer territorial change from the geographic distribution of material evidence.
xs: The absence of Gupta coins and inscriptions there shows **loss of Gupta control** over those territories — option **(3)**.
Notes: **No Gupta coins or inscriptions** in **western Malwa and Saurashtra** after **Skandagupta**.
xa: **Loss of western India** cost trade income and the **Roman silk trade**.
Those areas passed to powers like the **Maitrakas** (capital **Valabhi**).
⚠ **Nalanda** was founded by **Kumaragupta I** — unrelated to this evidence.

26.s: Which one of the following best explains the economic impact of the loss of western India on the Gupta Empire?
o: It brought the western feudatories under tighter imperial control.
It enabled the state to maintain a larger professional army.
It increased the inflow of gold from western ports.
It reduced trade income, including income connected with Roman silk trade.
26.x: The loss of western India reduced trade income and contributed to the loss of revenue from the Roman silk trade. This aggravated the financial and military weakness of the empire.
26.tq: Apply the economic-cause chain from territorial loss to declining state revenue.
xs: The **loss of western India** reduced **trade income**, including the **Roman silk trade** — option **(4)**.
With **land grants** also cutting revenue, the state could keep **no professional army** — so option (2) is the reverse.
Western feudatories **broke away** (Valabhi, Gujarat, western Malwa), not tighter control.
xa: Silk weavers migrated from **Gujarat to Malwa** (**AD 473**) and left their craft.
**No Gupta coins or inscriptions** appear in western Malwa and Saurashtra after **Skandagupta**.
The **Maitrakas** of **Valabhi** ruled Gujarat / western Malwa after the Guptas.

26.s: Which feature of later Gupta gold coins is cited as evidence of the empire's economic decline?
o: They contained less gold and more alloy
They were struck in larger numbers than ever before
They were replaced by Roman gold coins
They carried the portraits of Huna rulers
26.x: Later Gupta gold coins were debased, with less gold and more alloy, and coins gradually disappeared as payments shifted to land. There is no record of more coins being struck, of Roman coins replacing them, or of Huna portraits on Gupta coins.
26.tq: Decline evidence: debased coins (less gold, more alloy).
xs: Later Gupta gold coins had **less gold and more alloy** — debasement, option **(1)**.
The notes record no larger issues, Roman replacement or **Huna** portraits on Gupta coins.
xa: Coins **gradually vanish** post-Gupta → payments shifted to **land**.
Earlier, **Skandagupta's** gold coins showed **bow and arrow, Garuda standard, Lakshmi**.
Towns **decayed** as trade revenue fell.

26.s: Gupta land grants contributed to the empire's decline by encouraging the growth of:
26.x: Land grants encouraged feudatories, and hereditary governors grew into autonomous feudatories rather than strengthening central control.
xa: Gupta administration rested on feudatories, unlike the **centralised Mauryas**.
UPSC **2021**: **Guptas of Magadha, Pushyabhutis of Thanesar, Maukharis of Kannauj, Maitrakas of Valabhi**.
⚠ Not the **Paramaras** of Malwa or **Yadavas** of Devagiri (both later).

26.s: In the later Gupta period, land grants weakened the state's ability to keep a professional army by reducing its:
26.x: Land grants reduced the revenue available to the state, which weakened its ability to maintain a professional army.
xa: **Loss of western India** cost trade income and the **Roman silk trade**.
Silk weavers migrated from Gujarat to Malwa (**AD 473**) and left their craft.
Coins gradually vanished post-Gupta → **payments shifted to land**; towns decayed.

26.s: Which invasion is identified as a cause of the decline of the Gupta Empire?
26.x: Huna invasions, growth of feudatories and loss of western trade revenue were causes of Gupta decline; the Arab invasion was not.
xa: **Weak successors** after Skandagupta; last ruler **Vishnugupta** (**c. 540–550 CE**).

Later gold coins show **less gold, more alloy**.

He was the first mathematician to systematically study cyclic quadrilaterals and developed formulas for calculating their area, diagonals, and related geometric properties. His major works include the Brahmasphutasiddhanta and Khandakhadyaka, which dealt with planetary motions, eclipses, conjunctions, and other astronomical phenomena. In the Brahmasphutasiddhanta, he also hinted at gravitational attraction. Brahmagupta further referred to svayamvaha yantras (self-moving machines), reflecting an early awareness of the concept of perpetual motion. His works greatly influenced the development of mathematics and astronomy in India and beyond. Option (a) is incorrect: Aryabhata (c. 476 CE), often regarded as the Father of Indian Algebra and one of India's earliest astronomers, probably lived at Pataliputra. He authored the Aryabhatiya and the now-lost Aryabhatasiddhanta. His contributions laid the foundations of Indian mathematics and astronomy. Major Contributions: Explained that the Earth rotates on its axis and accurately estimated the length of a year as about 365.25868 days. Provided the first scientific explanation of solar and lunar eclipses, rejecting mythical interpretations. Developed sine tables and laid the foundation of Trigonometry. 25.x: Option (a) is correct: Ajanta Caves are located in the Aurangabad district of Maharashtra and are carved out of a steep cliff on the left bank of the Waghora River in the Ajanta hills. The complex comprises around 30 caves, including unfinished ones, of which five (Caves 9, 10, 19, 26, and 29) are chaityagrihas (prayer halls), while the rest serve as viharas (monasteries). Of these, 5 caves are associated with Hinayana Buddhism, while the remaining 25 are associated with the Mahayana tradition. The paintings in the caves were first outlined in red and then filled with other colours, depicting themes primarily from Jataka tales along with references to Chinese travellers such as Faxian and Xuanzang. The artwork follows the fresco technique, in which pigments are applied to freshly laid, damp lime plaster, allowing the colours to bond firmly with the surface and remain vibrant over time. The Ajanta Caves were inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1983. Option (b) is incorrect: Sanchi is located in the Raisen district of Madhya Pradesh, situated on an elevated plateau just west of the Betwa River. It has been an important centre of Buddhist faith, with the Great Stupa serving as its focal point since Ashoka's construction in the 3 rd century BCE. Originally built using bricks during Ashoka's reign, the Great Stupa was later encased in stone, and several architectural additions were made over time, enhancing its structure and significance. 25.x: Visakhadatta: Author of Mudrarakshasa and Devichandraguptam. The Mudrarakshasa, written by Visakadatta, is a Sanskrit drama. Although written during the Gupta period, it describes how Chandragupta, with Kautilya's assistance, overthrew the Nandas. It also gives a picture of the socio-economic conditions under the Mauryas. Devichandraguptam narrates the contest for the throne between Ramagupta and Chandragupta-II • Varahamihira: A mathematician and astronomer of the Gupta period. He composed Pancha Siddhantika, the five astronomical systems. One of these was Romaka Sidhanta, which was influenced by Greek ideas. His other works include the Brihadsamhita and the Brihadjataka. • Charaka: A court physician of King Kanishka, who authored Charaka Samhita, an authoritative treatise on Ayurveda. • Brahmagupta: He was a distinguished Indian mathematician and astronomer who made major contributions to geometry and astronomy. He was the first to develop formulas for the area and diagonals of a cyclic quadrilateral and other related geometric properties. His notable works include the Brahmasphutasiddhanta and Khandakhadyaka, which dealt with planetary motions, eclipses, conjunctions, and other astronomical phenomena. He also hinted at gravitational attraction and mentioned svayamvaha yantras (self-moving machines), reflecting an early awareness of perpetual motion.

With reference to the history of ancient India, Bhavabhuti, Hastimalla and Kshemeshvara were famous
27.x: Bhavabhuti was an eminent playwright and poet of the 8 th century CE, regarded as one of the greatest figures in Sanskrit drama. His celebrated works—Malatimadhava, Mahaviracharita, and Uttararamacharita—are often considered comparable to Kalidasa's. Known as the "Poet of Karuna Rasa," he is believed to have served as the court poet of King Yashovarman. In the later period of regional states (c. 800–1200 CE), playwrights such as Kshemeshvara and Hastimalla gained prominence. While earlier plays, such as those of Bhavabhuti, focused on subtle dramatic elements and emotional depth, the works of Kshemeshvara, Hastimalla, and their contemporaries like Murari and Rajashekhara emphasised sophisticated poetic and linguistic techniques. This shift highlighted a literary culture that valued reading and textual appreciation over theatrical presentation (Romila Thapar, A History of India).

Hastimalla is a Kannada poet and playwright during the reign of Hoysalas. Kshemeshvara (990-c. 1070 CE) was an 11th-century Sanskrit poet from Kashmir in India. One of the important works attributed to him is Dasavatar Charita.

27.s:
Consider the following statements:
1.
Assertion (A): Harshavardhana convened the Prayag Assembly.

Reason (R): He wanted to popularise only the Mahayana form of Buddhism. Options:

Both A and R are individually true, but R is NOT a correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
27.x: Assertion (A) is correct because Harshavardhana held the quinquennial Maha Moksha Parishad at Prayagraj. However, Reason (R) is incorrect. The Prayag Assembly was primarily a large charitable and religious gathering where Harsha paid homage to Buddha, Surya, and Shiva on successive days and distributed donations to followers of different faiths, including Buddhists, Brahmanas, and Jains. The assembly specifically associated with promoting Mahayana Buddhism and honouring Xuanzang was the Kannauj Assembly. Therefore, the use of the word "only" makes the Reason factually incorrect.

27.s: The place in U.P. where Harsh Vardhana organised the Buddha mega convention –
Harsha's Kannauj Assembly, attended by rulers of 20 countries, was held in:

n: Rulers of 20 countries attended the Kannauj Assembly. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #144 · pp 250-252]
Brahmins attended the Kannauj Assembly. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #144 · pp 250-252]
Shramanas attended the Kannauj Assembly. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #144 · pp 250-252]

Harsha held a religious assembly at Kannauj. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #144 · pp 250-252]

n: Rulers of 20 countries attended the Kannauj Assembly. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #144 · pp 250-252]

Figures on the Kannauj assembly **differ across sources**.

27.s: Harsha's Prayag assembly was held every:

xa: Prayag eclecticism: **Buddha, Sun and Shiva** worshipped on successive days.
⚠ **Kannauj** (643) = one-time Mahayana debate.

27.s: Which sequence correctly represents the stages of Harsha's religious life?
27.x: Harsha was initially a devout Saiva, later followed Hinayana Buddhism and was subsequently converted to Mahayana Buddhism.

xs: Harsha moved **Saivism → Hinayana Buddhism → Mahayana Buddhism** — option **(2)** is correct.

27.s: Which of the following statements about Harsha's punishments is NOT correct?

**Sriparvata vihara** lacked patronage.

27.x: The Vakataka dynasty was an ancient Indian royal dynasty that ruled over the central and southern parts of India from the 3rd century CE to the end of the 5th century and the beginning of the 6th century CE. The founder of this dynasty was Vindhyashakti, whose successor was Pravarasena I, who is also considered the actual founder of the Vakataka dynasty. During the time of Pravarasena I, the boundaries of the Vakataka dynasty reached from Bundelkhand in north to Deccan (including modern Hyderabad) in the south. The Vakataka rulers expanded their territory to include vast regions under their influence. Among the rulers of the Vakataka dynasty, Pravarasena I assumed the title of Samrat (Emperor) and performed several Ashvamedha Yajnas (horse sacrifices) and Vedic rituals. According to the Puranas, he is referred to as Pravira. Thus, all the given statements are correct.

86.s: Which inscription contains the 12 Sutras to be followed during the construction of Tataka?

The inscription demonstrates the advanced knowledge of irrigation engineering that existed in medieval Andhra. It is one of the most frequently asked inscriptions in APPSC examinations. Hence, the correct answer is Option (4).

• Importance – Twelve Sutras of Tank Construction

28.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The Cholas defeated Pandya and Chera rulers and established their domination over peninsular India in early medieval times.
2. The Cholas sent an expedition against Sailendra empire of South‑east Asia and conquered some of the areas. Which of these statements is/are correct?
28.x: Statement 1 is correct: Vijayalaya, a feudatory of the Pallavas in Uraiyur, conquered the Kaveri Delta from the Muttaraiyar. He captured Thanjavur (Tanjore) in 850 CE and established the Chola kingdom. Vijayalaya accepted the overlordship of Pallavas. Vijayalaya's son, Aditya I (c. 871 - 907 CE), expanded the kingdom by defeating both Pallavas and Pandyas. He defeated the last Pallava king, Aparajita, annexed their territory and put an end to the Pallava kingdom. He also weakened the Pandyas. Statement 2 is correct: Rajendra Chola led a naval expedition against the Sri Vijaya Empire in Southeast Asia. The empire was led by the Sailendra dynasty and extended over the Malay peninsula, Sumatra, Java and the neighbouring islands. The expeditions led to the conquest of Kadaram and several other places in the Malay Peninsula and Sumatra.

28.s: Who among the following led a successful military campaign against the kingdom of Srivijaya, the powerful maritime State, which ruled the Malay Peninsula, Sumatra, Java and the neighbouring islands?
28.x: Option (c) is correct: Rajendra Chola (1012- 1044 CE): He led the naval expedition against the Sri Vijaya empire of Southeast Asia. The empire was led by the Sailendra dynasty and extended over the Malay peninsula, Sumatra, Java and the neighbouring islands. The expeditions led to the conquest of Kadaram and several other places in the Malay Peninsula and Sumatra. He also led the expedition up to the Godavari River and sent a victorious expedition to north India. The Chola army crossed the Ganges by defeating a number of rulers on its way. To commemorate this successful north Indian campaign, Rajendra founded the capital near the mouth of the Kaveri River and named it Gangaikondacholapuram. He also constructed the famous Shiva temple in that city. Rajendra Chola also conquered southern Sri Lanka, effectively bringing the entire island under Chola rule during his reign. Rajendra Chola assumed the titles, such as:  Mudikonda Cholan (the crowned Chola)  Gangaikonda Cholam (Chola who conquered the Ganga)  Kadaramkondan (conqueror of Kadaram)  Pandita Cholan (scholarly Cholan) Option (a) is incorrect: The Rashtrakuta Dynasty, founded by Dantivarman, ruled parts of the Indian subcontinent from the 6 th to 10 th CE. Amoghavarsha I ruled the Rashtrakuta dynasty for 64 years (c. 814 – 878 CE). He was a follower of Jainism, and his reign was known for cultural development. He patronised many scholars, including Mahaviracharya, Jinasena (teacher of Amoghavarsha), Virasena, Shakataya

30.s: Which Article of the Constitution recognises the Gram Sabha under the Panchayati Raj framework?
30.x: Article 243A deals with the Gram Sabha. Article 243C concerns the composition of Panchayats, Article 243D reservations, and Article 243E duration.

**243C** = direct election; **243D** = **1/3** reservation for women; **243E** = **5-year** term.

30.s: Under the 73rd Amendment, the intermediate tier of Panchayats may be omitted in a State whose population does not exceed:
30.x: The intermediate tier is optional in a State with a population not exceeding twenty lakh.

30.s: Which Article of the Constitution reserves not less than one-third of Panchayat seats for women?
30.x: Article 243D reserves one-third of Panchayat seats and chairperson posts for women, unlike the Chola village assemblies, which had no quota for women.

30.s: Participation in Chola sabhas was associated with:
30.x: Sabha participation was tied to propertied, Vedic-learned Brahmins, so the system is criticised as elitist; it was not based on universal adult franchise.

30.s: Which one of the following statements is NOT correctly matched?
o: Nattar — direct universal adult franchise body under the 73rd Amendment
Burton Stein — segmentary state and local autonomy
Nilakanta Sastri — Chola local self-government as grassroots democracy

xa: PRIs are **directly elected** (**Art. 243C**) under the **73rd Amendment**.

30.s: Unlike the 73rd Amendment, Chola village assemblies had:
30.x: Chola assemblies had no women's quota, whereas Article 243D reserves at least one-third of seats for women.

30.s: Which historian described the Chola state as a 'segmentary state'?
30.x: Burton Stein called it a segmentary state where local autonomy stayed intact at the periphery; Nilakanta Sastri spoke of grassroots democracy.

29.s: Under the Cholas, the successor (yuvaraja) was generally named:
o: During the king's own lifetime, and made co-regent
By the nadu assembly in every case
29.x: Chola kings named the yuvaraja in their own lifetime and made him co-regent; Rajendra I became co-regent in 1012 and king in 1014.

29.s: Chola royal orders generally consisted of:
o: A Sanskrit preamble followed by a Tamil operative part
Tamil genealogy followed by a Sanskrit grant
29.x: The royal orders had a Sanskrit preamble containing genealogy and conquests, followed by the Tamil operative portion.

The Sanskrit preamble gave the **genealogy and conquests**. The order was neither in one language only nor in the reverse arrangement.

The **Leiden plates** follow the same pattern: **Sanskrit** genealogy and a **Tamil** grant.

29.s: Chola inscriptions praised the king as a warrior, a patron of the arts and the protector of:
29.x: Chola kings were compared to gods, their images were installed beside deities, and inscriptions praised them as warriors, patrons of art and protectors of varnashrama dharma.
xa: Inscriptional titles: **ko**, **perumal**, **raja-rajadhiraja**, **ko-konmai kondan**.
**Marco Polo** noted bodyguards ready to die for the king.
**Rajaraja I** directed the **sabhas of Cholamandalam** to perform services for the **Brihadeeswara** temple.

29.s: In which year did Rajendra I become co-regent?
29.x: Rajendra I was made co-regent in 1012 and became king in 1014.

29.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Chola kingship?
o: The successor was named only after the king's death.
Images of kings and queens were placed beside deities.
Royal orders had a Sanskrit preamble and a Tamil operative part.
Rajaraja I was called Ulakalanda Perumal.
29.x: The Chola king named his successor in his own lifetime and made him co-regent; the other statements are correct.

29.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Adhikari — Royal officer supervising local bodies
Nattar — Members of the royal court of justice
29.x: An adhikari was a royal officer supervising local bodies. Perundaram were the highest officials, sirudaram were lower officials, and nattar were members of the nadu assembly.
29.tq: Start with the functional description of adhikari and reject reversed ranks or substituted institutions.
xs: **Adhikari** = **royal officer supervising local bodies** is correctly matched, so option **(3)** is correct.
**Perundaram** were the **highest** officials, not lower ones, and **Sirudaram** were the **lower** officials.
**Nattar** were members of the **nadu assembly**. The royal court of justice was the **Dharmasana**.
xa: ⚠ Trap: **Perundaram** = highest, **Sirudaram** = lower.
**Tirumandira-olai** wrote down the king's oral orders; **Olai-nayagam** countersigned them.
Revenue department = **Puravu-varitinaikkalam / Shrikaranam**.

29.s: Who wrote down the king’s oral orders on palm leaf in the Chola administration?
29.x: The tirumandira-olai was the royal secretary who recorded the king’s oral orders on palm leaf.
29.tq: Distinguish the drafting official from the checking official.
xs: The **Tirumandira-olai** was the royal secretary who wrote the king's **oral orders** on **palm leaf (olai)**, so option **(4)** is correct.
The **Olai-nayagam** was the **chief secretary** who checked and countersigned orders.
A **Samanta** was a restored vassal king, and **Rajapratinidhi** was the title of the Vengi viceroys.
xa: ⚠ Trap: **Tirumandira-olai** writes, **Olai-nayagam** countersigns.
Orders were **bilingual**: a **Sanskrit preamble** (genealogy, conquests) and a **Tamil** operative part.
**Perundaram** = highest officials; **Sirudaram** = lower officials.

29.s: The principal function of the olai-nayagam was to:
29.x: The olai-nayagam, or chief secretary, checked and countersigned royal orders before they were sent to officials.
29.tq: Ask who would perform the final verification before dispatch.
xs: The **Olai-nayagam** (chief secretary) **checked and countersigned** royal orders before they went to officials, so option **(4)** is correct.
Water from tanks was distributed by the **eri variyam**, revenue in kind was **Kadamai**, and the **Kaikkolar** were infantry regiments.
xa: The **Tirumandira-olai** wrote down the king's **oral orders** on palm leaf.

**Dharmasana** = royal court of justice.

29.s: In Chola administration, the term 'Sirudaram' denoted the:
29.x: Sirudaram were the lower officials; Perundaram were the highest officials.

29.s: The Chola royal officer who supervised local bodies was the:
29.x: The Adhikari was the royal officer supervising local bodies; Nattar were members of the nadu assembly.

29.s: In Chola administration, the 'Nattar' were:
29.x: Nattar were the members of the nadu assembly; the highest officials were Perundaram.

29.s: A ‘Samanta’ in the Chola political system was:
o: A royal secretary who countersigned orders
A tank committee member elected by villagers
A temple servant given tax-free land
A defeated king restored after accepting overlordship, tribute and military obligations

29.tq: Use the political relationship rather than the official title alone.
xs: A **Samanta** was a **defeated king restored** on accepting **overlordship**, paying **tribute** and giving **military help**, so option **(4)** is correct.

xa: Some provinces were **samanta** (vassal) territories paying tribute; others were **annexed principalities**.
**Burton Stein** called the Chola state **"segmentary"**.
The **Leiden plates** seal carries the **Chola tiger**, **Pandya fish** and **Chera bow**.

29.s: Burton Stein described the Chola state as a:
29.x: Burton Stein used the concept of a segmentary state, while K.A. Nilakanta Sastri presented a more centralised picture.

Provinces mixed **annexed principalities** and **samanta** tributaries.
The bureaucracy weakened after **Kulottunga I** as local chieftains gained power.

29.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Chola administrative units?
o: Nadu was a unit above the Ur.
Kottam or Valanadu was a unit below the Nadu.

29.s: Chola provincial territories that were not annexed but paid tribute were known as:
29.x: Chola provincial territories included annexed principalities and samanta or vassal territories that paid tribute.
xa: A **samanta** was a defeated king restored on accepting **overlordship**.
**Burton Stein** called the Chola state **"segmentary"**, with local autonomy intact at the periphery.
Vengi viceroys (**Rajapratinidhi**) were **Kulottunga I's sons**.

29.s: Mummudicholamandalam referred to:

The **Kaveri delta** was **Cholamandalam**, and the former **Pallava** country was **Jayankondacholamandalam** (Tondaimandalam).
xa: **Rajaraja I** took **northern Sri Lanka** and the **Maldives**.
**Rajendra I** went on to take **all of Sri Lanka**.
Chola overseas footholds: **Sri Lanka**, **Maldives**, **Kadaram/Srivijaya**.

29.x: Jayankondacholamandalam was the former Pallava Tondaimandalam; Mummudicholamandalam was northern Sri Lanka.

29.x: Kulottunga I placed his sons in Vengi as viceroys called Rajapratinidhi.

o: Kasu – rural tax collected in cash

**Vetti** (also **muttaiyal**, **kudimai**) = forced labour owed to the state.

29.s: The normal rate of Chola land revenue was approximately:

xs: Chola land revenue was normally **1/6th of the produce**, so option **(3)** is correct.

**Kadamai** = land revenue collected in kind.

**Kasu** = gold coin.

29.s: The Chola land tax of one-sixth of the produce was comparable to the standard associated with the
29.x: The Chola rate of one-sixth matched the standard associated with the Pallavas and Kakatiyas. The Mughals and Sher Shah are associated with one-third, while the Gupta rate was about one-seventh.

xs: The Chola land tax of **1/6** matched the standard of the **Pallavas and Kakatiyas**, so option **(4)** is correct.
The **Mughals** and **Sher Shah** took **one-third**, and the **Gupta** rate was about **1/7**.

Chola revenue was paid in **cash, kind or both**.
**Kadamai** = revenue in kind; **Antarayam** = cash tax.

29.s: Besides being landholders, employers and lenders, Chola temples served as venues for meetings of the:

xa: The bureaucracy weakened after **Kulottunga I**.

29.x: Kadamai was land revenue in kind; Antarayam was the rural tax in cash.

29.x: Ayam meant royal dues; Irai was the tax on land, Kasu the gold coin and Eccoru the duty to feed visiting officials.

29.s: The land survey of the Chola empire is associated with:

**Brahmadeya** = rent-free land granted to **Brahmins**, run by a **sabha**.

29.s: In Chola land rights (kani), 'karanmai' meant:

xs: **Eripatti** land financed the **repair and maintenance** of village tanks, so option **(1)** is correct.

xa: **Eripatti** was a correct pair in **UPSC 2016**.

29.s: 'Pallichchandam' land in the Chola period was granted to:
29.x: Pallichchandam was land given to Jaina institutions; Shalabhoga was land for a school.

29.s: 'Shalabhoga' land in the Chola period was meant for the maintenance of a:

29.s: Rajaraja I was described by the title ‘Ulakalanada Perumal’ because he was regarded as:
o: the king who abolished hereditary officials
the ruler who measured the earth, like Vishnu’s three strides
the conqueror of the entire island of Sri Lanka
the patron who built all the major Chola temples

29.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?

Loyal bodyguard troops sworn to die with the king

88.s: Which Kakatiya ruler shifted the capital from Hanamkonda to Orugallu?
88.x:
Rudradeva (Prataparudra I) was the first powerful independent ruler of the Kakatiya dynasty. During his reign, he shifted the capital from Hanamkonda to Orugallu (present-day Warangal). The new capital was strategically stronger and better suited for administration and defence. Rudradeva strengthened the fortifications of Orugallu and laid the foundation for its development into one of the greatest capitals in medieval South India. Later rulers, particularly Ganapatideva and Rani Rudramadevi, further expanded and beautified Warangal, making it the political and cultural centre of the Kakatiya kingdom. Hence, the correct answer is Option (2).
Exam Note:
• Capital shifted to – Orugallu (Warangal)
• Ruler – Rudradeva
• Earlier Capital – Hanamkonda

88.s: Which ruler issued the famous Motupalli Charter?
88.x:
Ganapatideva, one of the greatest rulers of the Kakatiya dynasty, issued the famous Motupalli Charter to encourage overseas trade. The charter granted commercial privileges, protection and tax concessions to foreign merchants visiting the port of Motupalli. It assured traders of safety and promoted maritime commerce with countries such as China, Sri Lanka, Arabia and Southeast Asia. The Motupalli Charter reflects the Kakatiyas' farsighted economic policy and highlights the importance of maritime trade in medieval Andhra. Hence, the correct answer is Option (2).
Exam Note:
• Issued by – Ganapatideva
• Charter – Motupalli Charter
• Purpose – Promotion of Overseas Trade

88.s: Who among the following bears the title 'Rayagajakesari'?
88.x:
Prataparudra II, the last great ruler of the Kakatiya dynasty, bore the title "Rayagajakesari." The title literally means "a lion among kings and elephants," symbolizing bravery, military strength and royal supremacy. Prataparudra successfully defended the Kakatiya kingdom against several invasions before finally being defeated by Ulugh Khan in 1323 CE. His reign represents the final phase of Kakatiya political power. Hence, the correct answer is Option (4).
Exam Note:
• Title – Rayagajakesari
• Ruler – Prataparudra II

88.s: Who among the following was awarded the title 'Founder of Kakati Rajya'?
88.x:
Recherla Rudra was one of the most distinguished military commanders of the Kakatiya kingdom. After the death of Rudradeva, he played a crucial role in protecting the kingdom from external invasions and internal rebellions. During the captivity of Ganapatideva by the Yadavas, Recherla Rudra safeguarded the kingdom and later helped restore Kakatiya authority. For his immense contribution in strengthening and consolidating the Kakatiya kingdom, he was honored with the title "Kakati Rajya Sthapanacharya" (Founder/Restorer of the Kakatiya Kingdom). His services were instrumental in transforming the Kakatiyas into a powerful medieval empire. Hence, the correct answer is Option (4).
Exam Note:
• Recherla Rudra → Kakati Rajya Sthapanacharya
• Important general of Ganapatideva

88.s: Who were the kings who had the title 'Mahamandaleswara'?
88.x:
The title "Mahamandaleswara" literally means "Great Lord of Provinces". During the early phase of their political career, the Kakatiya rulers, while serving as feudatories under the Western Chalukyas, frequently used this title. It denoted powerful provincial governors or feudatory chiefs controlling large territories. Even after attaining independence, the title continued to appear in several Kakatiya inscriptions as a mark of prestige and authority. Hence, the correct answer is Option (4).
Exam Note:
• Mahamandaleswara → Prominent title of early Kakatiyas

88.s: To whom were the Kakatiyas feudatories before establishing their independent kingdom?
88.x:
The early Kakatiyas first served as feudatories of the Rashtrakutas. After the decline of the Rashtrakutas, they became vassals of the Western Chalukyas of Kalyani. Later rulers such as Prola II and Rudradeva (Prataparudra I) asserted independence and laid the foundation for the powerful Kakatiya kingdom with Orugallu (Warangal) as its capital. Thus, the Kakatiyas rose gradually from feudatories to one of the greatest dynasties of medieval Andhra. Hence, the correct answer is Option (4).

• Rashtrakutas → Western Chalukyas → Independent Kakatiyas

The Sanigaram Inscription belongs to the reign of Rudradeva and throws light on the consolidation of Kakatiya authority after they emerged as an independent power. The Anumakonda Inscription is associated with Prolaraja II and provides valuable information regarding the early expansion of the Kakatiya kingdom from Hanamkonda. The Bayyaram Inscription was issued by Mailamba, the sister of Ganapatideva. It is one of the most important sources for reconstructing the early genealogy of the Kakatiya dynasty and mentions several early rulers. The Motupalli Inscription belongs to Ganapatideva. Issued at the famous port of Motupalli, it guaranteed protection and commercial privileges to foreign merchants, encouraging overseas trade and making Motupalli one of the most important ports of medieval Andhra. Thus, the correct matching is a–IV, b–III, c–I, d–II, corresponding to Option (1).

• Motupalli Inscription – Foreign trade and merchant privileges.

89.s: Kakatiya Pratapa Rudra was held captive by whom at the end of his life?
89.x:
Prataparudra II, the last great ruler of the Kakatiya dynasty, faced repeated invasions from the Delhi Sultanate. In 1323 CE, Ulugh Khan (the future Muhammad bin Tughlaq) led the Delhi Sultanate army against Warangal. After a prolonged siege, Warangal fell into the hands of the Sultanate, and Prataparudra was taken prisoner. According to historical accounts, while being taken to Delhi, Prataparudra is believed to have ended his life on the banks of the Narmada River. The fall of Warangal marked the end of Kakatiya rule and paved the way for the emergence of regional powers such as the Musunuri Nayakas. Hence, the correct answer is Option (3).
Exam Note:
• Last Kakatiya Ruler – Prataparudra II
• Captured by – Ulugh Khan
• Year – 1323 CE

Motupalli was one of the most important medieval seaports of Andhra Pradesh. Historical records and literary works refer to it by another name, Deseeyakkonda Pattanam. 91.s: The main profession of Jayapa who wrote Nritta Ratnavali?
91.x:
Jayapa Senani, the celebrated author of Nritta Ratnavali, served as Gajasahini (Commander of the Elephant Corps) under the Kakatiya ruler Ganapatideva. Although he was a military commander, Jayapa possessed exceptional knowledge of dance and music. His Nritta Ratnavali is one of the most authoritative medieval treatises on Indian dance and describes Marga and Desi dance traditions, dance postures, mudras and performance techniques. The famous dance sculptures of the Ramappa Temple closely follow the principles laid down in this work, making it an invaluable source for the study of medieval Indian dance. Hence, the correct answer is Option (2).
Exam Note:
• Author – Jayapa Senani
• Position – Gajasahini
• Famous Work – Nritta Ratnavali

91.s: Which of the following is the city described in Vallabhamatya's Kridabhiramam?
91.x:
Kridabhiramam, written by Vallabhamatya, is one of the important literary sources for the history of medieval Andhra. The work gives a vivid description of Orugallu (Warangal), the capital of the Kakatiya kingdom. It describes:
• Fortifications and gateways
• Markets and commercial centres
• Temples and public buildings
• Social life, festivals and cultural activities Because of these detailed descriptions, historians use Kridabhiramam as an important source for reconstructing the urban history of the Kakatiya period. Hence, the correct answer is Option (3).
Exam Note:
• Kridabhiramam → Vallabhamatya
• Describes → Warangal (Orugallu)

93.s: Arrange the following Reddi rulers in chronological order. A. Kumaragiri Reddi B. Anavema Reddi C. Anavota Reddi D. Pedakomati Vema Reddi
93.x:
The Reddi Kingdom was founded by Prolaya Vema Reddi after the decline of the Kakatiyas. The rulers mentioned in this question succeeded one another in the following order: Anavota Reddi succeeded Prolaya Vema Reddi and consolidated the newly established kingdom. He was followed by Anavema Reddi, who further strengthened the administration and expanded the kingdom. After him came Kumaragiri Reddi, who was an able administrator and a great patron of literature, music and dance. His court became an important centre of Telugu culture. Finally, Pedakomati Vema Reddi ascended the throne. He was both a scholar and a capable ruler and continued the literary traditions established by his predecessors. Therefore, the correct chronological order is: Anavota Reddi → Anavema Reddi → Kumaragiri Reddi → Pedakomati Vema Reddi Hence, the correct answer is Option (4).
Exam Note:
• Founder – Prolaya Vema Reddi
• Capital – Addanki (later Kondavidu)
• Greatest literary patron – Kumaragiri Reddi

92.x:
After the decline of the Kakatiya Empire, several regional kingdoms emerged in Andhra Pradesh, among which the Reddi Kingdom and the Recherla Velama Kingdom became two powerful political forces. Both dynasties frequently competed for control over fertile territories and strategic trade routes. The Battle of Bhimavaram was fought between the Reddi rulers and the Velamas. In this battle, the Reddis achieved a decisive victory and successfully drove the Velamas out of the Palnadu region, thereby restoring their authority over the area. The victory greatly strengthened the Reddi Kingdom and enabled it to consolidate its political influence in Coastal Andhra. It also checked the expansionist ambitions of the Recherla Velamas for some time. Hence, the correct answer is Option (2).

• Importance – Strengthened Reddi control over Palnadu

87.s: Who were the ‘Ashtadiggajas’ in the court of Krishnadeva Raya?
87.x: The governance of Krishnadeva Raya is known as the golden age of Telugu literature. The ‘Ashtadiggajas’ were the eight great poets and scholars of Telugu in the Court of Vijayanagara. Telugu literature reached its peak during the reign of Krishnadeva Raya. He assumed the title ‘Andhra Bhoja’. ‘Peddana’ was ranked as the foremost of the 'Ashtadiggaja'. He had mastery over two languages, Telugu and Sanskrit. Krishnadeva Raya was an accomplished poet and writer. He authored ‘Amuktamalyada,’ which is considered as one of the five top Telugu epics. Krishnadeva Raya had a great interest in art and construction work. He is credited with the construction of Nagalpuram city. The Portuguese traveller Domingo Paes visited Vijayanagara during his reign. Babur mentioned Krishnadeva Raya as the most powerful of all the rulers of India in his autobiography.

87.x:
Ketana was a disciple of Tikkana and authored Andhra Bhasha Bhushanam, regarded as one of the earliest extant works on Telugu grammar. Marana translated the Markandeya Purana into Telugu under the patronage of the Kakatiyas, making it one of the earliest Telugu Puranas. Tikkana, one of the Kavitrayam, composed Nirvachanottara Ramayanam and translated fifteen parvas of the Mahabharata into Telugu. Manchena authored Keyurabahu Charitra, an important Telugu literary work based on courtly themes. Thus, the correct sequence is a–III, b–I, c–II, d– IV, corresponding to Option (2).

Assertion (A): Alauddin Khalji introduced price control in Delhi.
Reason (R) : He wanted to pay lower wages to the artisans building his palaces in Delhi.
Select the correct answer from the code given below :
o: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not a correct
32.x: Alauddin Khalji introduced the price control policy. He had appointed efficient officials for the success of his policy. He appointed Malik Kabool as Shehena, or inspector of the market, and provided him with a large detachment of cavalry and infantry to help him in the work. He gave him extensive authority. He controlled all the merchants and informed the king about fluctuations in price and general situation of the market. Barani describes the purpose of market reform to support a vast army against Mongols attacks and to control the potential rebellion by Hindus. He had nothing to do with paying low wages to the artisans. Hence, Assertion (A) is true, while Reason (R) is false.

32.s: The principal objective of Alauddin Khalji's market control regulations was to:
o: increase the profits of grain merchants in Delhi
maintain a large standing army on low, fixed salaries by keeping prices low
raise revenue for the construction of mosques and madrasas
promote free trade with Central Asian merchants
32.x: Prices of daily goods were lowered and fixed so that soldiers could live comfortably on low, fixed pay; military need shaped the economic policy. The regulations curbed merchants rather than enriching them, and they were not aimed at religious building or free trade.
32.tq: Cheap goods for a cheap army (APPSC G2 2017).
xs: The aim was to **maintain a large standing army on low, fixed salaries** by keeping prices low — so option **(2)** is correct.
Soldiers could live comfortably on low pay (APPSC G2 **2017** key); **military need shaped economic policy**.
The controls curbed merchants and **ended monopolies** — not merchant profit or free trade.
xa: Criticism: the controls may have been **confined to Delhi** and hurt **merchants and peasants**.
Mubarak Shah abolished them after **1316**.

32.x: The Lagaan system of Alauddin Khalji was not applicable across the state. Alauddin had taken away the right to charge taxes from traditional officers (Khut, Muqaddam and Chaudhary) and also abolished their privileges. He started charging tax on them also. As a result of which, there was little difference between Khut (Landlord) and Balahar (ordinary farmer/agricultural labourer).

32.s: The attempt of Alauddin Khalji to control the market prices
32.x: The attempt by Alauddin Khalji to control the market prices was highly successful. Alauddin Khalji's measures to control the market prices were one of the most important policy initiatives of his reign. Since Alauddin wanted to maintain a vast standing army, he therefore, lowered the prices of the commodities of daily use. He established separate markets in Delhi, (a) Grain Market (Mandi) (b) Clothes and Groceries market for clothes, sugar, dry fruits, butter and oil (c) Market for horses, slaves, cattle etc. (d) Market for miscellaneous commodities. To ensure implementation, each market was under the control of a superintendent called Shahna-i-Mandi who was assisted by an intelligence officer. Apart from Shahnai-Mandi Alauddin received daily reports of the market from two other independent sources, barids (intelligence officer) and munhiyans (Secret spies).

33.s: The Sultan of Delhi who is reputed to have built the biggest network of canals in India was
33.x: Feroz Shah Tughlaq (r. 1351–1388) is known for constructing the largest canal network among the Delhi Sultans. 33.x: Muhammad bin Tughlaq introduced a new gold coin known as the Dinar (called Dinar by Ibn Battuta). He also issued a silver coin called the Adli and undertook important currency reforms during his reign. Muhammad bin Tughlaq introduced a token currency around 1330 CE to tackle the shortage of silver in the royal treasury. Drawing inspiration from the currency system used in China under Kublai Khan, he issued copper coins (Jitals) and set their value at the same level as silver tankas. However, since the concept of token currency was unfamiliar in India and there was no effective control over minting, counterfeit coins were produced on a large scale. The widespread forgery disrupted the economy and undermined public confidence in the currency. Consequently, the Sultan withdrew the scheme and agreed to exchange the copper coins for silver coins.

33.s: Muhammad-Bin-Tughluq had transferred his capital from Delhi to –
33.x: Muhammad-Bin-Tughluq had shifted his capital from Delhi to Daulatabad (Devgiri). It was one of the most significant experiments of Muhammad-Bin-Tughluq. Various factors have been identified for this experiment. According to Barani, Devgiri probably was at the center of his empire. According to Ibn Battuta, the people of Delhi used to write undeferential letters to Sultan. To punish them he decided to make Devgiri his capital. Muhammad Tughluq was also the first Sultan of Delhi who tried to establish the administrative and cultural unity of northern and southern India. Probably this was also the main reason behind making Devgiri his capital. According to Dr. K.A. Nizami, Sultan Qutbuddin Mubarak Khalji had changed the name of Devgiri to Qutbabad and Muhammad Tughluq to Daulatabad.

Muhammad-Bin- Tughluq appointed him as Qazi of Delhi. Later in 1342 AD, he was sent to China as an ambassador of Sultan. Ibn Battuta had mentioned about his journey in his book Kitab-ul- Rihla.

33.s: For the first time the token currency was introduced in India by :
33.x: Muhammad-Bin-Tughluq launched different types of coins during his period and also decided on their reasonable prices. But the circulation of token currency was his specialty. According to Barani, due to lack of silver in treasury and policy of expanding the empire, Muhammad Tughluq had to launch the token currency. The token currency was launched in Iran during the regime of Gaykhatu, though, the experiment was unsuccessful. The token currency was successfully launched during the period of Kublai Khan. Innovative Muhammad- Bin- Tughluq was inspired by them. The modern historian also notes that there was a shortage of silver all over the world, and there was a severe shortage of silver in India too. Due to this reason, he launched token currency.
