33.s: On the death of which Muslim ruler, a historian said ‘the king was freed from his people and they from their king’?
33.x: When Muhammad-Bin-Tughluq was in Daulatabad, a revolt took place in Gujarat led by Taghi. Sultan dashed to Gujarat to quell the revolt. Taghi was defeated and fled to Sindh. After restoring peace in Gujarat, Sultan moved to Sindh to kill Taghi. Sultan fell sick on the way and died on March 20, 1351 A.D., near Thatta. On his death, Badayuni wrote, 'the king was freed from his people and the people from their king'.

33.s: ‘The king was freed from his people and they from their king.’ On whose death did Badayuni comment this ?
33.x: Badayuni made this statement about Muhammad-Bin- Tughluq in his work “Muntakhab-ut-Tawarikh.”

33.s: In 1342 Muhammad bin Tughlaq sent Ibn Battuta, the Qazi of Delhi, as envoy to:
33.x: Muhammad bin Tughlaq made Ibn Battuta Qazi of Delhi and sent him as envoy to China in 1342.
xa: He was a **Moroccan**, born at **Tangiers**, **1304**; real name **Abu Abdullah Muhammad**.
His **Rihla (Kitab-ul-Rehla)** is in **Arabic**.

33.s: Which of the following observations is associated with Ibn Battuta's account of the Delhi Sultanate?
o: Sati was permitted only to members of the royal family.
Sati was completely prohibited throughout the Sultanate.
Sati was not recorded by any contemporary traveller.
33.x: Ibn Battuta recorded the practice of sati and stated that it required the Sultan's permission.
33.tq: Select the precise recorded condition rather than an absolute statement about the practice.
xs: Ibn Battuta records that **sati required the Sultan's permission** — so option **(4)** is correct.
He also recorded the **spy system** and the **postal system**.
xa: He found MBT **eccentric**, **severe in temper**, but **generous**.
He was the **first foreign traveller** to visit **Vijayanagara**, in **Harihara I's** reign (APPSC PYQ).

33.s: Ibn Battuta, who came to India in 1333 during the reign of Muhammad bin Tughlaq, was a native of:
33.x: Ibn Battuta (Abu Abdullah Muhammad) was a Moroccan, born at Tangiers in 1304. He came to India in 1333, was made Qazi of Delhi and wrote the Rihla in Arabic. He was not from Persia, Egypt or Turkey.
xs: Ibn Battuta was from **Morocco** — so option **(2)** is correct.
He was born at **Tangiers** in **1304**; real name **Abu Abdullah Muhammad**.
He came in **1333** and was made **Qazi of Delhi**.
xa: He was sent as **envoy to China** (**1342**).
He wrote the **Rihla** in **Arabic**.

33.s: Which of the following statements about Ibn Battuta’s Rihla is correct?
o: It was written in Arabic and describes conditions in the Sultanate and the Deccan.
It was written in Persian and deals only with Central Asia.
It was written in Hindavi and describes only Vijayanagara.
It was written in Sanskrit under the patronage of Muhammad bin Tughlaq.
33.x: Rihla, also called Kitab-ul-Rehla, was written in Arabic and describes conditions in the Sultanate and the Deccan.
33.tq: Use the language-and-content combination to reject swapped literary traditions.
xs: Rihla **was written in Arabic and describes the Sultanate and the Deccan** — so option **(1)** is correct.
It is also called **Kitab-ul-Rehla**.
It was not Persian, Hindavi or Sanskrit.
xa: It records **uluq** and **dawa** couriers, the **spy system** and **sati**.
Its author, **Abu Abdullah Muhammad**, was a Moroccan born in **1304**.

33.s: Who described Muhammad bin Tughlaq as a 'mixture of opposites'?
33.x: Barani described Muhammad bin Tughlaq as a 'mixture of opposites'. Ibn Battuta characterised him as eccentric, severe in temper and generous.
33.tq: Separate the judgements of the court chronicler, foreign traveller and other contemporary figures.
xs: **Barani** called MBT a **"mixture of opposites"** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Ibn Battuta** called him **eccentric**, **quick-tempered**, but **generous**.
**Badauni** commented on his **death at Thatta (1351)**.
xa: Barani's **Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi** is the main account of these reigns.
Verdict: experiments **sound in idea, poor in execution**.

33.s: Ibn Battuta is described as the first foreign traveller to visit Vijayanagara during the reign of
33.x: Ibn Battuta is identified in this context as the first foreign traveller to visit Vijayanagara during the reign of Harihara I.
33.tq: Distinguish the earliest associated ruler from the more famous later Vijayanagara monarchs.
xs: Ibn Battuta was the first foreign traveller to visit Vijayanagara, in **Harihara I's** reign (APPSC PYQ) — so option **(2)** is correct.
Vijayanagara was founded in **1336** by **Harihara and Bukka**.
xa: He came to India in **1333** and served MBT as **Qazi of Delhi**.
He was sent as **envoy to China** in **1342**.

33.s: Ibn Battuta wrote his Rihla in:
33.x: Ibn Battuta's Rihla (Kitab-ul-Rihla) was written in Arabic.

33.s: Ibn Battuta was born at:
33.x: The Moroccan traveller Ibn Battuta (1304-1377) was born at Tangiers.

33.s: Which of the following works was written by Barani?
33.x: Barani wrote Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi and Fatawa-i-Jahandari; Futuhat-i-Firoz Shahi is Firoz's autobiography.

33.s: Who founded the Bahmani Empire?
33.x: In 1347 Alauddin Hasan Bahman Shah (Hasan Gangu) revolted against Muhammad bin Tughlaq and founded the Bahmani Empire.

33.s: Which one of the following statements about Malik Maqbul is correct?
o: He established the Bahmani kingdom under the title Hasan Gangu.
He was the founder of the Madurai Sultanate and was known as Ahsan Shah.
He founded Vijayanagara jointly with Harihara and Bukka.
He was originally a captured Brahmin named Jagannatha Pandit and later became Firoz Shah's wazir.
33.x: Malik Maqbul was originally the captured Brahmin Jagannatha Pandit, who converted to Islam and later became Firoz Shah's wazir, Khan-i-Jahan Maqbul.
33.tq: Trace a historical personality through a name change, conversion and later office.
xs: Malik Maqbul **was the captured Brahmin Jagannatha Pandit who became Firoz Shah's wazir** — so option **(4)** is correct.
He converted to Islam and became **Khan-i-Jahan Maqbul**.
**Hasan Gangu** founded the **Bahmani** kingdom; **Jalaluddin Ahsan Shah** the **Madurai Sultanate**; **Harihara and Bukka** Vijayanagara.
xa: After **1323** he assisted **Malik Burhanuddin** of Devagiri at **Warangal**.
As wazir he **paid compensation** to those who had suffered under MBT.

33.s: The Madurai Sultanate was established in:
33.x: The Madurai Sultanate dates to 1335, Vijayanagara to 1336 and the Bahmani kingdom to 1347.
xa: Madurai Sultanate: **Jalaluddin Ahsan Shah**.
Bahmani founder: **Alauddin Hasan Bahman Shah** (**Hasan Gangu**).

33.s: The Reddis expelled the Tughlaq forces from coastal Andhra around:
33.x: Coastal Andhra was freed around 1325, before the Madurai Sultanate (1335), Vijayanagara (1336) and the Bahmani kingdom (1347).
xa: **Kapaya Nayaka** recaptured Warangal also in **1336**.
These break-aways followed MBT's **badly carried out** schemes.

33.s: Harihara and Bukka founded Vijayanagara under the guidance of:
33.x: Harihara and Bukka, sent by Muhammad bin Tughlaq, founded Vijayanagara under Vidyaranya's guidance.
xa: **Ibn Battuta** visited Vijayanagara in **Harihara I's** reign.
⚠ In **1336** Kapaya Nayaka also recaptured **Warangal**.

33.s: Which one of the following is NOT correctly matched?
o: Coastal Andhra liberation — Prolaya Vema Reddi
Musunuri recapture of Warangal — Kapaya Nayaka
33.x: The Bahmani kingdom was founded by Alauddin Hasan Bahman Shah. Jalaluddin Ahsan Shah was associated with the Madurai Sultanate.
33.tq: Find the incorrectly assigned founder among otherwise familiar state–leader pairs.
xs: **Bahmani kingdom — Jalaluddin Ahsan Shah** is wrong — so option **(3)** is the answer.
The Bahmani founder was **Alauddin Hasan Bahman Shah** (Hasan Gangu); **Jalaluddin Ahsan Shah** founded the **Madurai Sultanate**.
The rest are correct: **Harihara and Bukka**; **Prolaya Vema Reddi**; **Kapaya Nayaka**.
xa: Years: Madurai **1335**, Vijayanagara **1336**, Bahmani **1347**.
Reddis freed coastal Andhra around **1325**.

33.s: The Vilasa copper plate of Prolaya Nayaka and Gangadevi's Madhura Vijayam are important for understanding:
o: The conditions under Tughlaq rule in the southern regions
The revenue system of the Bahmani kingdom
The maritime trade policy of the Madurai Sultanate
The succession disputes among the Mughal emperors
33.x: The Vilasa copper plate and Madhura Vijayam describe the conditions prevailing under Tughlaq rule in the southern regions.
33.tq: Associate each source with the historical situation it records, not with a later administrative theme.
xs: They describe **conditions under Tughlaq rule in the southern regions** — so option **(1)** is correct.
The **Vilasa copper plate** is **Prolaya Nayaka's**; **Madhura Vijayam** is **Gangadevi's**.
xa: Prolaya Nayaka led the fight to free Andhra (**Vilasa** grant, c. **1330**).
**Kapaya Nayaka** then **recaptured Warangal in 1336**.

33.s: Warangal was recaptured from the Tughlaqs in 1336 by:
33.x: Kapaya Nayaka of the Musunuri family, after Prolaya Nayaka, recaptured Warangal in 1336.

33.s: The Bahmani kingdom (1347) was founded by:
33.x: Alauddin Hasan Bahman Shah (Hasan Gangu) founded the Bahmani kingdom in 1347.

33.s:
Consider the following statements about the year 1336:
1. The Vijayanagara kingdom was founded.
2. Kapaya Nayaka recaptured Warangal.
3. The Bahmani kingdom was founded.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
33.x: Vijayanagara's founding and Kapaya Nayaka's recapture of Warangal both date to 1336; the Bahmani kingdom was founded in 1347.

33.s: The Madurai Sultanate was established by:
33.x: Jalaluddin Ahsan Shah established the Madurai Sultanate in 1335.

33.s: Firoz Shah Tughlaq was placed on the throne at Thatta in 1351 after the death of:
33.x: Firoz Shah succeeded Muhammad bin Tughlaq at Thatta in 1351 and ruled until 1388.
33.tq: Test succession through a direct ruler-event association.
xs: Firoz was enthroned at **Thatta** after **Muhammad bin Tughlaq** died there (**1351**) — so option **(4)** is correct.
**Jam Babaniya** of **Sind** only agreed to pay tribute; **Haji Iliyas** was Bengal's ruler.
xa: Firoz ruled **1351-88**.
Badauni: on MBT's death the Sultan was **freed from his people, and they from him**.

33.s: Firoz Shah Tughlaq made the iqtas:
33.x: Firoz made iqtas hereditary; he also wrote off taqavi loans, fixed land revenue and kept the four Islamic taxes.
xa: He levied **jizya** even on **Brahmins**, for the first time.
Hereditary iqtas and the slave corps **weakened central control**.

33.s: Which statement correctly describes the jizya policy of Firoz Shah Tughlaq?
o: He replaced jizya with the irrigation cess haq-i-sharb.
He abolished jizya for all non-Muslims.
He made jizya a separate tax and extended it to Brahmins.
He levied jizya only on Muslim peasants.
33.x: Firoz Shah made jizya a separate tax and, following the advice of the ulema, extended it to Brahmins for the first time.
33.tq: Discriminate between jizya, a religious tax, and haq-i-sharb, an irrigation cess.
xs: Firoz **made jizya a separate tax and extended it to Brahmins** — so option **(3)** is correct.
He did this on the **ulema's** advice.
**Haq-i-sharb** was an irrigation cess, not a replacement for jizya.
xa: He kept the **four Islamic taxes**: kharaj, jizya, khams, zakat.
His welfare state **won back nobles and ulema**.

33.s: Firoz Shah Tughlaq's two failed expeditions to Bengal were against:
33.x: Both Bengal campaigns against Haji Iliyas failed; Jam Babaniya of Sind agreed to pay tribute.
xa: Firoz did take **Jajnagar** and **Nagarkot**.
His military record is summed up as **mixed results**.

33.s: Firoz Shah Tughlaq abolished about how many taxes?
33.x: Firoz abolished about 24 taxes and kept only the four Islamic taxes.

33.s: Which of the following was NOT one of the four Islamic taxes retained by Firoz Shah Tughlaq?
33.x: Firoz kept kharaj, jizya, khams and zakat; haq-i-sharb was his irrigation cess.

33.s: Which ruler of Sind agreed to pay tribute to Firoz Shah Tughlaq?
33.x: Jam Babaniya of Sind agreed to pay tribute; Haji Iliyas of Bengal resisted Firoz's two expeditions.

33.s: With reference to medieval Indian rulers, which one of the following statements is correct?
o: Alauddin Khalji first set up a separate Ariz's department
Balban introduced the branding system of horses of military
Muhammad bin Tughlaq was succeeded by his uncle to the Delhi throne
Firuz Tughlaq set up a separate department of slaves
33.x: Firoz Shah Tughlaq established several separate departments during his reign, including the Diwan-i-Bandagan, which was specifically created to manage slaves.

33.s: Who among the following translated 300 volumes Sanskrit books collected by Firuz Tughluq during the campaign of Nagarkot?
33.x: During the Nagarkot expedition of Firuz Shah Tughlaq, he collected around 300 Sanskrit manuscript from Jawalamukhi temple library along with other loots. Later on, he got them translated into Persian by Azizuddin Khan.

33.s: Public Works Department was primarily established by-
33.x: The Public Works Department was primarily established by Firuz Shah Tughluq during the Sultanate period. It is said that he established 200 new cities. Fatehabad, Hisar, Firozpur, Jaunpur, Firozabad etc. are some of the main cities established by him. According to Firishta, Firuz had also constructed 40 Mosques, 30 schools, 20 palaces, 100 Inns, 100 hospitals, five tombs, 100 public bathrooms, ten pillars and 150 bridges. He had converted the name Ikdala to Azadpur and Pandua to Firuzabad during his Bengal campaign. Malik Ghazi Shehana was the main architect in his empire. The policy of each building as per its expected expenditure was put in front of ‘Diwan-i-Wazarat,’ only then could the fund be allowed on it.

33.s: The Sultan of Delhi who was very concerned about charity and alms and established a department called ‘Diwan-i-Khairat’ for it, was:
33.x: Firuz Shah Tughluq used to donate state and property to saints and religious people. He had established ‘Diwan-i- Khairat’ to provide financial help to poor Muslims, orphans, women, and widows and also arranged marriages of poor Muslim girls.

33.s: What was ‘Dar-ul-Shafa’ established by Firuz Tughluq?
Who among the following Sultans of Delhi established an ‘Employment Exchange’ to help the unemployed?
Under Firuz Tughlaq, about 1,300 Sanskrit manuscripts were obtained from the temple library of:
33.x: The manuscripts came from the Jawalamukhi temple library at Nagarkot, and Azizuddin Khalid Khani translated some into Persian.
n: Various scholars translated Sanskrit texts into Persian during Firuz Tughlaq’s rule. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #23-2 · pp 84-85]
Approximately 1,300 Sanskrit manuscripts were associated with the Jawalamukhi library. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #23-2 · pp 84-85]
Azizuddin Khan translated the Sanskrit manuscripts from the Jawalamukhi library into Persian. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #23-2 · pp 84-85]
xa: The translation was **Dalail-i-Firozshahi** by **Aizuddin (Azizuddin) Khalid Khani** (UPPSC **2023**).
**Ragadarpan**, on music, was also translated in his reign.
Firoz's autobiography: **Futuhat-i-Firoz Shahi**.
Firoz took **Jajnagar** and **Nagarkot**.

33.s: Which of the following Firoz Shah Tughlaq institution–function pairs is correctly matched?
o: Diwan-i-Istihqaq – Pensions and grants to deserving persons
33.x: Diwan-i-Istihqaq gave pensions and grants; Diwan-i-Khairat handled charity, Diwan-i-Bandagan slaves, and Dar-ul-Shifa was a free hospital.
xa: Diwan-i-Bandagan had about **1,80,000** slaves in the Sultan's service.
Firoz also ran an **employment bureau** and a **Public Works Department** (APPSC G2 **2017**).

33.s: Which of the following statements about Firoz Shah Tughlaq's canal policy is correct?
o: He built canals mainly to connect Bengal with Sind.
He abolished irrigation charges and prohibited the construction of canals.
He built the largest number of canals among the Delhi Sultans and levied haq-i-sharb.
His canals were drawn only from the Ganga and the Narmada.
33.x: Firoz Shah built more canals than any other Delhi Sultan and imposed an irrigation cess called haq-i-sharb.
33.tq: Use the superlative and the named levy together, while rejecting reversed policy statements.
xs: Firoz **built the largest number of canals** and levied **haq-i-sharb** — so option **(3)** is correct (BPSC **2019**).
His canals ran from the **Yamuna and Sutlej to Hisar**, not the Ganga and Narmada.
**Haq-i-sharb** was an irrigation cess of **one-tenth**.
xa: ⚠ **Ghiyasuddin** was the **first** to dig canals; **Firoz** dug the **most**.
His **Public Works Department** ran the building programme.

33.s: Firoz Shah Tughlaq's irrigation cess, haq-i-sharb, was:
33.x: Haq-i-sharb was one-tenth; his canals carried water from the Yamuna and Sutlej to Hisar.
xa: Firoz built **more canals than any other Sultan** (BPSC **2019**).
His towns include **Hisar Firoza** and **Fatehabad**.

33.s: The Ashokan pillars brought to Delhi during the reign of Firoz Shah Tughlaq came from:
33.x: Firoz Shah transported Ashokan pillars from Topra in the Ambala region and from Meerut to Delhi.
33.tq: Test the pair of source locations and reject the nearby religious and inscriptional sites.
xs: The Ashokan pillars came from **Topra** (Ambala) **and Meerut** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Jwalamukhi** at **Nagarkot** is where he seized **Sanskrit texts**, not pillars.
xa: Firoz founded **Firozabad** (Firoz Shah Kotla).
He laid about **1,200** fruit gardens around Delhi.

33.s: The autobiography of Firoz Shah Tughlaq is:
33.x: Futuhat-i-Firoz Shahi is the autobiography of Firoz Shah Tughlaq.
33.tq: Distinguish the ruler's autobiography from Barani's historical and political works.
xs: Firoz Shah's autobiography is **Futuhat-i-Firoz Shahi** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Dalail-i-Firozshahi** is the Persian translation of Sanskrit texts from **Nagarkot**, by **Azizuddin Khalid Khani**.
**Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi** and **Fatawa-i-Jahandari** were written by **Barani** under Firoz's patronage.
xa: **Ragadarpan**, a work on music, was also translated in his reign.
⚠ **Sikandar Lodi** had a Sanskrit medical treatise translated into Persian — a different Sultan.

33.s: Firoz Shah Tughlaq's Diwan-i-Bandagan dealt with:
33.x: Diwan-i-Bandagan looked after about 1,80,000 slaves; charity was Diwan-i-Khairat.

33.s: Under Firoz Shah Tughlaq, Diwan-i-Istihqaq was the department of:
33.x: Diwan-i-Istihqaq handled pensions and grants.

33.s: Firoz Shah Tughlaq's longest canal, about 150 miles, ran from:
33.x: The Yamuna-Hisar canal (150 miles) was the longest; the Sutlej-Ghaggar canal was 96 miles.

33.s: Firoz Shah's Rajabwah canal was restored in Akbar's time as the:
33.x: The Rajabwah was restored under Akbar as the Shihab (Shahab) Canal.

33.s: Azizuddin Khalid Khani's Persian translation of Sanskrit manuscripts from Jawalamukhi was titled:
33.x: Manuscripts from the Nagarkot campaign were translated as Dalail-i-Firoz Shahi.

33.s: Ain-ul-Mulk Multani did not serve under which of the following rulers?
33.x: Ain-ul-Mulk Multani served Under Alauddin Khilji, Muhammad bin Tughlaq and Firuz Shah Tughlaq. Alauddin Khalji sent him to central India in 1305 AD where he won Malwa.

33.s: Which Delhi Sultan set up a separate Public Works Department to run his building programme?
33.x: Firoz Shah Tughlaq created a Public Works Department for his canals, towns and buildings. Alauddin is known for market control, Muhammad bin Tughlaq for his experiments and Diwan-i-Amir-Kohi, and Sikandar Lodi for founding Agra.
xs: **Firoz Shah Tughlaq** set up a **Public Works Department** for his buildings (APPSC G2 **2017**) — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Alauddin** is known for **market control** and **dagh**; **MBT** for **token currency** and **Diwan-i-Amir-Kohi**.
xa: Firoz's other departments: **Diwan-i-Khairat**, **Diwan-i-Bandagan**, **Dar-ul-Shifa**, **Diwan-i-Istihqaq**.
**Sikandar Lodi** had a Sanskrit medical treatise translated into Persian.

33.s: The first Sultan of Delhi to dig canals was:
33.x: Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq first dug canals; Firoz Shah dug the largest number.
xa: Firoz's canals ran from the **Yamuna and Sutlej to Hisar**, with **haq-i-sharb** (one-tenth).
Ghiyasuddin also capped revenue rises at **one-tenth** and improved the **postal system**.

33.s: Which of the following Sultan–policy pairs is correctly matched?
o: Alauddin Khalji – Token currency and capital transfer
Firoz Shah Tughlaq – Canals, irrigation and public works
Muhammad bin Tughlaq – Blood and Iron policy
33.x: Firoz Shah Tughlaq built canals and public works; Alauddin brought market control, Balban Blood and Iron, and Muhammad bin Tughlaq token currency and the capital transfer.
n: Alauddin Khalji is associated with market and price control. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #97 · pp 181-183]
Balban is associated with the Blood and Iron policy. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #97 · pp 181-183]
Muhammad bin Tughlaq is associated with token currency. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #97 · pp 181-183]
Muhammad bin Tughlaq is associated with capital transfer. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #97 · pp 181-183]
Firoz Shah Tughlaq is associated with canals. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #97 · pp 181-183]
Firoz Shah Tughlaq is associated with irrigation. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #97 · pp 181-183]
Firoz Shah Tughlaq is associated with public works. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #97 · pp 181-183]
xa: Alauddin is also matched with **branding of horses (dagh)** (APPSC-G2 **2023**).
**Sher Shah Suri** — **roads, currency, administrative reforms**.
MBT's **Diwan-i-Amir-Kohi** = **agriculture** department.

33.s: Which of the following was NOT associated with Balban?
o: The doctrine of blood and iron
33.x: Branding of horses, or dagh, was a measure of Alauddin Khalji. Balban was associated with Sijda, paibos, the Zil-i-Ilahi theory and the policy of blood and iron.
33.tq: Find the one measure belonging to a neighbouring Sultan rather than the ruler named.
xs: **Branding of horses** (**dagh**) was not Balban's — so option **(4)** is the answer.
Dagh belongs to **Alauddin Khalji** (APPSC-G2 **2023** match key).
Balban's: **Zil-i-Ilahi** theory, **sijda and paibos**, **blood and iron**.
xa: Alauddin's other measures: **huliya**, **market control**, **land measurement**.
Balban also created **Diwan-i-Arz** and ended the **Chahalgani**.

33.s: Which one of the following pairs of a city of Delhi and its founder is correctly matched?
33.x: Siri was founded by Alauddin Khalji and Tughlaqabad by Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq. Firoz Shah founded Firozabad, not Tughlaqabad; Balban did not found Siri; Muhammad bin Tughlaq is linked with Daulatabad.
xs: **Siri — Alauddin Khalji** is correct — so option **(1)** is the answer.
**Tughlaqabad** was founded by **Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq**, not Firoz or MBT.
**Balban** did not found Siri.
xa: Firoz founded **Firozabad** (Firoz Shah Kotla).
MBT renamed **Devagiri** as **Daulatabad**.

33.s: Which of the following pairs is incorrectly matched?
o: Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq — Revenue increase limited to about one-tenth
33.x: The Zil-i-Ilahi theory was associated with Balban, not Iltutmish. Muhammad bin Tughlaq, Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq and Firoz Tughlaq are correctly matched with the measures given.
33.tq: Use the swapped ruler–reform trap to identify the incorrectly matched pair.
xs: **Iltutmish — Zil-i-Ilahi theory** is wrong — so option **(2)** is the answer.
**Zil-i-Ilahi** was **Balban's** theory; Iltutmish's were the **iqta**, **tanka/jital** and **Chahalgani**.
The rest are correct: **Firoz** — hereditary iqtas; **MBT** — token currency; **Ghiyasuddin** — revenue capped at **one-tenth**.
xa: MBT also set up **Diwan-i-Amir-Kohi** and moved to **Daulatabad**.
Firoz: **canals**, **Diwan-i-Khairat**, **Public Works Department**, **jizya on Brahmins**.

33.s: The Dahsala system is associated with:
33.x: Todar Mal devised the Dahsala; Abul Fazl wrote Akbarnama and Ain-i-Akbari.
n: Akbar is associated with Din-i-Ilahi. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #97 · pp 181-183]
Akbar is associated with Mansabdari. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #97 · pp 181-183]
Akbar is associated with Sulh-i-kul. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #97 · pp 181-183]
Abul Fazl is associated with Akbarnama. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #97 · pp 181-183]
Abul Fazl is associated with Ain-i-Akbari. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #97 · pp 181-183]
Todar Mal is associated with the Dahsala system. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #97 · pp 181-183]
Aurangzeb is associated with Jizya. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #97 · pp 181-183]
Aurangzeb is associated with Zinda Pir. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #97 · pp 181-183]
Aurangzeb is associated with Deccan policy. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #97 · pp 181-183]
Abul Fazl is associated with Akbar. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #97 · pp 181-183]
Todar Mal is associated with revenue reforms. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #97 · pp 181-183]
xa: Akbar also: **Rajput policy**.
**Shah Jahan** — **Taj Mahal**, Mughal architecture.
**Shivaji** — title **Chhatrapati**, **Ashtapradhan**.

33.s: Dagh, the branding of horses, was introduced by:
33.x: Dagh was Alauddin Khalji's measure, not Balban's.

33.s: Ain-ul-Mulk Multani won Malwa in 1305 for:

34.s: Who was the first Muslim ruler of Delhi?
34.x: Iltutmish was the first Sultan of Delhi who received the investiture from Caliph. In 1229 A.D., the Caliph of Baghdad, Al-Muntasir Billah, bestowed on Iltutmish the title of “Sultan-i- Azam” or the Sultan The Great. Thus, in this way, he was the first legally independent Sultan of Delhi. He was successful in keeping the throne of Delhi safe from the danger of Mongol invasion as well as from the attacks of both Taj ud-din Yalduz and Qabacha. He broke up the Rajput powers in the north and established his supremacy over them. He made his rule hereditary, issued coins with his name and made Delhi a beautiful capital. He is said to have introduced first Arabic silver (175gm) and copper currency which were two basic coins of the Sultanate period. Iltutmish belonged to the tribe of ‘Ilbari’ in the Eurasian Steppe of Turkestan. Iltutmish was first appointed governor of Badaun in recognition of his services during the campaign of Muhammad of Ghur against the Khokhars in 1205-06 A.D. Amirali Ismail invited Iltutmish for the coronation in Delhi with the approval of Turkish nobles after the death of Aybak. Iltutmish declared himself Sultan in 1211 A.D.

36.s: Which theory of conversion in medieval India is rejected by current scholarship as a colonial trope?
36.x: Current scholarship rejects the 'sword' theory as a colonial trope, holding that coercion was isolated; patronage and social liberation are seen as contributing or partial factors.
xa: **Sufi influence** was a major factor in **Bengal and Punjab**.
Conversion was **multi-causal** and **gradual**.

36.s: Along with agrarian expansion, Sufi influence was a major factor in conversion especially in:
36.x: Current scholarship sees Sufi influence, with agrarian expansion, as a major factor in Bengal and Punjab, working through pirs and dargahs.
xa: **Political patronage** (tax relief, office) was a contributing factor.
**Social liberation** was partial: caste-like stratification survived among converts.
Conversion was a **multi-causal**, gradual process.

36.s: The Meenakshipuram conversion of February 1981, when 558 Dalits embraced Islam, is cited as a case of which theory?
36.x: Meenakshipuram (1981) is the standard example of the social liberation theory of conversion.

36.s:
Consider the following statements about theories of conversion in medieval India:
1. Political patronage, such as office and tax relief, was a partial factor.
2. Under the social liberation theory, caste-like ranks disappeared among converts.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
36.x: Political patronage was a partial factor; social liberation is also only partial because caste-like ranks survived among converts.

36.s: Which musical instrument gained prominence during the Vijayanagara Empire?
36.x: The veena gained prominence under Vijayanagara; Krishnadevaraya himself is said to have studied it.

36.s: Who was the first woman to rule the Andhra region?
36.x: Kakatiya queen Rudramadevi (1262-1289) was the first woman ruler of the Andhra region.

36.s: In Qutb Shahi Golconda, foreign Muslims were known as:
36.x: Foreign Muslims in Golconda were the Afaqis; Brahmins received agraharas and Mustajir (tax-farming) rights.
xa: **Akkanna and Madanna** = "**Andhra Sultans**".
The **Qutb Shahis** were **Shia** and never imposed jizya.

36.s: The Bhakti movement had its indigenous roots in the:
36.x: The Bhakti movement had indigenous roots in the Alvars and Nayanars; Islam only reinforced its egalitarian and anti-ritual tendencies.
xa: Islam shaped later Bhakti's **egalitarianism** (**Kabir, Nanak, Ravidas**).
Khanqahs and dargahs drew **Hindus and Muslims** alike.

36.s: Which of the following pairs is INCORRECTLY matched?
o: Arthashastra – Compared by Al-Biruni with the Sufi idea of divine love
Amritakund – Translated into Arabic and Persian
Al-Biruni – Parallel between the Sufi idea of the soul and Patanjali's Yoga Sutra
36.x: Al-Biruni compared the Sufi idea of divine love with the Gita, not the Arthashastra; the other pairs are correct.
xa: **Nizamuddin Auliya** was struck by **Nath-yogic** body theory.
Amritakund = a **Hatha-yoga** text.

36.s: The Rishi movement of Kashmir was founded by:
36.x: Sheikh Nuruddin founded Kashmir's Rishi movement, practised vegetarianism and served all castes.
xa: **Amir Khusrau** is credited with the **sitar** and **qawwali**.
**Amritakund**, a Hatha-yoga text, was translated into Arabic and Persian (**13th** c.).
Breath control entered almost every Sufi order except the **Naqshbandis**.

36.s: Which Sufi order was especially associated with speaking to people in Hindavi?
36.x: Sufis, especially the Chishtis such as Muinuddin, Nizamuddin Auliya and Baba Farid, communicated with people in Hindavi.
xa: Chishti Sufis: **Muinuddin**, **Nizamuddin Auliya**, **Baba Farid**.
Chishtis **kept away from the court**; **khanqahs** were centres of charity.

36.s: The Sufi poem Padmavat was written by:
36.x: Padmavat is by Jayasi; Amir Khusrau is credited with the sitar and qawwali.
xa: **Gesu Daraz** wrote in Persian and early **Dakhni**.
**Raja Man Singh of Gwalior** wrote **Man Kautuhal**; **Pir Bhodan** was a Sufi musician.

36.s: Gesu Daraz, also known as Bandanawaz, is associated with which of the following?
o: Serving as Chief Qazi under Sikandar Lodi
Founding Kashmir's Rishi movement and writing only in Sanskrit
Imposing jizya on Brahmins and composing Padmavat
Moving to Gulbarga under Firoz Shah Bahmani and writing Mirqat-ul-Ashyaq in Persian and early Dakhni
36.x: Gesu Daraz moved to Gulbarga under Firoz Shah Bahmani and wrote in Persian and early Dakhni, including Mirqat-ul-Ashyaq.
36.tq: Match the saint with his movement, patronage context, languages and work.
xs: **Gesu Daraz (Bandanawaz)** moved to **Gulbarga** under **Firoz Shah Bahmani** and wrote **Mirqat-ul-Ashyaq** in **Persian and early Dakhni** — option **(4)**.
The **Rishi** movement was **Sheikh Nuruddin's**; **Padmavat** was **Jayasi's**.
xa: Deccan Sufi poetry was in **Dakhani** (early Urdu).
Islam reached Andhra with **Malik Kafur (1310)**.

36.s: Which Qutb Shahi ruler granted villages to the Bhadrachalam temple?
36.x: Abul Hasan Tana Shah granted villages to the Bhadrachalam temple; the Shia Qutb Shahis patronised Hindu temples.
xa: The Qutb Shahis **never imposed jizya**.
Brahmins got **agraharas** and **Mustajir** rights.

36.s: Which of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Raja Man Singh of Gwalior — Man Kautuhal
36.x: Dalail-i-Firozshahi was associated with Sanskrit texts translated during Firoz Tughlaq's reign, not with Baba Farid. Pir Bhodan, Raja Man Singh and Jayasi are correctly matched.
36.tq: Find the swapped author-work association among closely related cultural figures.
xs: **Baba Farid – Dalail-i-Firozshahi** is wrong: Baba Farid was a **Chishti Sufi** — option **(1)**.
The rest are correct: **Jayasi – Padmavat**; **Raja Man Singh of Gwalior – Man Kautuhal**; **Pir Bhodan – Sufi musician**.
xa: Other Chishtis: **Muinuddin**, **Nizamuddin Auliya**.
Padmavat uses **human love** as metaphor for **divine love**.

36.s: In the Vijayanagara empire, slavery was known as:
36.x: Vijayanagara slavery was called Benabaga; bandagan were the slaves of the Delhi Sultans.

36.s: Al-Biruni compared the Sufi idea of divine love with which text?
36.x: Al-Biruni compared Sufi divine love with the Gita, not the Arthashastra.

36.s: Dalail-i-Firozshahi, a Persian rendering of Sanskrit texts, was prepared under:
36.x: Dalail-i-Firozshahi rendered Sanskrit texts into Persian under Firoz Tughlaq, not Baba Farid.

36.s: Amritakund, translated into Arabic and Persian, was a text on:
36.x: Amritakund was a Hatha-yoga text translated into Arabic and Persian.

36.s: Which musical instrument is credited to Amir Khusrau?
36.x: Amir Khusrau is credited with the sitar and with qawwali.

36.s: Mirqat-ul-Ashyaq, an early Dakhni work, was written by:
36.x: Gesu Daraz (Bandanawaz), who moved to Gulbarga, wrote Mirqat-ul-Ashyaq.

36.s: Akkanna and Madanna, called the 'Andhra Sultans', belonged to which kingdom?
36.x: Akkanna and Madanna were the 'Andhra Sultans' of Qutb Shahi Golconda under Abul Hasan Tana Shah.

37.s: The arcuate style introduced by the Turks in India is primarily characterised by the use of:
37.x: The arcuate style uses arches, domes and vaults, in contrast to the trabeate system based on lintels, pillars and corbels.
37.tq: Use the architectural-terminology contrast to distinguish arcuate and trabeate construction.
xs: The arcuate style brought by the **Turks** rests on the **arch, dome and vault** — so option **(3)** is correct.
Its **true arch** is held in place by a **keystone**.
**Lintel, pillar and corbelled roof** describe the Indian **trabeate** style, which the Turks merged with the arcuate.
xa: **Squinch / pendentive** converted a **square room** into a round base for the dome.
New elements that came with it: **mihrab** (prayer niche), **minbar** (pulpit) and **minarets**.
⚠ **First true arch** = **Balban's tomb**; **first true dome** = **Alai Darwaza**.

37.s: In Indo-Islamic construction, 'surkhi' refers to:
o: Brick dust used in the mortar
37.x: Surkhi is brick dust mixed into the lime mortar in which rubble masonry was set.
xa: The **arcuate** style (arch, dome, vault) came with the **Turks**; the Indian **trabeate** style used lintel, pillar and corbel.
**Jali** = pierced stone screens; **arabesque** = floral vines.
Two broad styles: **Imperial** (Delhi Sultans) vs **Provincial** (regional dynasties).

37.s: In Indo-Islamic architecture, the 'mihrab' is the:
37.x: The mihrab is the prayer niche; the pulpit is the minbar and the jali is the pierced stone screen.
xa: **Arcuate** style (arch, dome, vault) was brought by the **Turks**; **true arch** held by a **keystone**.
**Trabeate** = Indian lintel, pillar, corbel style.
Rubble masonry used **lime mortar** with **surkhi** (brick dust).
Decoration avoided human/animal figures: **geometric** patterns, **arabesque**, **Quranic calligraphy**.

37.s: The decorative vocabulary of the Indo-Islamic style moved away from:
37.x: Indo-Islamic decoration moved away from human and animal figures towards geometric patterns, arabesque and Quranic calligraphy.
xa: **Jali** (pierced stone screens) was the other key decorative device.
The **Qutb Minar** carries **Quranic calligraphy bands** on its tapering storeys.
Two broad styles: **Imperial** (Delhi Sultans) and **Provincial** (regional dynasties).

37.s: Pierced stone screens in Indo-Islamic buildings are called:
37.x: A jali is a pierced stone screen; the mihrab is the prayer niche and the minbar the pulpit.

37.s: In the arcuate style, the true arch is held in place by a:
37.x: The true arch of the arcuate style is held by a keystone; lintel, pillar and corbel belong to the trabeate style.

37.s: The Indian trabeate style of building was based on:
37.x: Trabeate is the Indian lintel-pillar-corbel style; arch, dome and vault form the Turkish arcuate style.

37.s: The Horse-Shoe arch was first introduced in the -
37.x: The Horse-Shoe arch was first introduced in the Alai Darwaza. It was built by Alauddin Khalji.

37.s: The first true arch in the Sultanate memorial could be seen in
37.x: Tomb of Balban is located in Mehrauli, New Delhi. It was here that first true arches made their appearance in India.

37.s: Sultan Ghari, the first Indo-Islamic tomb in India, dates to:
37.x: Sultan Ghari dates to 1231, before Balban's tomb, Alai Darwaza and the octagonal tomb of Khan-i-Jahan Tilangani.
xa: ⚠ **Sultan Garhi – Balban's tomb – Alai Darwaza** = first **tomb – true arch – true dome**.
Sultan Ghari was the tomb of Iltutmish's son **Nasiruddin Mahmud**.
**Octagonal tombs** became a hallmark of the **Lodi** (and Sayyid) style.

37.s: The first true dome and the first building based fully on Islamic principles by Indian craftsmen are associated with:
37.x: Alai Darwaza is credited with the first true dome and with being the first building based fully on Islamic principles by Indian craftsmen.
37.tq: Distinguish the ‘first true dome’ from the separately tested first tomb and first true arch.
xs: The **first true dome** and first building on fully **Islamic principles** by Indian craftsmen = **Alai Darwaza** — option **(3)**.
Built by **Alauddin Khalji** in **1311** as the gateway of the **Quwwat-ul-Islam** mosque, Qutb complex.
**Sultan Ghari** is the first tomb; **Tughlaqabad** is Ghiyasuddin's fort-city; **Atala Masjid** is the Sharqi mosque of Jaunpur.
xa: Khalji hallmark: **horse-shoe arch with lotus-bud (spearhead) fringe**, red sandstone and marble inlay.
⚠ First tomb = **Sultan Garhi**; first true arch = **Balban's tomb**.
Alai Darwaza is part of the **UNESCO** site "Qutb Minar and its Monuments" (inscribed **1993**).

37.s: The first true arch in India is found in the:
37.x: Balban's tomb has the first true arch; Alai Darwaza has the first true dome and Sultan Ghari is the first Indo-Islamic tomb.
xa: ⚠ **Sultan Garhi – Balban's tomb – Alai Darwaza** = first **tomb – true arch – true dome**.
Sultan Ghari was the tomb of Iltutmish's son **Nasiruddin Mahmud**.
Khan-i-Jahan Tilangani's tomb dates from **Firoz Tughlaq's** reign.

37.s: Sadak-e-Azam of Sher Shah Suri, one of Asia's oldest major roads, is better known as the:
37.x: The Grand Trunk Road, called Sadak-e-Azam under Sher Shah Suri, is one of Asia's oldest major roads.
n: The Grand Trunk Road is one of Asia's oldest major roads. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 100-101]
The Grand Trunk Road is also known as Sadak-e-Azam. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 100-101]
xa: **Lingaraja Temple** = one of the oldest temples in **Bhubaneswar**.
**Gudimallam Shiva Linga** = the **earliest Shiva Linga**.
**Gupta period** = the **earliest freestanding temples**.

37.s: Iltutmish built Sultan Ghari, the first Indo-Islamic tomb, for his son:
37.x: Sultan Ghari (1231) was built by Iltutmish for his son Nasiruddin Mahmud.

37.s: The first octagonal tomb in India is that of:
37.x: Khan-i-Jahan Tilangani's tomb, of Firoz Tughlaq's reign, is the first octagonal tomb.

37.s: The earliest Indo-Islamic building and first major Sultanate mosque in India is the:
37.x: The Quwwat-ul-Islam Mosque in Delhi is the earliest Indo-Islamic building.

37.s: Which of the following features is associated with Sayyid and Lodi architecture rather than with the principal Tughlaq style?
o: False arches influenced by Syrian and Byzantine forms
Hindu-style gateways, plaster ornament and external drip-stones
37.x: Sayyid and Lodi builders reintroduced Hindu-style gates or façades, plaster ornament and external drip-stones.
37.tq: Identify the feature belonging to the neighbouring dynasties rather than the Tughlaq architectural vocabulary.
xs: **Hindu-style gateways, plaster ornament and external drip-stones** belong to the **Sayyid and Lodi** builders — option **(4)**.
Massive plain fort-like buildings, **battered walls**, pointed domes and **false arches** (Syrian/Byzantine) are **Tughlaq** features.
xa: Tughlaq style arose from the **Mongol threat** and finances — the "**crisis period of architecture**".
Lodi (also Sayyid) features: **octagonal tombs** and **double dome**.
Lodi Garden tombs date to the **15th-early 16th c.**

37.s: Which of the following statements regarding double domes is correct?
o: The Tughlaqs used double domes exclusively in fort gateways.
The Lodis pioneered the use of double domes on tombs, while Mughal architecture associated its first full double dome with Humayun’s Tomb.
Double domes were first introduced by the Sharqis at Atala Masjid.
Humayun’s Tomb was the first monument in India to use any form of double dome.
37.x: The Lodis pioneered double domes on tombs, while Humayun’s Tomb is credited in Mughal architectural history with the first full double dome.
37.tq: Separate the Lodi innovation from the Mughal claim concerning the first full double dome.
xs: The **Lodis pioneered** the double dome on tombs, while **Humayun's Tomb** has the first full double dome in **Mughal** architecture — option **(2)**.
So option (4) is wrong: Humayun's Tomb was not the first use of any double dome in India.
The **Tughlaqs** are known for battered walls, and the **Sharqi** Atala Masjid for its **propylon** — not double domes.
xa: Lodi examples: **Sikandar Lodi's tomb**, **Bara Gumbad**, **Shisha Gumbad** (Lodi Garden).
Lodi (and Sayyid) tombs were typically **octagonal**.
⚠ "Introduced" for Humayun's Tomb means the first **full** double dome in Mughal architecture.

37.s: The tomb of Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq at Tughlaqabad is noted for:
o: A double dome on an octagonal plan
Sloping walls and a marble dome
A horseshoe arch with lotus-bud fringe
37.x: Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq's tomb is noted for its sloping (battered) walls and marble dome.
xa: **Tughlaqabad** fort-city was built by **Ghiyasuddin Tughluq** — massive, rugged, built for security.
Tughlaq style is called the "**crisis period of architecture**" (Mongol threat, finances).
Qutb complex holds the **Tomb of Iltutmish**, not the Tughlaq tombs.

37.s: The horseshoe arch with a lotus-bud fringe is a feature of which architecture?
37.x: The lotus-bud horseshoe arch is Khalji; battered walls are Tughlaq, octagonal tombs and double domes Lodi, and the propylon screen Sharqi.
xa: **Sayyid and Lodi** revived Hindu elements: Hindu-style gateways, **plaster ornament**, external **drip-stones**.
Tughlaq period = "**crisis period of architecture**", due to the **Mongol threat** and finances.
Lodi examples: **Sikandar Lodi's tomb**, **Bara Gumbad**, **Shisha Gumbad** (Lodi Garden).

37.s: The domes and false arches of Tughlaq architecture show the influence of:
37.x: Tughlaq domes and false arches show Syrian and Byzantine influence.
xa: The Tughlaq period is called the "**crisis period of architecture**".
Examples: **Tughlaqabad** fort-city and **Ghiyasuddin's tomb** (battered walls, **marble dome**).
First **octagonal** tomb (Khan-i-Jahan Tilangani's) also dates from the **Tughlaq** period.

37.s: Sloping (battered) walls are characteristic of which dynasty's architecture?
37.x: Tughlaq buildings are plain and fort-like with sloping (battered) walls.

37.s: Who amongst the following got ‘Purana Quila’ of Delhi built in the present form?
37.x: Purana Quila is one of the oldest forts in Delhi. Its current form was built by Sher Shah Suri, the founder of the Sur Empire. Humayun raised the citadel of Purana Qila, which had an extensive area sprawling around it.

37.s: Which one of the following is a monument constructed by Sher Shah?
37.x: The short reign of Sher Shah is a revolutionary era in the history of Indian architecture. Qila-i-Kuhna, built in 1541 A.D., is famous for its elegant architectural qualities in historical monuments of northern India.

37.s: From where did Fareed, who later on became Sher Shah Suri, get his education :
37.x: Farid Khan, who later became Sher Shah Suri, got his education from Jaunpur. 37.s: Which one of the following sultans provided employment to the unemployed?
37.x: Firuz Shah Tughluq started some welfare programmes for common people. He tried to solve the problem of unemployment by opening an office for the appointment (employment office) and also appointed many qualified people by their qualification and merits.

37.s: The Lal Darwaza Mosque is an example of which architectural style?
37.x: Lal Darwaza is a Sharqi mosque; Moth ki Masjid is Lodi.
n: The Quwwat-ul-Islam Mosque was the first major mosque of the Delhi Sultanate. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #74 · pp 152-153]
The Adhai Din Ka Jhopra is an early Sultanate mosque. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #74 · pp 152-153]
The Moth Ki Masjid represents Lodi architecture. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #74 · pp 152-153]
The Lal Darwaza Mosque represents Sharqi architecture. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #74 · pp 152-153]
xa: ⚠ Pair asked: Quwwat-ul-Islam and Adhai Din ka Jhonpra = **Delhi and Ajmer**.

37.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Red Palace — tomb of Alauddin Khalji
Sultan Garhi — tomb of Nasiruddin Mahmud
Jamat Khana Masjid — tomb of Iltutmish
Firoz Shah Kotla — fortress of Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq

xs: **Sultan Garhi** is the tomb of **Nasiruddin Mahmud**, son of **Iltutmish** — option **(2)**.

**Firoz Shah Kotla** (Firozabad) was **Firoz Tughlaq's**, not Ghiyasuddin's.

37.s: The tank at Hauz Khas, known as Hauz-i-Alai, was dug by:
37.x: Alauddin Khalji excavated the Hauz-i-Alai; Firoz Shah Tughlaq later added the madrasa and tomb.

37.s: The Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque and the Adhai Din ka Jhonpra, both built by Qutbuddin Aibak, are located respectively at:

xa: Quwwat-ul-Islam reused **temple pillars** and stands in the **Qutb complex** (APPSC 2024).
Adhai Din ka Jhonpra is the "mosque at Ajmer" of the imperial style (JPSC 2021).
The **Iron Pillar** (Gupta era) stands in the Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque court.

37.s: Which of the following monuments was built earliest?
37.x: The Qutb Minar (early 13th century) predates Tughlaqabad Fort (1320s), the Lodi Garden tombs (15th–early 16th century) and Fatehpur Sikri (1570s).

37.s: The Adhai Din ka Jhonpra at Ajmer was built by:
37.x: Adhai Din ka Jhonpra at Ajmer was built by Qutbuddin Aibak, not Iltutmish.

o: Hazar Sutun was constructed by Sher Shah Suri.
Hauz-e-Alai was constructed by Alauddin Khalji.
Alai Darwaza was constructed by Alauddin Khalji.

Hazar Sutun was built by Alauddin Khalji. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 146-147]

37.x: Tughlaqabad was built by Ghiyasuddin Tughluq. The Qila-i-Kuhna Mosque is Sher Shah Suri's, the Moth Masjid dates from Sikandar Lodi's reign and the Kirti Stambha is Rana Kumbha's.

Who among the following witnessed the reign of Seven Sultans of Delhi?

94.s: The kingdom of Vijayanagara was founded by-
94.x: The Vijayanagara empire was founded by Harihara and Bukka in 1336. This dynasty is known as Sangama Dynasty after their father’s name. Harihara and Bukka were the feudatories of the Kakatiyas of Warangal. After the fall of Warangal at the hands of Delhi Sultan, they shifted to Kampili and became ministers. Muhammad Tughluq invaded Kampili and arrested Harihara and Bukka. Both were forced to convert to Islam. Later, both were sent to the south to suppress a rebellion. They could not succeed, but under the influence of Saint Vidyaranya, they again reverted to Hinduism to establish the Vijayanagara Dynasty. They were inspired by their spiritual teacher Vidyaranya and Sayan, a noted commentator of Vedas. Four Dynasties ruled under this empire. (i) Sangama dynasty (1336-1485 A.D.). (ii) Saluva dynasty (1485-1505 A.D.), (iii) Tuluva dynasty (1505-1570 A.D.) and (vi) Aravidu dynasty (1570-1672 A.D.). These dynasties ruled over three hundred years. The capitals of Vijayanagara were Anegundi, Vijayanagara, Penukonda and Chandragiri respectively.

According to Portuguese writer Nuniz, the women in Vijayanagara Empire were experts in which of the following areas?
1. Wrestling
2. Astrology
3. Accounting
4. Soothsaying
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
94.x: All are correct: The Vijayanagara Empire was ruled by four successive dynasties: the Sangama (c. 1336–1485 CE), Saluva (c. 1485–1503 CE), Tuluva (c. 1503–1570 CE), and Aravidu dynasties, the last continuing till the end of the 17th century. A significant understanding of the empire's history comes from the accounts of two Portuguese Medieval Indian History PMF IAS IH – 41 chroniclers, Domingo Paes and Fernao Nuniz. Writing in the sixteenth century, their narratives provide valuable first-hand insights. Domingo Paes recorded his observations during 1520–22, in the reign of Krishnadevaraya, while Fernao Nuniz wrote around 1535–37, during the rule of Achyuta Deva Raya. Both rulers were key figures of the Tuluva dynasty. Women in Vijayanagara society enjoyed a notable status and actively participated in political, social, and cultural life. They were engaged in activities such as wrestling, swordsmanship, the use of shields, music, and other fine arts, and some also received substantial literary education. Nuniz notes that women held diverse roles, including wrestling, astrology, and soothsaying. He also notes the presence of women officials who kept expense records in the palace and documented administrative affairs, often cross-checking these records with those kept by external scribes.

96.s: In ancient medieval times Pradvivaka was the advisor to the king in this department?
96.x:
The Pradvivaka (Pradvivaka or Pradvivakudu) was the chief judicial adviser to the king in ancient and medieval Indian administration. He assisted the ruler in legal matters, interpreted Dharmashastra, advised on judicial decisions and supervised the administration of justice. His position was equivalent to that of a chief judge or legal expert in the royal court. Several ancient legal texts refer to the office of the Pradvivaka as an important component of judicial administration. Hence, the correct answer is Option (4).

o: Administrative unity and unity in Law
40.x: Akbar was the first among the monarchs of medieval India to raise the policy of religious tolerance to the pinnacle of secularism. The socio-political condition of the country was such that Akbar thought it was advisable to adopt independent views in religious matters. The non-Muslims constituted the majority of his Indian subjects. Without winning their confidence and active support, Akbar could not hope to establish and consolidate the Mughal rule in India. Religion had played the role of a divisive force in Indian society ever since the advent of Islam which most of its people had refused to embrace. Akbar fully understood the centrifugal tendencies of the complex Indian sociopolitical order and made a serious attempt to eliminate these by separating religion from politics. To win the goodwill of Hindus, he abolished the pilgrimage tax and Jizya. Freedom of worship, matrimonial alliances with Hindus, high civil and military positions to Hindus, translation of Hindu scriptures, establishment of Ibadatkhana, issue of infallibility decree, freedom to construct temples, land grants, considerations of Hindu sentiments, reforms in Hindu society were some measures adopted by Akbar to establish religious harmony but he had not forsaken Islam.

40.s: Which Mughal Emperor was known as "Zinda Peer" ?
40.x: Aurangzeb was a remarkable man. Among the Mughals, he possessed extraordinary personal qualities. He maintained high moral standards and was far from vices, pleasures and extravagance. Some recommended him ‘Shahi Darvesh’ and some Muslims accepted him as "Zinda Peer".

40.s: During whose reign did the “Mughal Painting” flourish?
40.x: Jahangir (1605-27) had an artistic inclination. During his reign, Mughal painting developed further as Jahangir was fascinated with art, science and architecture from a young age. He showed a leaning towards painting and had an atelier of his own. His interest in portraiture led to much development in this art form. The art of Mughal painting reached great heights during Jahangir’s reign. His interest in painting also served his scientific interest in nature. Painter Ustad Mansur became one of the best artists to document the animals and plants which Jahangir either encountered on his military expeditions or received as donations. Jahangir maintained a huge aviary and kept a record of every specimen and organized experiments. He patronized the European and Persian arts.

40.s: Which of the following Mughal Emperors wrote his autobiography in Persian ?

40.s: The first matrimonial alliance with the Rajputs was established by Akbar with the house of :
40.x: The first matrimonial alliance with the Rajputs was established by Akbar with Kachhwaha Rajput. He went on a pilgrimage to the Mausoleum of Shaikh Muinuddin Chishti at Ajmer in 1562 A.D. His route laid through the Rajput state of Amber. Its ruler Raja Bihari Mal (Bharmal), with a view of safeguarding his position, offered his submission to Akbar at Sanganer and voluntarily proposed his daughter, Princess Harkhabai (Jodha) marriage with the young monarch. Akbar accepted the offer and on his return from Ajmer, married in 1562 AD. It was the first marriage of Akbar with any Rajput girl. Thus, Raja Bharmal was the first Rajput king who accepted Akbar’s supremacy of his accord. Salim (later Jahangir), heir to the throne was born of this wedlock on August 30, 1569 AD.

43.s: Banjaras during the medieval period of Indian history were
43.x: During the medieval period, the Indian trading classes were large in number, widely spread throughout the country, and well organised. Seth, bohra traders specialised in long-distance trade, while local traders were called banik. Another class of traders, known as banjaras, specialised in carrying bulk goods and used to travel long distances with their goods on the backs of oxen (their caravans were called Tanda). Interestingly, the trading community did not belong to one caste or religion. For instance, the Gujarati merchants included Hindus, Jains, and Muslims, Oswals, Maheshwaris, and Agarwals came to be called the Marwaris, while in South India, the Chettis on the Coromandel coast and the Muslim merchants of Malabar formed important trading communities.

(a) Wellesley (b) Warren Hastings (c) Lord Cornwallis (d) Lord Dufferin U.P. P.C.S. (Pre) 1991 Ans. (c) The Permanent Settlement (1793 AD) was introduced by Lord Cornwallis. This system was launched in Bengal, Bihar, Odisha, Varanasi (U.P.) etc. It is also known as Istimarari Maalguzari, Bishwedari etc. The Permanent Settlement stood on the following features - It recognized the landlords as the proprietors of the land. It also recognized the rights of a hereditary successor or lawful successors of the landlords. The government believed that these landlords would remain faithful to the British. The landlords were given the right to transfer or sell their land. All the rights of the landlords depended on their payment of the fixed revenue on the fixed date at the treasury of the government. All their rights ended if they failed to pay. This was one reason for increased litigation. An increase in intermediaries between farmers and landlords was another reason for increased litigation. The total amount of revenue to be paid by each landlord for his Zamindari was fixed once and for all. It was agreed that the tax rate would not increase in the future.

44.x: In c.1575 CE, Akbar constructed the Ibadat Khana (Hall of prayers) at his new capital, Fatehpur Sikri, wherein Akbar invited learned scholars from all religions, like Hinduism, Jainism, Christianity, and Zoroastrianism and used to conduct religious discussions with them. Some of the prominent scholars associated with Akbar's court included Purushottam Das, a Hindu Dastur; Maharji Rana, a Parsi scholar from Navsari; and Hira Vijaya Suri, a Jain saint from Kathiawar. Among the Christian scholars were Aquaviva and Monserrate, who were sent by the Portuguese at Akbar's request. In c.1582 CE, he promulgated a new religion called Din-i-Ilahi/Tauhidi-Ilahi (Divine Monotheism), which believes in one God and in Sulh-i-Kul/peace to all. It contained the good points of all religions, and the basics were rational. However, his new faith proved to be a failure. It fizzled out after his death. Even during his lifetime, it had only followers, including Birbal, Abul Fazl, and Abul Faizi.

When Akbar heard of his prodigious talent, he sent a 'firman' to the king asking for Tansen and made him one of the Navaratnas in his court. Akbar gave him the title of 'Mian'. Tansen composed numerous dhrupads dedicated to deities such as Ganesha, Shiva, Parvati, and Rama, as well as compositions for his royal patrons. Tansen is also known for composing in his favourite ragas, including Multani, Bhairavi, and Todi. He is credited with creating several new ragas, such as the night raga Darbari Kanhra, morning raga Mian Ki Todi, midday raga Mian Ki Sarang, and the seasonal raga Mian Ki Malhar. His descendants and disciples are called Seniyas.

51.s: What was the immediate reason for Ahmad Shah Abdali to invade India and fight the Third Battle of Panipat?

51.s: A historian witness to the third battle of Panipat. Who was he?

51.s: Which of the following was NOT a major cause of the Maratha defeat at Panipat?
o: Alienation of some regional powers through earlier plunder
Heavy baggage and the presence of non-combatants
Strong and sustained support from the Jats and Rajputs
Collapse of supplies and starvation in the camp

xs: Option **(3)** was NOT a cause: there was **no strong support from the Jats and Rajputs** — they stayed away.
Real causes: **no allies in the north**, **supply collapse and starvation**, **heavy baggage and non-combatants**, and earlier **plunder** that alienated Rajputs and Jats.

51.s: The Third Battle of Panipat, fought on 14 January 1761, was fought between

the Marathas and Ahmad Shah Abdali
the Mughals and Ahmad Shah Abdali

xs: Third Panipat (**14 January 1761**) was between **the Marathas and Ahmad Shah Abdali** — option **(2)** (APPSC-G1 **2018**).
**Shah Alam II** was the Mughal emperor, not a combatant.
xa: Abdali's motive: the Marathas had driven his son **Timur Shah** out of the Punjab.
Maratha commander: **Sadashiv Rao Bhau**.

xs: Abdali's allies were **Najib-ud-Daula** (Rohilla) and **Shuja-ud-Daula** of Awadh — option **(2)**.

51.s: Abdali's son whom the Marathas drove out of Lahore in 1758 was:
51.x: The expulsion of Timur Shah from Lahore (1758) was Abdali's immediate motive for the Panipat campaign.

51.s: The Treaty of Salbai of 1782 was concluded between

51.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched? Treaty — Provision or event
o: Treaty of Surat — Bombay government agreed to support Raghunath Rao with 2,500 troops
Treaty of Purandar — British retained Salsette and secured twenty years of peace
Treaty of Salbai — Calcutta Council annulled the Treaty of Surat

51.tq: Match the treaty with its distinctive provision, watching for reversed outcomes.
xs: **Treaty of Surat** — Bombay backed **Raghunath Rao** with **2,500 troops** — option **(1)**.
**Purandar (1776)**: the **Calcutta council annulled** Surat — so option 3 misplaces it under Salbai.
**Wadgaon (1779)**: the British were **defeated and forced to give up gains**.

51.x: After the British defeat at Talegaon, the Convention of Wadgaon forced them to give up their gains, but Warren Hastings rejected it.
xa: ⚠ **Surat (1775)** = British back Raghunath Rao; **Purandar (1776)** = annulled; **Salbai (1782)** = end.

Outcome: **Peshwaship abolished in 1818**.

xs: **Assaye** is the battle NOT of the Third Anglo-Maratha War — option **(4)**.
The Third war's battles were **Khadki (Kirkee)**, **Koregaon**, **Sitabuldi** and **Mahidpur**.

o: The Pindari campaigns were a cause

51.x: On July 10, 1806 AD, a military uprising took place at the Vellore Fort in Tamil Nadu, known as the Vellore Mutiny. Nana Phadnavis, a prominent political leader of the Maratha society, passed away in March 1800 AD. Lord Wellesley served as Governor-General from 1798 AD to 1805 AD. Due to his aggressive expansionist policies and military campaigns, the British government faced financial difficulties and recalled him in 1805 AD. Lord Hastings (1813–1823 AD) later oversaw the Anglo- Nepalese War (1814–1816 AD), which concluded with the Treaty of Sugauli.

46.s: Who were the first Vaishnavite devotees in South India?
46.x: The Alwars were the early Vaishnava saints of South India; the Nayanars were Shaiva.

46.s: Who were the first Vaishnavite devotees in South India?
46.x:
The Alwars were the earliest Vaishnavite Bhakti saints of South India who flourished between the 6th and 9th centuries CE. They composed devotional hymns in praise of Lord Vishnu, which were later compiled into the Nalayira Divya Prabandham. Their teachings emphasized personal devotion (Bhakti) rather than rituals and played a crucial role in spreading the Bhakti Movement throughout South India. Hence, the correct answer is Option (1).
Exam Note:
• Alwars → Vaishnavite saints
• Nayanars → Shaivite saints

46.s: The Bhakti movement was started by –
46.x: The Bhakti Movement is a Hindu religious movement in which the main spiritual practise is loving devotion among the Shaiva Nayanars and the Vaishnava Alvars. Devotional worship had a long history of almost a thousand years across the sub-continent. The early medieval Bhakti movement originated in Dravida region and began to spread to the north during the late medieval ages (during 13th-14th centuries onwards) when North India was under Islamic rule. The Bhakti movement was started in the 8th century by the great philosopher Adi Shankaracharya.

46.s: The word ‘bhakti’ is derived from the root ‘bhaj’, which means:
46.x: The word bhakti is derived from the root bhaj, meaning to share or participate.
xs: **Bhaj** means **to share or participate** — option **(3)**.
Bhakti derives from this root.
xa: The **Bhagavata Purana** first put bhakti at the **centre of religion**.
It lists **ninefold (navadha) bhakti**: shravana, kirtana, smarana, padasevana, archana, vandana, dasya, sakhya, atmanivedana.

46.s: Which text put bhakti at the centre of religion and described a ninefold bhakti?
46.x: The Bhagavata Purana put bhakti at the centre; its ninefold bhakti includes kirtana, smarana and atmanivedana.
xa: Dating: some notes say the **6th c.**; most scholars **c. 9th-10th c.**
Other roots of bhakti: the **Upanishads** and the **Bhagavad Gita**.

46.s: Which of the following is NOT regarded as a root of the Bhakti movement?
46.x: The Upanishads, Bhagavad Gita and Bhagavata Purana are identified as roots of the Bhakti movement; the Arthashastra is not.
xa: **Gita Chapter 12 = Bhakti Yoga**.
Both streams drew on the **Upanishadic doctrine of Advaita**.

46.s: Which one of the following sequences represents the beginning of the Bhakti movement and its later spread most accurately?
o: Tamil region in the sixth–ninth centuries, followed by spread to northern India by the fifteenth century
Northern India in the fifteenth century, followed by spread to Tamil Nadu in the eighteenth century
Bengal in the ninth century, followed by spread to Tamil Nadu in the twelfth century
Rajasthan in the sixth century, followed by spread to Tamil Nadu in the fifteenth century
46.x: The movement first developed in the Tamil region through the Alvars and Nayanars during the sixth–ninth centuries and reached the northern belt by the fifteenth century. Its overall span is described as the sixth to the eighteenth century.
46.tq: Use the first regional centre and the later northern expansion to establish sequence.
xs: Bhakti began in the **Tamil region (6th-9th c.)** and reached **northern India by the 15th c.** — option **(1)**.
It started with the **Alvars and Nayanars**.
xa: Overall span: **6th to 18th c.**
**Ramananda** brought it to the north.

46.s: The Bhakti movement arose partly because ordinary people found which paths difficult?
46.x: The paths of knowledge (gyana) and action (karma) were considered difficult for ordinary people, alongside reaction against ritualism, priestly dominance and caste.
xa: Core beliefs: **monotheism**, **guru essential**, **salvation through devotion**.
Limit: it only **moderated** caste rigidity.

46.s: The Bhakti movement challenged caste hierarchy by placing devotion above:
46.x: The Bhakti saints placed devotion above birth and status, and that is how they challenged caste hierarchy.
n: The Bhakti Movement emphasized devotion over birth and status. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #22 · pp 80-82]
The Bhakti Movement challenged caste hierarchy. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #22 · pp 80-82]
xa: **Guru Nanak**'s **Guru Ka Langar** = common dining without caste discrimination.
**Alvars and Nayanars** came from **all castes, high and low**.
Limit: it only **moderated** caste rigidity to an extent.

46.s: Modern scholars trace the indigenous roots of the Bhakti movement to the:
46.x: Modern scholars emphasise the movement's indigenous Alvar–Nayanar roots and see Islam as influencing mainly its later egalitarianism.
xa: Bhakti began in the **Tamil region (6th-9th c.)**.
It brought **Hindus and Muslims closer**, but lasting unity was not achieved.

46.s: Which chapter of the Bhagavad Gita is the Bhakti Yoga?
46.x: Gita Chapter 12 is Bhakti Yoga; it holds both Saguna and Nirguna valid.

46.s: Vaishnavism was propagated by Alvar saints of Tamil Nadu. Who was the only female Sadhvi among the Alvar saints?
46.x: The Alvar saints propagated Vaishnavism in South India. There are a total of 12 Alvar saints, and among them, the only female saint was Andal.

46.s: The Alvars and Nayanars, who challenged Brahmanical dominance, came from:
46.x: The Alvars and Nayanars came from different castes, high and low, and challenged Brahmanical dominance.

Nayanar lives: **Periya Puranam** by **Sekkizhar**.

46.x: The Nalayira Divya Prabandham contains 4,000 Alvar hymns and was compiled by Nathamuni.

**Alvars = 12** Vishnu devotees.

46.x: Andal was the only female Alvar.

**Shankaracharya** (**788-820**) was a forerunner.

46.s: Who is regarded as the foremost Alvar, author of the Tiruvaymoli?
46.x: Nammalvar is the foremost Alvar; his Tiruvaymoli has 1,102 verses.

46.s: Karaikkal Ammaiyar was one of the women saints among the:
46.x: Karaikkal Ammaiyar was one of three women among the 63 Nayanars, and the only female Nayanar whose poems survive.

46.s: The Periya Puranam, the lives of the 63 Nayanars, was written by:
46.x: Sekkizhar wrote the Periya Puranam under Kulottunga II; it is the 12th book of the Tirumurai.

46.s: The Tevaram contains the hymns of:
46.x: The Tevaram holds the hymns of the Nayanars Appar, Sambandar and Sundarar; Poigai, Bhoothath and Pey were the first three Alvars.

46.s: Vallabhacharya, the exponent of Pushtimarg, was:
o: A Telugu Brahmin who visited Krishnadevaraya's court
