49.s:
Given below are two statements, one is labelled as
Assertion (A) and the other as
Reason (R).
Assertion (A) : Many Sanskrit works on music were translated into Persian during the medieval period.
Reason (R) : The early Chishti Sufis were fond of musical assemblies called, 'sama'.
Select the correct answer from the codes given below:
o: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is correct
Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is not the correct
49.x: In the medieval period, many Sanskrit books on music were translated into Persian. Translation of these Sanskrit books into Persian, was possible due to the interest of rulers. Mahmud of Ghazni took many books with him to Ghazni. Firuz Tughluq and Sikandar Lodi got books from various areas written especially in Sanskrit translated into Persian. Later, Mughal emperors also translated various books of Sanskrit in Persian. Therefore, it is clear that the statement is correct. 'Sama' was the music assembly. Chishtis were the supporter of music and considered music a medium to reach God. Hence, it is clear that the reason is also true, but the reason (R) is not the correct interpretation of the statement.

49.s: Which one of the following Sufi orders was opposed to musical practices such as sama?
49.x: The Naqshbandis opposed sama and associated musical practices, in contrast to the Chishti and Suhrawardi traditions mentioned in this context.
49.tq: Test the exception among Sufi orders associated with devotional music.
xs: The **Naqshbandi** order opposed sama — option **(1)** is correct.
**Chishtis and Suhrawardis** held **"Majlis-i-Sama"** gatherings.
xa: Naqshbandis also stood apart on **breath control**, the one order that did not adopt it.
**Naqshbandi orthodoxy** was the main pushback against Sufi-Bhakti liberalism.

49.s: The Qaul, associated with the early development of qawwali, was introduced by
49.x: Amir Khusrau is credited with introducing the Qaul, which became associated with qawwali traditions around Sufi shrines.
49.tq: Use the author-or-originator association to identify the correct contributor to a musical form.
xs: **Amir Khusrau** introduced the **Qaul** — option **(3)** is correct.
**Faqirullah** wrote **Raga Darpan**; **Chaitanya** = **sankirtan**; **Annamacharya** = Telugu padam / keertana.
xa: **Qawwali** grew around **Sufi shrines**.
**Hindustani music** absorbed Persian, Bhakti and Sufi influences (**Amir Khusrau**, **Tansen**).

49.s: Which music tradition remained closely tied to temple Bhakti?
49.x: Carnatic music remained linked with temple Bhakti, while Hindustani absorbed Persian, Bhakti and Sufi influences.
xa: Hindustani influences: **Amir Khusrau**, **Tansen**.
Carnatic's temple link: the **Trinity**.
Persian works on Indian music: **Ghunyat-ul-Munya** (**1375**) and **Raga Darpan** (Faqirullah).

49.s: In medieval India, many Sanskrit works on music were translated into:
49.x: Many Sanskrit musical works were rendered into Persian; the early Chishtis too were fond of music.
xa: **Chishti and Suhrawardi** held **"Majlis-i-Sama"**; the **Naqshbandis** opposed it.
**Ghunyat-ul-Munya** (**1375**) and **Raga Darpan** are Persian works on Indian music.

49.s: Lahjat-i-Sikandar Shahi, a Persian rendering of Sanskrit music works, is linked with:
49.x: Lahjat-i-Sikandar Shahi is associated with Sikandar Lodi.

49.s: Ghunyat-ul-Munya, a Persian work on music, dates to:
49.x: Ghunyat-ul-Munya dates to 1375.

49.s: The Melakarta raga system is associated with:
49.x: Venkatamakhin is linked with the Melakarta raga system; Shyama Shastri was a Carnatic composer.

49.s: A common feature of all Bhakti Saints was that they –
o: Composed their verses in the language understood by
Rejected the authority of the priestly class
Encouraged women to go to the temples
49.x: The conduct of Bhakti saints was of a very high standard. Many of them visited the country and met many people having different views. They also contributed to the advancement of Hindi, Kannada, Punjabi, Bengali, Telugu, Tamil and other languages. The Saints of Bhakti Movement gave their verses in regional and local languages so that their followers could easily understand them. This was the main reason behind the development of local languages.

49.s: The Jnaneshwari belongs to the literature of which language?
49.x: The Jnaneshwari is a Marathi work; Bengali is associated with Padavali kirtans.

49.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched?
49.x: Jnaneshwari was composed by Jnaneshwar in Marathi. Kaalagnanam was composed by Potuluri Veerabrahmam, while the other two pairs have incorrect authors and languages.
49.tq: Test the three-part association of work, author and language.
xs: **Jnaneshwari — Jnaneshwar — Marathi** is correct — option **(1)**.
**Kaalagnanam** is **Potuluri Veerabrahmam's**, not Potana's; **Basava Puranam** is **Palkuriki's** (Telugu).
**Ramcharitmanas** is **Tulsidas's** (Hindi), not Annamacharya's.
xa: Marathi also: **Abhangas** of **Tukaram**; **Namdev**.
**Potana's** Telugu work is the **Bhagavatamu**.

49.s: Who among the following used satire in common Telugu to criticise birth-based inequality?
49.x: Vemana, associated with the seventeenth century, used satire in common Telugu against birth-based inequality.
49.tq: Link the poet’s language and literary method with the social theme.
xs: **Vemana** (**17th c.**) used **satire in common Telugu** against **birth-based inequality** — option **(1)** is correct.
**Baba Farid** = Punjabi verses; **Surdas** = Hindi; **Amir Khusrau** = Urdu / Hindavi.
xa: Vemana is part of Andhra's pre-colonial reform line with **Veerabrahmam**, **Nasaraiah**, **Brahmanaidu**.
Telugu bhakti literature also includes **Annamacharya's sankirtanas** and **Kaalagnanam**.

49.s: Bhakti and Sufi saints spread their teaching mainly through:
o: The speech of the common people
49.x: The saints used the people's speech instead of relying exclusively on Sanskrit, which helped regional languages such as Hindi, Marathi and Bengali grow.

49.s: Kaalagnanam in Telugu is associated with:
49.x: Kaalagnanam is by Veerabrahmam; Vemana wrote 17th-century satire on birth inequality.

49.s: Amir Khusrau is associated with the growth of literature in:
49.x: Amir Khusrau is linked with Urdu and Hindavi.

49.s: Which of the following was a social impact of the Bhakti and Sufi movements?
o: They closed khanqahs to lower social groups
They weakened priestly and Brahmanical dominance
49.x: The movements weakened priestly dominance and khanqahs welcomed different groups, but caste was not completely abolished.

49.s: The Rishi movement of Kashmir emphasised:
o: Universal love, service to all castes and vegetarianism
Courtly luxury, military conquest and Persianisation
Purdah, child marriage and priestly monopoly
Caste exclusiveness, animal sacrifice and compulsory meat-eating
49.x: The Rishi movement served all castes, emphasised universal love and adopted vegetarianism, although the Shariat permitted meat.

49.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched with the occupational or caste background of the saint?
49.x: Namdev belonged to a tailor family. Kabir was a weaver, Ravidas a leather tanner or shoemaker, Sena a barber and Dhanna a Jat cultivator.
49.tq: Use occupation-based discrimination among closely associated Bhakti figures.
xs: **Namdev — tailor** is correct — option **(4)**.
**Kabir** was a **weaver**, not a barber; **Dhanna** was a **Jat cultivator**, not a weaver.
**Sena** was a **barber**; the tanner was **Ravidas**.
xa: These **low-caste saints** helped weaken **priestly and Brahmin dominance**.
**Ramananda's** disciples: **Dhanna**, **Sena**, **Raidas**, **Kabir**.

49.s: Veerashaivism associated with Basava advocated which one of the following combinations?
o: Vedic ritualism, animal sacrifice and purdah
Caste hierarchy, child marriage and widow seclusion
Priestly monopoly, child marriage and caste exclusiveness
Caste opposition, widow remarriage and gender equality
49.x: Basava’s Veerashaivism condemned caste and child marriage and supported widow remarriage and gender equality.
49.tq: Match the reform movement with its positive social reforms.
xs: Basava's Veerashaivism stood for **caste opposition, widow remarriage and gender equality** — option **(4)** is correct.
It **opposed** caste, **animal sacrifice**, **Vedic ritualism** and **child marriage** — so options (1)-(3) are its opposite.
xa: It spread in Andhra through **Mallikarjuna, Inpati and Manchana Panditas**.
⚠ Limitation: it at times turned to violence, spread by the **"Sivapasa"** (sword).
**Lingayat / Veerasaiva** sect: founder **Basaveswara**; region **Karnataka, Andhra**.

49.s: Which Andhra saint had disciples like Siddayya (a Dudekula) and Kakkaiah (a Madiga)?
49.x: Veerabrahmam's disciples cut across castes and he admitted women; he opposed untouchability and idol worship.
xa: **Nasaraiah**, a Sayyid reformer (until **1825**), was popular among the **Madigas** of Vinukonda and Narasaraopeta.
Nasaraiah also opposed **untouchability** and **idol worship**.

49.s: Who is regarded as the first medieval reformer to denounce caste outright, with disciples such as Kabir, Raidas, Sena and Dhanna?
49.x: Ramananda was the first medieval reformer to denounce caste outright; his disciples included Kabir (weaver), Raidas (shoemaker), Sena (barber) and Dhanna (Jat cultivator). Ramanuja preached Vishishtadvaita, Basavanna led Veerashaivism, and Chaitanya is linked with sankirtan; none had this group of disciples.
49.tq: Ramananda: first to denounce caste; disciples Kabir, Raidas, Sena, Dhanna.
xs: **Ramananda** was the **first medieval reformer to denounce caste outright** — option **(3)** is correct.
His disciples: **Kabir** (weaver), **Raidas** (shoemaker), **Sena** (barber), **Dhanna** (Jat cultivator).
**Ramanuja** is linked with **Srivaishnavism**; **Basavanna** with **Veerashaivism**; **Chaitanya** with **sankirtan**.
xa: ⚠ Even with Srivaishnavism and Veerashaivism, **caste inequalities could not be eradicated**.
**Namdev** the tailor was another low-caste saint.

49.s: Which statement about women in the Bhakti and Sufi movements is correct?
o: Women were excluded from spiritual expression in both
Only royal women could express spirituality publicly
The movements gave women room for open spiritual expression
Women were admitted to Sufi orders but to no Bhakti order
49.x: Both movements created space for women's open spiritual expression; Veerabrahmam also admitted women to his order.
xa: Veerabrahmam's granddaughter **Eswaramma** became a yogi.
⚠ Limitation: the movements **did not end purdah** or restrictions on women's public life.

49.s: Which of the following pairs of traditions formed part of the pre-colonial social-reform line in Andhra?
49.x: The Andhra pre-colonial reform line included Veerashaivism and Srivaishnavism, along with figures such as Brahmanayudu, Vemana, Veerabrahmam and Nasaraiah.

o: Kabir, Dadu Dayal and Guru Nanak

49.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Ajivika sect:
1. Belief in determinism
2. The order of reincarnation can be changed.
3. Belief in austerity.
Select the correct answer using the codes given below:
49.x: The Ajivika sect, which is an ancient religious and philosophical tradition of India, believes in determinism (fatalism). According to this belief, all events that occur in a person's life—both joys and sorrows—are preordained and governed by an unchangeable cosmic order.They held that the universe follows a strict, predetermined course, where everything happens due to past conditions, and there is no scope for individual free will or moral efforts to change one's fate. They practised severe austerities, such as remaining silent for long periods and fasting, as they believed these acts were part of their predestined path. Because they did not believe in free will or individual effort, they also rejected the idea that one's rebirth cycle could be altered by personal or religious actions.Thus, it is clear that statements 1 and 3 are correct, while statement 2 is incorrect.

52.s: The 1717 farman of Farrukhsiyar is popularly known as the:
52.x: The 1717 farman granted important trading privileges to the Company and is popularly called the Magna Carta of the Company.
52.tq: Recall the distinctive title associated with the 1717 farman.
xs: The **1717 farman** of **Farrukhsiyar** is called the **"Magna Carta" of the Company** — option **(3)**.
It gave **duty-free trade** in Bengal for **Rs 3,000** a year.
xa: **Diwani** = **revenue + civil justice** — a later grant (**1765**), not the farman.
**Dastak** misuse caused quarrels with **Siraj** and later **Mir Qasim**.

52.s: A dastak under the Bengal trading system was a:
o: land grant issued to a zamindar
permit for fortifying a European settlement
military order issued by the Nawab
52.x: A dastak was a free pass that enabled duty-free trade. Its misuse became a major source of conflict between the Company and the Nawabs.
52.tq: Test the precise meaning of a confusable administrative term.
xs: A **dastak** was a **free pass for duty-free trade** — option **(4)**.
**Company servants misused dastaks** for **private trade**, draining the Nawab's revenue.
xa: Dastak misuse caused quarrels with **Siraj** and later **Mir Qasim**.
**Mir Qasim** **abolished all internal trade duties**, so the dastak advantage vanished.

52.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the Diwani granted to the East India Company?
o: The right to collect revenue and administer civil justice in Bengal, Bihar and Orissa
The right to appoint the Mughal Emperor and control Delhi
The right to conduct foreign affairs on behalf of Awadh

**Criminal justice and police** form the **Nizamat**, kept by the Nawab.
xa: Granted by **Shah Alam II** under the **Treaty of Allahabad (1765)**.
**Naib diwans**: **Muhammad Reza Khan** (Bengal) + **Raja Shitab Rai** (Bihar).

52.s: Under the Dual Government in Bengal, criticised as "power without responsibility", the Nawab formally retained the:
52.x: The Company enjoyed the financial power of the Diwani, while the Nawab formally retained the Nizamat and its responsibilities.

52.s: Under the farman of 1717, the Company could trade in Bengal without customs duties for a fixed annual payment of:
52.x: Farrukhsiyar's farman let the Company trade duty-free in Bengal for a fixed Rs 3,000 a year.

52.s: The farman of 1717 granting the Company duty-free trade in Bengal was issued by:
52.x: The 1717 farman, the "Magna Carta" of the Company, was issued by Farrukhsiyar.
52.tq: one-liner

52.s: Which of these Nawabs of Bengal abolished all duties on internal trade?
Who was the Nawab of Bengal when the Battle of Buxar was fought?
52.x: On 22/23 October, 1764 A.D. British Army defeated allied forces of Mir Qasim, Nawab of Oudh Shuja-ud-Daula and Mughal emperor Shah Alam II. British Army’s command was in the hands of Major Hector Munro in the Battle of Buxar. The battle of Buxar assured the result of Plassey battle and established British supremacy on Banaras and Allahabad (Prayagraj) across the Ganges. The battle of Buxar made way for British and proved that there was no strong competitor before the British. The battle of Buxar completed what Plassey had begun. During the battle of Buxar Nawab of Bengal was Mir Jafar. According to Sir James Stephen, ‘’The battle of Buxar deserves more credit than the battle of Plassey as the origin of British power in India”. If the results of both significant battles are analyzed, it can be said that the battle of Plassey was won by treachery, but the battle of Buxar showed the supremacy of English armies and military skills. Plassey made the English the only controllers of Bengal while Buxar raised the political prestige of the Company throughout India.

52.s: Najm-ud-Daula, who became Nawab of Bengal in 1765, was the son of:
52.x: Najm-ud-Daula was Mir Jafar's son; he held the Nizamat in name only.
xa: **Diwani** = revenue + civil justice; **Nizamat** = police, criminal justice.
**Dual Government** lasted **1765-72**; **Warren Hastings** ended it.
**Raja Shitab Rai** was naib diwan for **Bihar**.

52.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?

Sarfaraz Khan – Stopped both companies fortifying Calcutta and Chandannagar
Alivardi Khan – Killed Shaukat Jang at Manihari

**Siraj-ud-Daulah** was **Alivardi's grandson**.

52.s: Who was the Nawab of Bengal at the time of the Battle of Buxar (October 1764)?
52.x: Mir Jafar had been restored in 1763 and was Nawab during Buxar. Mir Qasim fought at Buxar as the deposed ex-Nawab, Siraj died after Plassey (1757), and Najm-ud-Daula became Nawab only in 1765.
52.tq: Buxar: Mir Qasim = ex-Nawab; Mir Jafar = sitting Nawab
xs: **Mir Jafar**, restored in **1763**, was Nawab during Buxar — option **(4)**.
**Mir Qasim** fought as the **deposed** Nawab; **Siraj** was executed after **Plassey**.
**Najm-ud-Daula** became Nawab only from **1765**.
xa: Mir Jafar's second term: **1763-1765**; he died soon after Buxar.
In this term he accepted **limits on the size of his army**.

52.s: Under Najm-ud-Daula (1765), defence and administration were handed to the Naib Subahdar:
52.x: The 1765 arrangement handed defence and administration to the Naib Subahdar Muhammad Reza Khan; the Nawab kept the Nizamat in name only.

52.s: Sirajuddaula was defeated by Lord Clive in the battle of-
52.x: Sirajuddaula was defeated by Lord Clive in the battle of Plassey in 1757 A.D.

52.s: The battlefield of Plassey is situated in –
52.x: Plassey (present name - Palasi) battlefield is located on the banks of the Bhagirathi River in Nadia district of West Bengal. On 23 June 1757 AD, the troops of the British East India Company led by Robert Clive defeated Nawab of Bengal Sirajuddaula, in the historic Battle of Plassey.

52.s: Following the Battle of Plassey, which one of the following combinations of concessions was obtained by the Company?
o: Kora and Allahabad, together with the Nizamat of Bengal
Diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa and control of Awadh
The whole of Bengal without the appointment of a Nawab
Zamindari of the 24 Parganas, duty-free trade and resources to fight the French

52.tq: Group the immediate commercial, territorial and strategic results of one event.
xs: After Plassey the Company got the **zamindari of the 24 Parganas**, **duty-free trade** in Bengal, Bihar, Orissa, and **resources to beat the French** — option **(4)**.
**Diwani** and **Awadh's** dependence came after **Buxar**; **Kora and Allahabad** went to **Shah Alam II** in **1765**.
xa: Mir Jafar became Nawab and paid **Rs 1.77 crore**.
Plassey: **puppet Nawab, 24 Parganas**; Buxar: **Diwani**, Awadh dependent.

52.s: Who was the last independent Nawab of Bengal?
52.x: Siraj-ud-Daulah, the last independent Nawab, was defeated by Clive at Plassey despite French support.
xa: Conspirators inside his army: **Mir Jafar**, **Rai Durlabh**, **Jagat Seth**, **Omichund**, **Manik Chand**.

52.s: Which of the following was NOT a cause of conflict between the English Company and Siraj-ud-Daulah?
o: Fortification of Calcutta without the Nawab's consent
Misuse of dastaks by Company servants
Sheltering of the Nawab's enemies by the Company
French refusal to obey the Nawab's order to stop fortification

52.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched with the conspiracy surrounding the Battle of Plassey?
o: Mir Madan — principal conspirator against Siraj
Governor Drake — leader of the anti-Company faction
52.x: Mir Jafar, who held the office of Mir Bakshi, was a principal conspirator against Siraj-ud-Daulah. Mir Madan was loyal to Siraj, while Holwell and Drake were associated with the British side.

xs: **Mir Jafar — Mir Bakshi** is correctly matched — option **(1)**.
**Mir Madan** was **loyal** to Siraj, not a conspirator.
**Holwell** was a European prisoner in the Black Hole; **Drake** was the Governor who fled to **Fulta**.

52.s: Which one of the following was a consequence specifically associated with the Battle of Buxar rather than the Battle of Plassey?
o: The Company restored the privileges of the 1717 farman.
The Company obtained the zamindari of the 24 Parganas.
Mir Jafar became Nawab of Bengal.
The Company secured the Diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa and made Awadh dependent.

xs: **Diwani of Bengal, Bihar, Orissa** and a **dependent Awadh** came from **Buxar** — option **(4)**.
**1717 farman privileges** were restored at **Alinagar (Feb 1757)**.
**24 Parganas** and **Mir Jafar as Nawab** were results of **Plassey**.
xa: Buxar's enemy: **Bengal + Awadh + Mughal Emperor** together.
Plassey's result: **puppet Nawab**, **24 Parganas**.

52.s: The Battle of Plassey was fought on which of the following dates and at which place?
52.x: The Battle of Plassey was fought on 23 June 1757 at Palashi, also known as Plassey, on the Bhagirathi River.

xs: Plassey: **23 June 1757**, at **Plassey (Palashi)** — option **(3)**.

**22 October 1764** is **Buxar**, fought in Bihar.

52.s: Which one of the following was NOT a conspirator against Siraj-ud-Daula at Plassey?

52.s: Which of the following correctly represents the two periods of Mir Jafar's tenure as Nawab of Bengal?

xs: Mir Jafar ruled **1757-1760** and again **1763-1765** — option **(4)**.

xa: Mir Jafar was removed in **1760** — he could not meet **Company demands**.

52.s: Which one of the following was a reason for Mir Jafar's removal from office in 1760?
o: He surrendered Bengal to the Dutch.
He refused to accept the grant of Diwani to the Company.
He could not meet the Company's demands.
52.x: Mir Jafar was removed in 1760 because he could not meet the increasing demands of the Company.

52.s: Who was the ruler of Delhi at the time of the battle of Buxar?
52.x: On 22/23 October, 1764 A.D. British Army defeated allied forces of Mir Qasim, Nawab of Oudh Shuja-ud-Daula and Mughal emperor Shah Alam II. British Army’s command was in the hands of Major Hector Munro in the Battle of Buxar. The battle of Buxar assured the result of Plassey battle and established British supremacy on Banaras and Allahabad (Prayagraj) across the Ganges. The battle of Buxar made way for British and proved that there was no strong competitor before the British. The battle of Buxar completed what Plassey had begun. During the battle of Buxar Nawab of Bengal was Mir Jafar. According to Sir James Stephen, ‘’The battle of Buxar deserves more credit than the battle of Plassey as the origin of British power in India”. If the results of both significant battles are analyzed, it can be said that the battle of Plassey was won by treachery, but the battle of Buxar showed the supremacy of English armies and military skills. Plassey made the English the only controllers of Bengal while Buxar raised the political prestige of the Company throughout India.

52.s: Which one of the following is the correct chronological order of the battles fought in India in the 18 th Century?

The Battle of Plassey established British political influence in Bengal. The Battle of Wandiwash decisively ended French ambitions in India by securing British supremacy in the Carnatic region. 52.s: Which one of the following rulers had granted Diwani to the East India Company?
52.x: As per the first Treaty of Allahabad (August 1765 A.D.), the Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II was taken under the Company’s protection and was to reside at Allahabad. The Emperor issued an order dated 12th August, 1765 granting Company the Diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa. During this time Robert Clive was Governor of East India Company in Bengal. The emperor’s order legalized the political authority of Company in Bengal and British rule expanded all over India including Delhi. Successors of Shah Alam II i.e. Akbar II (1806-37 A.D.) and Bahadurshah II (1837-57 A.D.) became pensioners of East India Company.

52.s: Who was appointed Deputy Diwan of Murshidabad by Robert Clive after the Allahabad Treaty?
52.x: According to the Treaty of Allahabad (August, 1765 A.D.), Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II was taken under the Company’s protection and had to reside at Allahabad. Shah Alam II conferred Diwani (fiscal revenue collection authority) of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa to the Company by issuing ‘Farman’ on 12 August, 1765 A.D. Nazm-ud-duala (son of Mir Jafar) was accepted as Nawab of Bengal. In return, the company had to pay the emperor an annual sum of Rs 26 Lakhs as pension. At that time, the Company was neither interested in taking responsibility for tax revenue collection nor was it capable of doing so. Therefore, the Company appointed two Diwans- Mohammad Raza Khan for Bengal and Raja Shitab Rai for Bihar. Thus, all business of Diwani and Nizamat was conducted by Indians but authorized by the British Company.

54.s: Who was the first Indian ruler to accept Lord Wellesley's Subsidiary Alliance?
54.x:
The Subsidiary Alliance System was introduced by Lord Wellesley in 1798 to expand British political control over Indian states. The Nizam of Hyderabad became the first Indian ruler to accept this alliance in 1798. Under the treaty, the Nizam agreed to maintain a permanent British force in his territory and surrendered control over foreign affairs. In return, the British promised military protection. This marked the beginning of British political supremacy in the Deccan and reduced Hyderabad's independence. Hence, the correct answer is Option (3).
Exam Note:
• First ruler under Subsidiary Alliance – Nizam of Hyderabad
• Year – 1798

54.s: Which one of the following statements does not apply to the system of Subsidiary Alliance introduced by Lord Wellesley?
o: To maintain a large standing army at others expense
To keep India safe from Napoleonic danger
To secure a fixed income for the Company
To establish British paramountcy over the Indian States
54.x: Statement (c) does not apply to the system of Subsidiary Alliance: The primary objective was to establish military and political dominance rather than ensuring a stable revenue for the Company. Though the Subsidiary Alliance system was quite old, Wellesley gave it a definite shape. Under the system, the ruler of the allied Indian state was compelled to accept the permanent stationing of a British force within his territory and to pay a subsidy for its maintenance. The ruler, unable to pay the expenses, had to cede a part of his kingdom to the British. The British agreed to defend the ruler from his enemies. They also controlled the defence and foreign relations of the protected ally. In return, the Indian ruler of the protected state should keep a British Resident at his court and disband his own army.  Indian rulers should not employ Europeans in their service without the approval of the British.  Indian rulers should not negotiate with any other Indian ruler without consulting the Governor-General. • The System of Subsidiary Alliance was also aimed at preventing French influence (the Napoleonic threat) from entering India. This system enabled the British to uphold a substantial army, with the financial burden falling Modern Indian History PMF IAS IH – 154 on the local rulers (it helped the British to have paramountcy over the Indian States), and was not implemented for securing a fixed income for the East India Company.

54.s: Which one of the following statements does not apply to the system of Subsidiary Alliance introduced by Lord Wellesley?
o: To maintain a large standing army at other’s expense
To keep India safe from Napoleonic danger
To secure a fixed income for the company
To establish British paramountcy over the Indian States
54.x: Governor-General Lord Wellesley came to India in 1798 A.D. at a time when the British were locked in a life and death struggle with France all over the world. The fear of Napoleon haunted the Britishers everywhere. To achieve his political aims, Wellesley relied on the system of Subsidiary Alliance. While the practice of helping Indian rulers with a paid British force was quite old, it was given shape by Wellesley who used it to sub-ordinate the Indian states to the paramountcy of the company. Under the subsidiary Alliance system, the ruler of the allying state was compelled to accept the permanent stationing of a British force within his territory and to pay a subsidy for its maintenance. However, to secure a fixed income for the company was not under the agenda of the Subsidiary Alliance.

o: provide direct British administration at the lowest possible cost

54.x: Wellesley designed the system to counter French influence and establish British paramountcy without assuming the cost of direct administration.
54.tq: Identify the stated aim rather than confusing political control with direct annexation.
xs: The aim was to **counter French influence** and **establish British paramountcy** without the cost of **direct administration** — option **(4)**.
Option (1) is the opposite: the system avoided direct administration.
Another aim: maintain a large army **at the Indian states' cost**.
xa: Introduced by **Lord Wellesley**, **1798**.
First state: **Hyderabad (1798)**.

xa: The ruler **paid for its upkeep**, in cash or by **ceding territory**.
In return the Company **protected the state's borders**.

o: Thomas Munro — Introduced Ryotwari and surveyed the districts from 1802 to 1807

o: He introduced mahalwari settlement from Punjab into the Ceded Districts and died at Hyderabad in 1827.

xs: **Munro** brought **Ryotwari** from the **Bara Mahals** to the Ceded Districts and died as Governor at **Pattikonda** in **1827** — option **(4)**.

101.s: In which year did Collector's administration come into force in place of the Revenue Board?
101.x:
In 1786, the British administration replaced the Board of Revenue system with the Collector system in order to improve revenue administration. District Collectors became the chief executive officers responsible for revenue collection, judicial administration and maintenance of law and order. This system later became the backbone of British district administration throughout India. Hence, the correct answer is Option (1).
Exam Note:
• Collector System Introduced – 1786
• Purpose – Efficient Revenue Administration

101.s:
Assertion (A): In 1794 the Chief-and-Council system in the Northern Circars was replaced by District Collectors.
Reason (R): The Permanent Settlement was introduced in the Northern Circars in 1802.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
101.x: Both are true but R does not explain A: Collectors replaced the Chiefs and Councils in 1794, while the Permanent Settlement came later, in 1802, so it cannot explain the earlier change.
101.tq: Check the dates: a later reform cannot explain an earlier one.
n: The Collector’s administration came into existence in place of the Board of Revenue in 1794. [AP History · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 15-16]
The Office of Collector was introduced in the North Sarkar region in 1802. [AP History · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 15-16]
xs: **Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A** — option **(2)**.
A: in **1794** the **Chiefs and Councils** were replaced by **District Collectors**.
R: the **Permanent Settlement** reached Andhra in **1802** — later, so it cannot explain A.
xa: ⚠ Exam key: "Collector's administration in place of the Revenue Board" = **1786** (APPSC G2 **2012**).
From **1794** each Collector handled land revenue, law and order and magistracy; judicial powers removed in **1816**.
The **Office of Collector** reached the **North Sarkar region** in **1802**.

101.s: Under Company revenue administration, the officer at the taluk level was the:
101.x: The Board of Revenue was at state level, the Collector at district, the Tahsildar at taluk and the Karanam and Munsab at village level.
xa: Division: **Sub-Collector / Revenue Officer**; Firka: **Deputy Tahsildar / Firka Revenue Inspector**.
Karanam and Munsab were **hereditary** village officers.

101.s: The Circuit Committee, while examining revenue administration in the Andhra region, recommended which of the following?
o: Replacement of ryotwari by permanent settlement
Abolition of the auction system of revenue collection
Continuation of the auction system with higher minimum bids
Transfer of revenue collection entirely to village panchayats

Auctions hurt both the government and the **ryots**.
xa: **Munro** then abolished auctions in **Rayalaseema**.
Before **1802**, zamindaris were given by **auction**; the **Permanent Settlement** replaced auctions with a fixed demand.

101.tq: PYQ wording 'Collector in place of Revenue Board' = 1786.
xs: In the PYQ wording, the Collector's administration replaced the Revenue Board in **1786** — option **(2)** (**APPSC G2 2012** key).
The notes date the **Collector system** in coastal Andhra to **1794**; for this exact wording, answer **1786**.
xa: **1786** is also the year of the **Madras Board of Revenue**.
**1816**: Collectors lost judicial powers.
**1802**: Permanent Settlement in Andhra; Ryotwari in the Ceded Districts.

xs: The **Ceded Districts (1800)** = **Kadapa, Kurnool, Anantapur and Bellary** — option **(1)**.

xa: **1911** = **Chittoor** carved out, giving **Kadapa** its present area.
Coastal Andhra had **5 districts**: **Ganjam, Visakhapatnam, Godavari, Krishna, Nellore**.
⚠ Exam angle: the **Kadapa 1911** trap.

101.s:
Statement (A): Moturpha is a salt tax levied by the British East India Company.
Statement (B): The revenue collected by the British East India Company from the Zamindars is called Peshcush.
101.x:
Statement (A) is false. Moturpha was not a salt tax. It was a professional or trade tax imposed on artisans, craftsmen, traders and occupational groups by the British East India Company. The salt tax was a separate levy imposed on the manufacture and sale of salt.
Statement (B) is true. Peshcush refers to the fixed annual tribute or land revenue paid by Zamindars to the British East India Company under the Zamindari system. It became an important source of revenue during British rule in the Madras Presidency. Therefore, Statement (A) is false and Statement (B) is true. Hence, the correct answer is Option (4).
Exam Note:
• Moturpha – Tax on professions, trades and occupations.
• Peshcush – Fixed revenue paid by Zamindars to the British.

101.s: What does "Moturpha" refer to?
101.x:
Moturpha was a professional tax imposed on artisans and craftsmen, particularly on weavers and their looms. It was one of the important taxes collected during the colonial period and was strongly opposed by the weaving community because it increased their economic burden. Hence, the correct answer is Option (3).
Exam Note:
• Moturpha – Tax on Looms

101.s: Moturpha indicates:
Statement (A): Moturpha is a salt tax levied by British East India Company. Statement (B): The revenue collected by the British East India Company from the zamindars was called ' Peshcush '.
101.x: Moturpha was a profession or trade tax on artisans, weavers and traders, not a salt tax-so Statement A is false. ' Peshcush ' correctly refers to the fixed tribute that zamindars and other intermediary revenue-holders paid to the East India Company under the Permanent Settlement, making Statement B true. Distinguishing colonial revenue terms is a frequently tested area.

101.s:
Which of the following statements is/are correct regarding the Revenue system in the Andhra Region during the British Period?
A) British Administrative System has divided their land tax management systems into three methods
B) They imposed Zamindari system in Uttara Sarkaru districts; Ryotwari system in Datta mandals
Which of the following was a major consequence associated with the Ryotwari system in the Andhra region?
o: Abolition of direct contact between cultivator and government
Over-assessment, indebtedness to moneylenders and land alienation
Fixed revenue payable only by zamindars
101.x: Ryotwari areas experienced heavy assessment, often exceeding 50 percent of the produce, along with dependence on moneylenders and alienation of land.
101.tq: Link the revenue arrangement with its stated economic consequences.
xs: **Ryotwari** brought **over-assessment** (often **50%+** of produce), **moneylenders** and **land alienation** — option **(2)**.
Ryotwari was settled with the **ryot directly** — it did not abolish that contact or work through zamindars.
xa: First region: **Baramahal (1792)** under **Captain Alexander Read** with **Munro**.
In Andhra it began in the **Ceded Districts in 1802**; extended across Madras in **1820**.
Zamindari's effect: absentee landlordism, impoverished tenants.

101.s: Which of the following correctly represents the regional distribution of Zamindari and Ryotwari in Andhra?
o: Zamindari in the Northern Circars and Ryotwari in Rayalaseema, later extending to most of Andhra
Zamindari in Rayalaseema and Ryotwari in the Northern Circars
Ryotwari in the Northern Circars and Zamindari in the Ceded Districts
Both Zamindari and Ryotwari were confined to Nellore
101.x: Zamindari prevailed in the Northern Circars, while Ryotwari was associated with Rayalaseema and later covered most of Andhra.
101.tq: Use the AP regional contrast as the decisive clue.
xs: **Zamindari** in the **Northern Circars**; **Ryotwari** in **Rayalaseema**, later most of Andhra — option **(1)**.
Circar estates: **Vizianagaram, Bobbili, Pithapuram**; Ryotwari began in the **Ceded Districts in 1802**.
xa: **Mahalwari** is placed in **Nellore**.
Zamindari settled with the zamindar (intermediary); Ryotwari with the ryot directly.
Effects: zamindari → absentee landlordism; ryotwari → over-assessment, moneylenders.

101.s: The Permanent Settlement, introduced by Cornwallis in 1793, was applied to the Andhra zamindaris in:
101.x: It was applied in Andhra in 1802, replacing the earlier auction of zamindaris with a fixed demand. 1794 is when the Collector system began. 1800 is the cession of the Ceded Districts. 1820 is when Ryotwari was extended across Madras under Munro.
xs: The **Permanent Settlement** (**Cornwallis**, **1793**) was applied in Andhra in **1802** — option **(3)**.
**1802** is also when **Ryotwari** began in the **Ceded Districts**.
xa: Before **1802**, zamindaris were given by **auction**.
**1794** = Collector system; **1800** = Ceded Districts; **1820** = Ryotwari across Madras.

101.s: Vizianagaram, Bobbili and Pithapuram were estates under the ____ system.
101.x: Vizianagaram, Bobbili and Pithapuram were Zamindari estates; Ryotwari dealt directly with the ryot.
xa: Ryotwari began in **Rayalaseema** and later spread to most of Coastal Andhra.
Zamindari abolished by the **Madras Estates Act, 1948**.

101.s: An important effect of the Zamindari system in the Northern Circars was:
o: uniform assessment limited to one-fourth of the produce
transfer of all land rights to village headmen
absentee landlordism and impoverishment of tenants
101.x: The Zamindari system encouraged absentee landlordism and impoverished tenants.
xa: Estates: **Vizianagaram, Bobbili, Pithapuram**, under the **Permanent Settlement (1802)**.
Ryotwari's effect, by contrast: **over-assessment** (often **50%+** of produce), moneylenders and land alienation.
Abolished by the **Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948**.

101.s: ‘Peshkash’ refers to:
o: The share of revenue paid by zamindars to the British
Revenue collected by zamindars from farmers
101.x: Peshkash was the share of revenue paid by zamindars to the British.
101.tq: Discriminate among closely related colonial revenue terms.
xs: **Peshkash** = the share of revenue / tribute **zamindars paid to the British** — option **(2)**.
**Haveli lands** = land under direct British control; **Korunu** = revenue zamindars collected from farmers; **Moturpha** = tax on looms.
xa: **APP** spells it "**peshcush**"; "Peshcush is the revenue collected from zamindars" is true (**PYQ 2025**).
Zamindari lands: **9/10** of estimated revenue to government, **1/10** to the zamindar.
⚠ "**Moturpha** is a salt tax" is false — it was a **tax on looms** (**APPSC G2 2011**).

101.s: Haveli lands in coastal Andhra were lands:
o: Assigned to the Nizam as military grants
101.x: Haveli lands were under the direct control of the British in coastal Andhra.
101.tq: Identify the exact ownership or control category.
xs: **Haveli lands** were lands **held directly under British control** in coastal Andhra — option **(3)**.
Lands held by zamindars were **zamindari lands**, a separate category.
xa: Zamindari lands: **9/10** of estimated revenue to government, **1/10** to the zamindar; agreements ran for **10** years.
**Peshkash** = tribute zamindars paid to the British; **Korunu** = revenue zamindars collected from farmers.
⚠ **Peshkash** = zamindar → British; **Korunu** = farmer → zamindar.

101.s: Under Company rule, 'Sayer' referred to:
o: a tax on looms and occupations
inland transit and customs duties on goods
101.x: Sayer was the inland transit and customs duty; Abkari was excise on liquor and Moturpha a tax on looms and trades.
xa: The Madras Native Association's **1861** petition complained about Moturpha.
⚠ **Peshkash** = zamindar → British; **Korunu** = farmer → zamindar.
**Haveli lands** = under **direct British control** in coastal Andhra.

101.s: Moturpha was levied mainly on which of the following?
o: Trades and occupations such as looms, shops and artisan activities
101.x: Moturpha was imposed on trades and occupations, including looms, shops and artisans. It was not a salt tax.
101.tq: Separate the look-alike revenue terms by identifying the actual taxable activity.
xs: **Moturpha** was a tax on **trades and occupations — looms, shops, artisans** — option **(1)**.
It was **not a salt tax**; liquor and toddy fell under **Abkari**, and zamindars' land revenue was **Peshkash**.
xa: **APPSC G2 2011** key: Moturpha = **tax on looms**.
The **Madras Native Association's 1861** petition complained about it.
**Sayer** = inland transit and customs duties.

101.s: Abkari under Company rule referred to:
101.x: Abkari was the excise on liquor and toddy; Sayer was transit duty and Moturpha a loom tax.

101.s: 'Korunu' referred to the revenue collected by:
101.x: Korunu was what zamindars collected from farmers; Peshkash was what zamindars paid the British.

101.s: In Andhra, the Ryotwari system was first introduced in:
101.x: Ryotwari came first to the Ceded Districts (1802); its first region overall was Baramahal (1792).

101.s: Which system of land revenue was associated with Nellore?
101.x: Nellore had the Mahalwari system, settled with village headmen.

101.s: Ryotwari was extended across the Madras Presidency under Governor Munro in:
101.x: In 1820 Ryotwari was extended across Madras under Governor Munro.

101.s: The Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948 came into force on:
101.x: The Act came into force on 19 April 1949; the first estates were taken over from 7 September 1949.

101.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Peshkash – Tribute paid by zamindars to the British
101.x: Peshkash was the fixed tribute zamindars paid to the British; Sayer was transit duty, Moturpha a loom tax, and Haveli lands were under direct British control.

101.s: Which of the following are present-day silk hubs of Rayalaseema?
101.x: Dharmavaram and Madanapalle are present-day silk hubs; sericulture was promoted by the British in the Ceded Districts in the late 19th-early 20th centuries.
xa: Ceded Districts = **Kadapa, Kurnool, Anantapur, Bellary**.
Name **Rayalaseema** adopted in **1928**.

101.s: The growing divergence between the fertile and educated Circars and the arid and neglected Ceded Districts later influenced debates surrounding the:
101.x: The contrasting development of the Circars and the Ceded Districts later shaped the Sri Bagh Pact debate. The other pacts belong to different political contexts.
101.tq: Link a regional socio-economic contrast with the agreement it later influenced.
xs: The divergence between the **fertile, educated Circars** and the **arid, neglected Ceded Districts** later shaped the **Sri Bagh Pact** debate — option **(2)**.
The Circars came to the Company in **1766**; the Ceded Districts only in **1800**, and they grew apart under British rule.
xa: Ceded Districts = today's **Rayalaseema**; name adopted at **Nandyal, 1928**.
The Circars correspond to **Srikakulam, Vizianagaram, Visakhapatnam, East and West Godavari, Krishna + Guntur**.

101.s: The Zilla or District Court functioned under a District Judge. The post of District Judge was created by the:
101.x: The post of District Judge was created under the Cornwallis Code of 1793. The Madras Regulations of 1816 related chiefly to Munsiff and Panchayat courts.
101.tq: Use the legislation–office association and reject neighbouring judicial enactments.
xs: The **District Judge** post was created by the **Cornwallis Code, 1793** — option **(1)**.
The **Madras District Police Act** came in **1859**; the **Madras Regulations of 1816** set up **Munsiff** and **Panchayat** courts.
xa: District courts were also called **Zilla** courts.
After the **1816** separation, civil justice stayed with the District Judge.

101.s: The introduction of British judicial procedure in place of village panchayats was criticised mainly because it:
o: was slow and costly and contributed to litigation and debt
made justice quicker and less expensive
reduced litigation and eliminated rural debt
transferred all judicial powers to hereditary village officers
101.x: British judicial procedure displaced village panchayats and was criticised as slow and costly. It increased litigation and contributed to indebtedness.
101.tq: Select the option that combines all the stated consequences without reversing the criticism.
xs: British procedure was **slow and costly** and fed **litigation and debt**, displacing village panchayats — option **(1)**.
It did not make justice quicker or cheaper, nor reduce rural debt.
xa: **Munro**'s **1816** Regulations set up **Munsiff** and **Panchayat** courts as courts of first instance.
Village officials handled **petty thefts**.
The **District Collector** became the pivot of British rule and ended village autonomy.

101.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched with the judicial hierarchy in the Madras Presidency?
101.x: The Munsiff Court functioned at the taluk level, while the Zilla Court functioned at the district level. Sadar Adalats were apex courts for natives at Madras.
101.tq: Use the administrative level as the anchor for matching the court.
xs: **Taluk — Munsiff Court** is correct — option **(3)**.
The **Zilla Court** was at the **district** level; **Sadar Adalat** was the apex civil court at Madras.
xa: Appeal: **Provincial Courts of Appeal / Circuit courts** (powers expanded in **1820**).
Apex criminal court: **Sadar Faujdari Adalat**.
**Madras Supreme Court (1801)** for British subjects in Madras town.

101.s: The Indian Penal Code was enacted in:
101.x: The IPC dates to 1860; the CPC to 1859 and the CrPC to 1861.
xa: **Madras District Police Act** — also **1859**.
Criticism: slow, costly British procedure displaced village **panchayats** → litigation and debt.

101.s: Thomas Munro was President of the Judicial Commission constituted in:
101.x: Munro presided over the Judicial Commission of 1814; its report was submitted in April 1816 and largely accepted.
xa: Result: the **Madras Regulations of 1816** — Munsiff and Panchayat courts.
**1818**: magistrates got powers to punish.

101.s: The Madras Regulations of 1816 provided for:
o: Abolition of all village-level judicial institutions
Munsiff and Panchayat courts as courts of first instance
Transfer of civil justice from District Judges to Collectors
Creation of the Madras High Court
101.x: The Madras Regulations of 1816 established Munsiff courts and Panchayat courts in every large village and district as courts of first instance.
101.tq: Match the regulation with its immediate institutional reform.
xs: The **Madras Regulations of 1816** set up **Munsiff and Panchayat courts** as **courts of first instance** — option **(2)**.
They strengthened, not abolished, village-level justice: village officials handled **petty thefts**.
xa: Panchayat courts were set up in every large village and district.
Same year (**1816**): Collectors lost judicial powers; civil justice stayed with **District Judges**.
Munro (**1816**) moved **police supervision** from judges to **Collectors**.

101.s: Who created thanas under the supervision of darogas in the early British police administration?
101.x: Cornwallis created thanas under darogas, who were Indian officers assisted by constables. Darogas were criticised for abusing their power.

53.x: Marathas opposed the British vigorously in India. Maratha were suppressed after three Anglo-Maratha Wars. On the ruins of Mughal Empire, Maratha laid down their foundation and British also took advantage of these circumstances. British lost first Anglo-Maratha war badly and this war ended with the Treaty of Salbai. Lord Wellesley trapped Peshwa in the cage of Subsidiary Alliance in 1802. Lord Hastings established British supremacy after the devastation of remnant strength of Marathas in 1818. Regional States : Punjab and Mysore *Ranjit Singh was born to the chief of Sukerchakia Misl on 13 th November, 1780 A.D. Treaty of Amritsar was signed between Maharaja Ranjit Singh and British East India Company on 25 th April, 1809 A.D. Ranjit Singh captured Multan in 1818 A.D., Kashmir in 1819 and Peshawar and North-West frontier (Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa) in 1834 A.D.. *In 1798 AD, Zaman Shah attacked Punjab. While returning, his cannons accidentally fell into the Jhelam River (some sources refer for Chenab River but Jhelam River is authenticated by many historians). These cannons were sent back to Jaman Shah by Ranjit Singh. Happy with this gesture of Ranjit Singh, Jaman Shah allowed Ranjit Singh to rule Lahore. As a result, in 1799 A.D., Ranjit Singh took control of Lahore and made it his Capital. 53.x: Second Anglo-Maratha War from 1803 to 1805 A.D. was fought during the period of Lord Wellesley. The third Anglo- Maratha War (1817-18 A.D.) took place in the reign of Lord Hastings. After defeating Marathas in third Anglo-Maratha War, Lord Hastings abolished the title of Peshwa and merged all the regions of Peshwa in the Bombay presidency. Apart from this, the Company took over the political authority of Bundelkhand, Malwa and rest of India ( Peshwa dominating regions). Other three options are correctly matched.

53.s: Subsidiary Alliance was implemented during the reign of –
53.x: Lord Wellesley (1798-1805) cleverly used a subsidiary alliance as a tool to make Indian provinces puppets of Britishers. He did not discover this method. This method was in practice earlier also but it gradually evolved and the final shape was provided by Wellesley. Dupleix was the first European to give his army to an Indian ruler on the promise of a fixed payment to the Company. Britishers used these tactics too. First Subsidiary Alliance was signed in 1765 with Awadh where Company promised to protect the boundaries of Awadh on a fixed payment to the Company. The evolved version of the Subsidiary Alliance was accepted by the Princely States in the following Sequence- Hyderabad (1798 AD and 1800 AD), Mysore (1799 AD), Tanjore (1799 AD), Oudh (1801 AD), Peshwa (1802), Bhonsle of Barar (1803 AD), Sindhiya (1804 AD), Holkar (1818 AD), Jodhpur, Jaipur, Machheri, Bundi and Bharatpur. Note : Hyderabad will be the answer if it is asked first state to join Wellesley's subsidiary alliance.

60.s: Who was mainly responsible for introducing the Ryotwari System in the Madras Presidency?
60.x:
The Ryotwari System was introduced in the Madras Presidency by Sir Thomas Munro during the early nineteenth century. Under this system, the government collected land revenue directly from individual cultivators (Ryots) instead of through Zamindars or intermediaries. Every ryot was recognized as the proprietor of his land, provided he regularly paid the land revenue fixed by the government. The system was first experimented with in parts of South India and later became the principal land revenue system in the Madras Presidency. It aimed to eliminate intermediaries, but in practice the heavy land tax often placed a severe burden on cultivators. Hence, the correct answer is Option (2).

With reference to Ryotwari Settlement, consider the following statements

60.x: All statements are correct: Under the Ryotwari Settlement (Munro System), the cultivator (ryot) was recognised as the owner of his land, subject to paying land revenue. 61.s: The artificially fixed rupee-sterling exchange rate prescribed by the Hilton-Young Commission (1926) was adopted by the British Government for which one of the following reasons?
o: Aiding the flow of remittances from India and maintaining India's creditworthiness
Encouraging the export of cotton produce from India
Preventing depreciation of the Rupee in terms of gold
61.x: Statement (a) is the correct answer: The Hilton-Young Commission recommended fixing the rupee-sterling exchange rate at 1s. 6d. (one rupee = 1 shilling and 6 pence). This was an artificially high (overvalued) rate compared to what many Indian nationalists and economists demanded (1s. 4d.). The British Government adopted this rate to facilitate the smooth and cheaper transfer of remittances from India to Britain. These included pensions of British officials, interest on public debt, military expenses, and dividends of British companies. A stronger rupee meant fewer rupees were needed to buy the required sterling for these remittances. It helped maintain India's creditworthiness in the London money market, making it easier for the Government of India to raise loans in Britain. Statement (b) is incorrect: An overvalued rupee made imported British goods cheaper for Indian buyers, benefiting British manufacturers and hurting Indian industries, which faced stiff competition from cheaper imports. Indian importers benefited, but this was not the main British motive. Statement (c) is incorrect: The artificially fixed high exchange rate hurt Indian exports (including cotton). Statement (d) is incorrect: The rate was fixed in relation to sterling, not primarily to prevent depreciation against gold. • Note: The Hilton-Young Commission (1926) has recently been in the news because 2026 marks the 100 th anniversary of its recommendations, which ultimately paved the way for the establishment

59.s: Wellesley established the Fort William College at Calcutta because:
o: He was asked by the board of directors at London to do so
He wanted to revive interest in oriental learning in India
He wanted to provide William Carey and his associates with employment
He wanted to train British civilians for administrative purposes in India
59.x: In 1800, Wellesley, the Governor-General, observed that despite ruling over vast areas, civil servants were sent to India at a young age without proper training, leading to a lack of necessary skills and knowledge of Indian languages. Therefore, on 24 November 1800, Wellesley established the College of Fort William at Calcutta to educate young recruits to the Civil Service. The college provided two years of training in literature, science, and languages in India. The Directors of the Company disapproved of the action of Wellesley and, in 1806, replaced the College of Fort William with their own East Indian College at Haileybury in England. The East Indian College provided training in oriental language, literature, and history.

59.s: Who was the first Indian to resist for the political reforms?
59.x: Raja Ram Mohan Roy was the first Indian to resist for political reforms. He wrote about human rights and the development of democratic valves. According to Bipin Chandra Pal, Ram Mohan Roy was first Indian political reformer. Although, some historians gave this credit to Surendra Nath Banerjee.

59.s: Who established the judicial organization in India?
59.x: Lord Cornwallis introduced criminal and judicial regulations to a significant degree which is still underpins the Indian Judicial system. Cornwallis gave limited judicial powers to the company’s revenue collectors, who already served as civil magistrates. In 1790 AD the company took over the administration of justice from Nawab and Cornwallis introduced a system of circuit courts with a superior court that met in Calcutta and had the power of review over the circuit court decision.

59.s: Which one the following social reformers strongly opposed Jury Act of 1826’?
59.x: The Jury Act of 1826 was the manifestation of the idea of religious superiority of the British government that introduced the nation of religious distinctions in the judicial system of the country. According to the act, only Christians had the right to sit as Jurors involving trials of Christians (whether Indian or European). He can also judge cases of the natives (Hindu and Muslims). The natives (Hindus and Muslisms) could sit as Jurors in the cases of trails of Hindus and Muslims but not of Christians. Ram Mohan Roy strongly opposed this act and the flagrant injustice contained under the act.

xs: The **Hindu Widow Remarriage Act** was passed in **1856** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Sati** was abolished in **1829**; the **Caste Disabilities Removal Act** is of **1850** (**1856** is the trap date).
xa: ⚠ Some notes date the Religious Disabilities Act to **1856**; the Act is of **1850**.
**1856** also = **General Service Enlistment Act** and the annexation of **Awadh**.

55.s:
Consider the following statements about the abolition of Sati:
1. It was carried out in 1829 under Lord Dalhousie.
2. Orthodox sections resented it as interference in custom.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
55.x: Statement 1 is wrong: Sati was abolished in 1829 under Lord William Bentinck, not Dalhousie. Statement 2 is correct: it was resented as interference in custom. So B; A and C accept the false statement 1, D rejects the true statement 2.
xs: Only statement **2** is correct — so option **(2) 2 only** is correct.
Statement 1 wrong: **Sati** was abolished in **1829** by **Bentinck**, not Dalhousie.
Statement 2 correct: it was resented as **interference in custom**.
xa: **Lex Loci Act (1850)**: converts could **inherit ancestral property**.
**Hindu Widow Remarriage Act (1856)** challenged orthodox norms.

55.s:
Consider the following statements about the Lex Loci Act (Religious / Caste Disabilities Act):
1. It was enacted in 1856.
2. It allowed converts to Christianity to inherit ancestral property.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
55.x: Statement 1 is wrong: the Act is of 1850 (1856 is the trap date of the Widow Remarriage Act). Statement 2 is correct: converts could inherit ancestral property, seen as an incentive to convert. So B; A and C accept the false date, D rejects the true statement 2.
xs: Only statement **2** is correct — so option **(2) 2 only** is correct.
Statement 1 wrong: the **Lex Loci / Caste Disabilities Removal Act** is of **1850**; **1856** is the trap date.
Statement 2 correct: converts to Christianity could **inherit ancestral property**, seen as a state **incentive to convert**.
xa: **1856** = **Hindu Widow Remarriage Act**.
**1829** = abolition of **Sati** (Bentinck).

55.s: Which developments before 1857 generated fears of mass conversion among Indians?
o: Ending of the Company's trade monopoly
Western education, railways and the telegraph
55.x: Western education, railways and the telegraph, along with missionaries preaching under police protection, created fears of mass conversion and loss of caste.
xa: Other grievances: **taxation of temple and mosque lands**; **racial arrogance** of officials.
After **1858** the Crown promised **religious neutrality** and withdrew state patronage from missionary work.

55.s: After 1858, the British Crown's policy towards religion in India was one of:
55.x: After 1858 the Crown promised religious neutrality and withdrew state patronage from missionary work.
xa: Before 1857, missionaries **preached under police protection** and attacked Hindu and Islamic practice.
The **Lex Loci Act (1850)** let converts **inherit ancestral property**, seen as an incentive to convert.

55.s: The Lex Loci (Caste Disabilities Removal) Act was passed in:
55.x: The Lex Loci Act is of 1850; 1856 is the Hindu Widow Remarriage Act.

55.s:
Consider the following statements about social measures before 1857:
1. Sati was abolished in 1829 under William Bentinck.
2. The Hindu Widow Remarriage Act was passed in 1856.
3. The Lex Loci Act allowed converts to Christianity to inherit ancestral property.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
55.x: All three are correct: Sati abolition (1829, Bentinck), Widow Remarriage Act (1856) and Lex Loci Act (1850) letting converts inherit.

55.s: Before 1857, Christian missionaries in India preached under:
55.x: Missionaries preached under police protection, which added to fears of mass conversion.

55.s: Which of the following was not a reason for making the sepoys of the East India Company rebellious?
o: The efforts of the officers of the company to spread
The order to the sepoys to travel on ships
55.x: The inefficiency of the officers was not a cause for the Sepoy Mutiny. The Indian Rebellion of 1857 occurred as a result of an accumulation of factors over time, rather than any single event such as an effort by officers to spread Christianity among the soldiers, which led to interference in the religious matters of the people. The order of the Company to the sepoys to travel on a ship was another reason as in Hinduism it was believed that travelling by sea could deprive them of their religious status of being a Hindu. A more immediate cause of the sepoy’s dissatisfaction was the recent order that they would not be given the foreign service allowance (Bhatta/Batta) when serving in Sindh or Punjab along with rumors of the use of animal fat in the cartridges of the New Enfield Rifle.

55.s: The General Service Enlistment Act, 1856 was passed under which Governor-General?
55.x: The Act was Canning's (1856); it required recruits to serve anywhere, including overseas, which orthodox Hindu sepoys feared would cost them caste.
xa: The order to travel by ship **was** a cause (BPSC key).
Earlier: **Barrackpore 1824** — refusal to go to **Burma by sea**.

55.s: Before 1857, 'bhatta' paid to sepoys was:
55.x: Bhatta was the foreign service allowance; it was withdrawn for service in Sindh and Punjab once they became British territory.
xa: **Bhatta mutinies** of the **1840s**: **34th NI 1844**, **66th NI 1849-50**.
Stopping of bhatta **was** a cause (BPSC **2018** key).

55.s: An Indian sepoy in the pre-1857 army could ordinarily rise no higher than:
55.x: Racial discrimination restricted the highest rank ordinarily attainable by an Indian soldier to Subedar.
55.tq: Test the exact promotion ceiling rather than general discrimination.
xs: An Indian could rise **no higher than Subedar** — so option **(2)** is correct.
This was part of the **racial discrimination** in pay and promotion.
xa: **APPSC-GS 2023** keyed the Subedar ceiling as correct.
Sepoys got **lower pay** than British soldiers and faced **racial contempt**.
Indians were also shut out of **high civil and military posts**.

55.s: On the eve of the Revolt of 1857, the approximate ratio of Indian sepoys to European soldiers in India was:
55.x: There were about 2.3 lakh Indian sepoys and 45,000 European soldiers, giving an approximate ratio of 5:1.
55.tq: Convert the supplied troop figures into the approximate ratio.
xs: About **2.3 lakh sepoys to 45,000 Europeans** — roughly **5:1** — so option **(4)** is correct.
So sepoys far outnumbered Europeans; ratios like **2:1** or **3:1** understate the gap.
xa: Europeans had been drawn off for the **Crimean and Persian wars**.
**Awadh** was the **"nursery of the Bengal Army"**.

55.s: The expression “peasants in uniform” referred to the fact that the sepoys:
o: Were recruited only from European farming communities
Were trained exclusively in agricultural work
Received land grants instead of salaries
Carried rural and village grievances into the army
55.x: The sepoys were largely drawn from rural communities, so their grievances reflected those of the villages from which they came.
55.tq: Translate a descriptive phrase into its historical implication.
xs: **"Peasants in uniform"**: sepoys **carried rural and village grievances into the army** — so option **(4)** is correct.
Their grievances **mirrored the village's**.
xa: Peasants suffered **heavy land revenue**, **debt** and loss of land to **moneylenders**.
**Awadh** = **"nursery of the Bengal Army"**.

55.s: Before the Revolt of 1857, mysterious chapatis were passed from village to village across:
55.x: The chapatis passed village to village across North India, not South India.
xa: The **Enfield** cartridges were believed greased with **cow and pig fat**.
All read as a plot to **force conversion**.

55.s: Which of the following was NOT a military grievance of the Indian sepoys mentioned in relation to the Revolt of 1857?
o: The ceiling of promotion at the rank of Subedar
55.x: Inefficiency of officers was identified as not being a cause of sepoy anger. Lower pay, racial contempt and the Subedar ceiling were genuine grievances.
55.tq: Find the one item expressly excluded from the list of grievances.
xs: **Inefficiency of officers** was **not** a cause — so option **(3)** is the answer (**BPSC 2018** key).
**Lower pay** than British soldiers, **racial contempt** and the **Subedar** ceiling were real grievances.
xa: **APPSC-GS 2023**: Subedar ceiling + greased cartridges both correct.
Missionary pressure, the order to travel by ship and stopping of **bhatta** **were** causes.

55.s: Bhatta, the foreign service allowance, was stopped for sepoys serving in:
55.x: Bhatta was withdrawn for service in Sindh and Punjab, which had become British territory.

55.s: Which region was called the 'nursery of the Bengal Army'?
55.x: Awadh supplied over 75,000 sepoys and was called the nursery of the Bengal Army.

55.s: On the eve of 1857, European troops in India were reduced because they were drawn off for the:
55.x: Europeans were drawn off for the Crimean and Persian wars, leaving about 45,000 against 2.3 lakh sepoys.

55.s: The revolt of 1857 was by?
55.x: The revolt of 1857 began as a mutiny of sepoys against the British.

55.s: The symbol of 1857 independence struggle was –
55.x: The symbol of 1857 Independence struggle was Chapatis (bread) and Lotus as the message was conveyed by these two. A class of historians considers that this mutiny was a wide and well-planned conspiracy. They mentioned the reach of Chapatis and Lotus in remote villages of North India and prophets, hermits and plays of Madaris to prove that fact.

55.s: When was the new Enfield Rifle with greased cartridges introduced in the British Indian Army?
55.x: The Company decided to use the new Enfield Rifle musket instead of old Brown Bess Standardised musket in December, 1856 A.D. The training for the use of this rifle was organized in Dum Dum, Ambala, and Sialkot. The rifle required an extraordinary kind of loading of a cartridge in the magazine and hence the soldiers while in the ensuing fight, had to bite off the outer covering of the cartridge while loading it down into the rifle’s muzzle. The cartridge was rumoured to have been greased with animal fat (Pig fat and Cow fat). The soldiers believed that this was an intentional act of the British to besmirch their religion. This became the immediate cause of the first Independence Struggle of India in 1857 A.D. 2. The immediate cause of India’s first war of independence was: (a) Doctrine of Lapse by Lord Dalhousie (b) Suspicion about British interference in religion (c) Military discontent (d) Economic exploitation of India R.A.S./R.T.S. (Pre) 1993 Ans. (b) See the explanation of the above question.

55.s: The annexation of princely states became a cause of discontent before the Revolt of 1857 because it—
o: ended the drain of wealth to Britain
created employment for thousands of court officials and soldiers
restored the authority of all displaced rulers
threw officials, retainers and soldiers of princely courts out of work
55.x: Annexations displaced thousands of officials, retainers and soldiers who had depended on princely courts for employment and patronage.
55.tq: Trace the administrative consequence of annexation.
xs: Annexations **threw officials, retainers and soldiers of princely courts out of work** — so option **(4)** is correct.
They did the opposite of creating jobs; and Company rule kept the **drain of wealth** going.
xa: In Awadh (**1856**), the deposition of **Wajid Ali Shah** cost lords, officials, retainers and soldiers their livelihoods.
**Pindaris and irregular soldiers** were also disbanded.
Annexations also ended **princely/court patronage** of artisans.
55.fixed: stem said annexation hurt the colonial administration, which the answer does not support

55.s: Who is regarded as the first martyr of the Revolt of 1857?
55.x: Mangal Pandey is identified as the first martyr of the Revolt of 1857.
55.tq: Test a first-in-sequence fact directly, while using other prominent figures as nearby distractors.
xs: **Mangal Pandey** is the **first martyr of 1857** — so option **(4)** is correct.
He attacked **Lt Baugh** and **Sergeant-Major Hewson** at **Barrackpore** on **29 March 1857**.
xa: He was hanged on **8 April 1857**; his regiment (**34th Bengal NI**) was disbanded.
On **21 July 2026** the PM paid tribute on his birth anniversary (born **19 July 1827**).
**Bahadur Shah II** was proclaimed **Shahenshah-e-Hindustan** on **11-12 May 1857**.

55.s: The Vellore mutiny of 1806 was chiefly triggered by which of the following measures?
o: Introduction of a new dress code and prohibition of caste marks and earrings
Refusal to cross the sea to Burma
Refusal to use the new rifle cartridges
55.x: The new dress code, including a turban with a leather cockade and restrictions on caste marks and earrings, caused resentment among the sepoys at Vellore.
55.tq: Distinguish the cause attached to a specific mutiny.
xs: **Vellore (July 1806)** was triggered by a **new dress code** — turban with **leather cockade**, ban on **caste marks and earrings** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Burma by sea** = **Barrackpore 1824**; **bhatta** = **1840s**; cartridges = **1857**.
xa: **Tipu's sons** were lodged in the Vellore fort.
UPPSC match key: **Vellore = July 1806**; **Barrackpur = Nov 1824**; **Santhal = 1855-56**.

55.s: The Barrackpore mutiny of November 1824 was caused by the sepoys’ refusal to—
55.x: The 47th Native Infantry at Barrackpore refused to go to Burma by sea during the First Anglo-Burmese War.
xs: The **47th NI** at Barrackpore (**November 1824**) refused to **go to Burma by sea** — so option **(2)** is correct.
It came during the **First Anglo-Burmese War**.
xa: ⚠ **Barrackpore 1824** (47th NI, Burma) ≠ **Barrackpore 1857** (**Mangal Pandey**, 34th Bengal NI).
**38th NI (1852)** also refused to go to **Burma**.

55.s: Why did the cartridges of the new Enfield rifle offend both Hindu and Muslim sepoys?
o: They were believed to contain cow and pig fat, and had to be bitten open.
They required sepoys to cross the sea before use.
They were made exclusively from animal skin.
They were distributed only to European soldiers.
55.x: The greased-paper cartridges were believed to contain cow fat, offensive to Hindus, and pig fat, offensive to Muslims. Sepoys had to bite them open before loading.
55.tq: Identify the religious implication of the practical loading procedure.
xs: The cartridges were believed to contain **cow and pig fat** and had to be **bitten** open — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Cow** fat offended **Hindus**; **pig** fat offended **Muslims**.
xa: They were read as proof of a **colonial-missionary plot** to force conversion.
Rumours also spoke of **bone dust** in Company flour.

55.s: The Meerut rising of the Revolt of 1857 began on:
55.x: The Meerut rising began on 10 May 1857; Mangal Pandey's action at Barrackpore was on 29 March and the 19th Native Infantry refused at Berhampur in February 1857.
xa: Mangal Pandey was hanged on **8 April 1857**.
**9 May**: **85** sepoys of the **3rd Cavalry** sentenced to **10 years**.
**11-12 May**: rebels reach **Delhi**.

55.s: What immediately preceded the Meerut rising of 10 May 1857?
o: The proclamation of Bahadur Shah II as Shahenshah-e-Hindustan
The sentencing of 85 sepoys of the 3rd Native Cavalry to ten years’ imprisonment
The disbandment of Mangal Pandey’s regiment
The refusal of the 19th Native Infantry to use the rifle
55.x: On 9 May 1857, 85 sepoys of the 3rd Native Cavalry at Meerut were sentenced to ten years. The rising followed on 10 May, when officers were shot and imprisoned comrades were freed.
55.tq: Identify the immediately preceding event rather than the later consequence.
xs: On **9 May 1857**, **85** sepoys of the **3rd Native Cavalry** were sentenced to **10 years** — so option **(2)** is correct.
The rising followed on **10 May**: officers shot, comrades freed, **"Delhi Chalo"**.
**Bahadur Shah II** was proclaimed only after it (**11-12 May**); the other events were earlier.
xa: Mangal Pandey's regiment was disbanded on **8 April 1857**.
**19th NI** refused the cartridges at **Berhampur** in **February 1857**.

55.s: The rebels who reached Delhi on 11–12 May 1857 proclaimed whom as Shahenshah-e-Hindustan?
55.x: After reaching Delhi, the rebels proclaimed Bahadur Shah II as Shahenshah-e-Hindustan on 11–12 May 1857.
55.tq: Match the political title with the associated leader.
xs: Rebels reaching Delhi (**11-12 May 1857**) proclaimed **Bahadur Shah II** **Shahenshah-e-Hindustan** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Kunwar Singh** was at Jagdishpur; **Wajid Ali Shah** had been deposed in **1856**; **Nana Sahib** was at Kanpur.
xa: They came from the **Meerut rising** (**10 May**) with the cry **"Delhi Chalo"**.
Bahadur Shah Zafar's successors were to lose the **Red Fort** and **royal title**.

55.s: The 19th Native Infantry at Berhampur refused the new cartridges in:
55.x: The Berhampur refusal came in February 1857; Vellore was July 1806, the Barrackpore mutiny November 1824 and Mangal Pandey's attack 29 March 1857.

55.s: The Santhal revolt of 1855–56 is distinguished from the mutinies listed in the context of the 1857 uprising because it was—
o: the first mutiny of the 34th Native Infantry
a civil revolt rather than a sepoy revolt
an uprising caused by the new cartridges
a military revolt over sea service
55.x: The Santhal revolt of 1855–56 was a civil revolt and not a sepoy mutiny.
55.tq: Separate a civil revolt from a military mutiny.
xs: The **Santhal revolt (1855-56)** was a **civil revolt, not a sepoy revolt** — so option **(2)** is correct.
It had nothing to do with cartridges or sea service; those drove the sepoy outbreaks of **1824** and **1857**.
xa: UPPSC key: **Santhal revolt = 1855-56**; **Vellore = July 1806**; **Barrackpur = Nov 1824**.
Bhatta mutinies: **34th NI 1844**, **66th NI 1849-50**.

55.s: The Enfield rifle introduced in December 1856 replaced the:
55.x: The Enfield rifle replaced the Brown Bess musket; training was at Dum Dum, Ambala and Sialkot.

55.s: Besides the greased cartridges, a rumour before 1857 said that the Company's flour was mixed with:
55.x: A rumour spread that bone dust was mixed in Company flour.

55.s: Mangal Pandey belonged to the:
55.x: Mangal Pandey was of the 34th Bengal NI; the 47th NI mutinied at Barrackpore in 1824.

55.s: Mangal Pandey was hanged on:
55.x: He attacked Lt Baugh on 29 March and was hanged on 8 April 1857.

He belonged to Arrah in Bihar during the mutiny. When the people of all parts of India rose against British authority in 1857 A.D., Babu Kunwar Singh was nearly eighty years old. At that age, he fought against the English East India Company. Despite his age and failing health, Kunwar Singh plunged into the thick of it and battled against the British forces with grim determination and undaunted courage. In Bihar, Kunwar Singh was the Leader against the British. He assumed command of the soldiers who had revolted at Danapur on 25th July 1857 A.D. Two days later he occupied Arrah, the district headquarters. Major Vincent Eyre relieved the town in August 1857, defeated Kunwar Singh’s force and destroyed Jagdishpur. Kunwar Singh left his ancestral village and reached Lucknow in December 1857 A.D. In March 1858 A.D., he occupied Azamgarh. However, he had to leave the place soon. He was pursued by Brigadier Douglas, and he retreated towards his home in Bihar. On 23 April 1858 A.D., Kunwar Singh had a victory near Jagdishpur over the force led by Captain Le Grand, but on 26 April 1858 A.D., he died in his village. The mantle of the old chief now fell on his brother Amar Singh who, despite heavy odds, continued the struggle and for a considerable time ran a parallel government in the then district of Shahabad. 56.s: The real name of which one of the following leaders of 1857 was ‘Ram Chandra Pandurang’?
56.x: Ramachandra Pandurang Tope, known as Tatya Tope, was an able leader of the great uprising of 1857. He was a personal adherent of Nana Saheb of Kanpur. He progressed with the Gwalior contingent after the British reoccupation of Kanpur and forced Lieutenant General Charles Ash Windham to retreat from Kanpur. Later on, he came to the rescue of Rani Lakshmibai. However, he was defeated by General Napier's troops and was executed by the British Government (after he was captured in the forest of Paron due to betrayal of his friend Mansingh) at Shivpuri on 18th April 1859. One of the greatest heroes of the Great Uprising of 1857, Tatya Tope was born in 1814 at Yeola in Maharashtra. He was the only child of Pandurang and his wife, Rukhmabai. Having been brought up in Bithoor, he came into contact with Nana Saheb Peshwa. He was a great admirer of Nana Saheb and was ready to sacrifice his life for him. Tatya Tope was the only person who witnessed the rebellion from the Kanpur revolt until his end on 18th April 1859.

58.s:
Consider the following statements about the centenary histories of 1857:
